Model Output:
# Brainstorming ## What the prompt offers "Gods wore sneakers" is a collision of the sacred and the mundane. Sneakers imply: walking (gods arriving among mortals), running/speed (Hermes, Nike), flight (winged sandals → Air Jordans), commerce and hype culture, status, sweatshop labor, mass production vs. the singular relic, comfort vs. ancient regalia, and disguise/incarnation. The prompt practically begs the question: *why* would gods wear sneakers? Answerable as satire (they've gone corporate), melancholy (they've lost their temples and need to blend in), economics (worship moved to consumer goods), or tenderness (they just wanted to walk comfortably among us). ## Possible premises **A. The Goddess of Victory, Incorporated.** Nike — the actual goddess — is a historical footnote: no myths of her own, always an attendant of Athena or Zeus, a headless statue in the Louvre. Then a sportswear company takes her name. She becomes the most recognized "deity" on Earth while being completely hollowed out. Story: Nike navigates the strange afterlife of being a brand. Is the swoosh her severed wing? Is "Just Do It" her only surviving commandment? Does the logo feed her or starve her? **B. The Grail Pair (sneakerhead magical realism).** First-person teen protagonist, a reseller in New York / Lagos / Manila, queues for a hyped drop. Rumor says one pair in every release is "grailed" — a god lives in it. The kid wins/acquires it, and small miracles follow: never-scuffed leather, laces that retie themselves, improbable luck on resale. But the god inside is starving — buying isn't believing. To save her, the kid must *give the shoes away*, which is unthinkable for someone saving up for their mother's rent. Theme: value vs. worth, hype vs. holiness, scarcity vs. gift. **C. The Last Cobbler (episodic commissions).** A mortal shoemaker — last of a workshop dating back millennia — receives divine customers. One chapter per pair: sandals for Ereshkigal's long climb *up* out of the underworld; retirement loafers for a war god; shoes for a god so forgotten no one remembers their face, only their feet. The throughline: the cobbler's own arc (grief? a debt? their own approaching death), ending with the final pair — perhaps for their own last walk. Literary, elegiac, Gaiman/Oyeyemi flavored. **D. Hermes, Gig Worker.** Comedy: the messenger god thrives in the delivery economy. Winged sandals are a liability at the sorting facility, so — sneakers. He's the most employed god alive and utterly miserable/envious of gods who still get temples. Workplace satire with a melancholy undertow. **E. The Race.** Every century the gods race for the world's belief, disguised as a city marathon, all in ordinary sneakers. A mortal pacer is accidentally hired to set the tempo and ends up changing the outcome. Kinetic, cinematic, lighter. **F. Gods in a Walk-Up (ensemble).** A pantheon shares a cramped apartment above a laundromat, pooling tips; sneakers are the one luxury anyone can agree on. A new arrival seeks asylum — a dead meme? an algorithm? Pratchett-ish satirical warmth. Risk: ensemble sprawl at 8,000 words. ## Tones available Wry satire (Pratchett); melancholy urban fantasy (Gaiman's *American Gods*); warm magical realism with social teeth; teen-voice contemporary; full farce; literary elegy. ## Structural approaches - Linear single-protagonist arc (setup ch1–2, escalation ch3–6, turn ch7, resolution ch8) - Object-in-transit vignettes (sneakers passed god to god, era to era) - Alternating dual POV (mortal/god chapters interlocking) - Frame device: interviews, forum posts, resale-listing descriptions between scenes ## Character seeds - A teenage reseller with a sharp, funny, hungry voice; mother working double shifts; knows the exact resale value of everything and nothing's actual worth - Nike as faded divinity: proud, bewildered, funny about her own branding, secretly terrified of irrelevance — she *chose* the deal centuries ago (or Hermes brokered it) - Hermes as the smooth talent agent / repo man who cut the original deal and now collects on defaults - An old woman who works at an outlet store and turns out to be a retired priestess — the only person still performing the rites correctly, by accident, while folding hoodies ## Thematic veins Worship migrating into consumption; authenticity vs. counterfeit (fakes as theological problem — what happens to a god whose power is bootlegged?); victory and what it costs; the ethics of who makes the shoes; wanting vs. having; everything holy eventually wears out. # Reflection Looking across these ideas, my first filter is: **does the sneaker carry the theology, or is it just set dressing?** Concepts D and E are fun but the shoes are incidental — you could swap in any modern object. A, B, and C genuinely build meaning into the sneaker itself, which is what will make the piece feel like it answers the prompt rather than merely obeys it. **Concept C (the cobbler)** is the most beautiful on paper, but I worry about it at this length. Eight vignettes with one connecting thread is hard to land emotionally in ~1000-word chapters; vignette pieces often feel cumulative rather than propulsive, and the cobbler's inner arc risks being crowded out by the novelty of each divine client. If I used it, I'd have to cut the cast down hard. It's a strong candidate for a longer form than this one. **Concept A (Nike)** has the best built-in irony I've ever been handed by a prompt: the goddess of victory is also the most famous logo in human history, and historically she really was a mythological nonentity — no stories, just wings and presence. There's a real poignancy there: she traded a name with no stories attached for a name everyone knows. But as a standalone premise it risks becoming a concept piece — one extended wink. It needs a human anchor and a plot engine, not just irony. **Concept B (the grail pair)** has the strongest plot engine and the most direct answer to "why sneakers": because worship changed shape. Hype culture *is* liturgy — the queue, the drop, the relic, the pilgrimage to the store, the resale market as indulgence economy. And it hands me an automatic emotional dilemma: a kid who desperately needs money holding an object that can only be saved by giving it away. That's a real choice, not a contrived one. What excites me most, though, is that **B and A aren't competing — they fuse.** The grail pair contains Nike herself. She's the perfect starving god: nominally the most worshipped figure alive, actually nourished by almost none of it, because a billion people saying her name aren't praying to her. Hermes slots in cleanly as the entity who brokered her name away and now repossesses defaulted gods. The old priestess at the outlet store gives me exposition that doesn't clunk. And the finale writes itself toward a place where genuine awe — not purchase — is what feeds a god. Pitfalls I need to watch: - **Preachiness about consumerism.** The easy version of this story lectures. The better version stays ambivalent: the brand also *kept her alive*. Starving is still alive. Nike shouldn't simply regret the deal — she should be conflicted about biting the hand that feeds her, especially when the alternative was vanishing entirely. - **One-joke stretch.** Mitigated by giving the protagonist a concrete material stake (mother's rent, a specific number) and letting each chapter advance both the miracle-mystery and the money-pressure simultaneously, so plot and theme braid instead of alternating. - **Teen voice over eight chapters.** The voice must be specific and consistent — first person, past tense, funny but not quippy-for-its-own-sake. I'll need a strong opening line that establishes register immediately. - **Chapter shape.** At ~1000 words each, every chapter needs its own micro-arc: a want entering, a turn, a button. I'm tentatively sketching beats — queue night and acquisition; the shoes misbehave; the god surfaces; backstory of the deal via the priestess or dreams; Hermes arrives with an offer that would solve everything; the low point where the kid uses the shoes selfishly and the luck curdles; the public act of giving; restoration and changed terms on both sides — but I'm treating that as provisional scaffolding, not commitments. - **Ending trap.** "Kid learns money isn't everything" is a cliché. The sharper resolution is mutual transformation: she doesn't ascend back to Olympus — she chooses to stay small, patron of one neighborhood track, and the kid doesn't stop wanting things, but learns the difference between price and worth. Both walk away changed, neither gets a sermon. My leaning, then: a fused A/B — first-person teen reseller, the starving goddess in the grail pair, Hermes as antagonist-with-a-point, an outlet-store priestess, and an ending staged at a place where running still means something before it means winning. Tone: warm, wry magical realism with teeth — Gaiman's melancholy crossed with a teenager's gallows humor about money. I haven't locked names, city, or the exact mechanics of how the god ended up in the shoes; those are decisions for the next pass.

Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>

# Intention ## Premise (locked) A fused concept from brainstorming: **first-person teenage sneaker reseller acquires a "grailed" limited-edition pair that contains the starving goddess Nike herself.** Setting: Philadelphia (quiet thematic bonus — the City of Brotherly Love, in a story about the difference between selling and giving). Title candidate: **"Dead Stock"** — a reseller term for inventory that's never been worn, which is exactly what a god in an unopened shoebox is. ## Core mechanics (stated once in-story, then dramatized, never re-explained) - **Gods eat intention, not money.** Billions speak Nike's name daily, but as brand invocations — noise, not food. What nourishes her is a human genuinely reaching for victory *through* her: lacing up before a moment that matters. - **The historical hook is real and does my plotting:** the ancient Athenians erected a *wingless* Nike ("Nike Apteros") so Victory could never fly away from the city. The grail pair is the limited-edition **"Apteros"** (500 pairs, de-winged silhouette, swoosh hidden on the insole — the wing where you can't see it). The shoe is simultaneously cage and lifeboat, exactly like the statue. - **Backstory:** After the temples died, Nike starved in the Louvre (living off coins tossed into fountains). In 1971 Hermes brokered her name to a startup — her survival in exchange for becoming a logo. The swoosh is her signature; the brand kept her alive and hollowed her out at once. Ambivalence preserved: she does not simply regret the deal. - **Theological physics of the plot:** Bought things can be repossessed; given things cannot. If Imani sells the shoes, Hermes lawfully collects the god. Only a free gift — the oldest rite — releases her. This makes the central dilemma structural, not moralizing: the rent money and the goddess's life are literally the same transaction. ## Cast - **Imani Brooks**, 17, reseller. Sharp, price-fluent, funny from specificity. Runs the 400m until sophomore year, when money got tight. Her hoard of unworn "grails" is love-for-her-mom, not greed — the story treats her hustle sympathetically. - **Nike**, the god: proud, bewildered, dry-witted about her own branding; terrified of irrelevance; conflicted about biting the hand that feeds her. - **Hermes**: antagonist-*with-a-point*, not a villain. Courier-mogul, charming, fast, wears collabs that haven't released yet, barcode tattoo where the caduceus should be. He genuinely believes he saved her — and partly did. His temptation offer must be legitimately attractive. - **Callie Stavros**, 70s, returns desk at the outlet store; granddaughter of a shrine-keeper from near Samothrace. Performs correct rites without knowing it (blesses damaged returns; ritually "smites" defective goods). - **Bea**, freshman sprinter on Imani's old team, talented, can't afford proper shoes — eventual recipient. - **Mom**: night shifts at a hospital laundry; light-touch presence, one late revelation ("Never sell what was given to you"). ## Voice & style - First person, past tense, Imani throughout. Register set by the opening line: *"The night I queued for the Apteros, I didn't believe in anything I couldn't resell."* - Two or three short **dream sequences** (italic/section breaks) carry backstory: Samothrace, the museum decades, the 1971 signing. - Sensory theology ladder, recurring: myrrh-and-ozone smell, warmth, faint hum, rain-on-cinders — escalating as Nike fades, then returns. - Comedy from sneaker-culture realism: raffles, lowball offers, fake-PayPal scams, the blasphemy of creasing a grail (which doubles as the reason she's starving — dead stock can't perform its sacred function). ## Things to aim for - Each chapter as its own micro-arc: a want enters, a turn happens, a button lands. - Plot and theme braided: every chapter advances both the money-pressure and the mystery simultaneously. - Scale-subversion at the end: small victories, sincerely meant, are the point. "Just do it" reclaimed as sincere advice. - Mutual transformation: Imani learns price vs. worth *through action*; Nike chooses to shrink down and stay — "Olympus is a museum too." ## Things to avoid - Lectures about consumerism; ambivalence instead (the brand also saved her). - Divine bailout of the rent — Imani solves money herself by liquidating her own dead stock. - Villainizing Hermes or the Company (execs oblivious, not sinister). - Horror inflections, dream-cheats ("it was all a dream"), ensemble sprawl, quippy-for-its-own-sake dialogue. # Chapter Planning **Ch. 1 — The Drop.** Queue night for the Apteros raffle. Establish Imani's world: the app, the odds, her collection of never-worn grails, the eviction-notice math ($1,860 by the 1st), the seed of her abandoned 400m. She wins the draw. Button: at home, the box is wrong — tissue smells of myrrh and storm; the laces are knotted in a pattern she doesn't know. **Ch. 2 — Dead Stock.** She refuses to wear them (creasing a grail is blasphemy) except once, to shoot listing photos. One walk to the bus: impossible green lights, a $20 bill, strangers smiling. Lists at $2,400. Night: first dream fragment — wings, sea, marble; a voice: *"Take me outside."* Button: the listing has vanished overnight. **Ch. 3 — Market Pressure.** Relisting chaos: lowballs, a scam attempt, forum creepypasta about "haunted grails" (the community half-knows). Eviction notice posted. Miracles curdle — luck overshoots, feels borrowed. Comic beat: pigeons bow to the box. Button: at the outlet store, an old woman grips her arm — *"Child. Where did you get those?"* **Ch. 4 — Callie.** The priestess explains: Apteros history, the two-way chain, what feeds a god and what starves her; the rule — *"Bought things can be collected. Given things can't. You don't sell a god."* Interleaved dream: the Louvre decades; Hermes in a powder-blue suit; her signature drying into a swoosh. Imani pushes back — she needs the sale. Button: a business card appears in the shoebox: HERMES LOGISTICS — *We deliver everything eventually.* **Ch. 5 — The Offer.** 3 a.m. depot meeting. Hermes, charming and half-right, lays out options: sell him the pair (clean cash, "climate-controlled storage"), or sign as Nike's First Athlete — money, college, mom fixed — and formalize the leash forever. Imani nearly signs. Button: she asks what happens to Nike; he answers honestly — *"Nothing. Nothing happens to her. Forever. That's the product."* She stalls until the 1st; deadlines are his favorite holiday. **Ch. 6 — The Run.** Rent panic; Mom wrecked from double shifts. Imani arranges a private sale to a collector — but the shoes arrive *dead*: gray, weightless, scentless. Days listed as inventory nearly finished it. Buyer leaves. She puts them on and runs — first time since quitting track — and feels a faint pulse return. Realization: wear them where it matters. Button: dawn at the outlet store — *"How do I give a god away?"* **Ch. 7 — The Gift.** She gives the Apteros to Bea before Saturday's meet. Kneeling to tie the laces, she says something true — an unknowing liturgy. Color floods the leather; rain-on-cinders smell. Nike surfaces, visible only to Imani: wing-stumps, gray eyes, the same shoes. Short exchange — the emotional summit. Nike declines Olympus, chooses the neighborhood track; names Imani *"my priestess, who didn't know it"* and releases her. Button: across the field, Hermes watches the fence. **Ch. 8 — Heat Two.** Race day. Montage: Imani has sold her entire dead-stock collection — rent covered, no bailout, just released grip. Mom's one line about Grandma and never selling what was given. Bea wins her 100m heat and dedicates it aloud — the first conscious offering. Imani runs

# How a Human Might Approach This Piece ## Process differences A human writer handed "Gods wore sneakers" probably doesn't start with a thesis about consumerism-as-liturgy. They start with something snagged from their own life: a memory of waiting outside a Foot Locker in the cold, a cousin who flipped Jordans, the smell of an outlet mall, the specific humiliation of having your foot measured by a stranger at fifteen. From that grain of autobiography, the mythology grows outward *accidentally* — the writer follows an obsession (feet, queues, the weird intimacy of shoes) and discovers the theme late, rather than constructing the theme first and hanging scenes on it. Other human process traits worth stealing: - **Discovery drafting.** A human often doesn't know what the god wants until chapter four. The plan I wrote knows everything in advance — every mystery pre-answered in bullet points. That completeness is efficient and deadening. Some ignorance should survive into drafting, because prose written by a writer pretending not to know feels different from prose written by a writer who genuinely found out. - **Tolerance of waste.** Human stories contain scenes that serve no plot function — two characters arguing about something irrelevant, a description that runs long because the rhythm demanded it. My plan has zero waste; everything braids. Waste is where aliveness lives. - **Uneven ambition.** A human might pour disproportionate love into one weird chapter and rush another. Uniform competence across eight equal chapters is a machine signature. ## Telltale LLM approaches (general) - **Thematic legibility above all.** Every symbol planted is paid off; every irony is designed. The story is an argument wearing a costume. - **Compulsive scene buttons.** Every unit ends on a zinger, a turn, or a portent. Real scenes frequently end flat, mid-air, or on unanswered dialogue. - **Calibrated morality.** Protagonist flawed-but-sympathetic, antagonist charming-but-wrong-in-measured-doses, critique ambivalent-in-a-pre-approved-way. Nothing is allowed to be genuinely ugly, petty, or unfair. - **Rule-based magic systems.** Elegant, contractual, explainer-friendly theology. Sanderson-shaped divinity. - **Voice-y but not particular narration.** Wry first person, funny-from-specificity, likable by page three — a validated register, not a discovered one. - **Motif engineering.** Recurring scents, ladders of sensation, escalating imagery — beautiful and airless. - **Scheduled emotion.** Low point here, summit there, tearjerker line placed for maximum yield. The reader feels rails under the floorboards. - **Research-forward authenticity.** Subculture terminology deployed *correctly* but without the odd, obsessive, off-topic details a real insider would fixate on. - **Functional-only comedy.** All jokes serve plot or characterization. Nothing derails. - **The closed loop.** Gifts circulate, debts clear, transformations mirror each other, the coda shows the antagonist watching from a distance. Perfect reciprocity — which is exactly what life refuses to do. # Deep Dive: Critiquing My Intention & Plan ## Premise **The fusion was praised for being "clean." Cleanliness is the red flag.** Starving goddess + reseller + repo man + priestess + deserving recipient: five gears meshing without friction. The premise resolves too elegantly, and the elegance will show. **Philadelphia chosen by pun.** Selecting the city because "City of Brotherly Love" rhymes with the theme is a designer's move, not a dweller's. A human picks a city they can render from the inside — the specific corner, the transit line, the local track meet — and the theme either follows or it doesn't. (Ironically, Philadelphia *does* host one of the biggest track events in America — but reaching for that as a fact is research-flexing unless it grows from genuine knowledge.) **Stacked ironies.** Apteros/wingless statue, hidden swoosh-on-the-insole, dead stock/unworn god, "Just Do It" reclaimed, brotherly-love setting. Each is individually nice; together they're an exhaustion of cleverness, and the reader starts hearing the writer applaud herself. A human keeps one central irony and lets the others arrive crooked or not at all. **The swoosh-is-a-wing observation** is genuinely resonant but also widely circulated internet lore — reaching for it is predictable. Usable, but only if complicated or degraded, not presented as a pristine reveal. ## Mechanics **The theology is contract law.** "Bought things can be collected; given things cannot" is tidy, dramatic, and structurally load-bearing — but it's a puzzle-box rule, and readers can feel the mechanism click. Real myth contradicts itself. Gods are inconsistent. A human version might keep the *folklore* of this rule while letting it be garbled, disputed, or occasionally false — uncertainty is more alive than physics. **"Stated once, dramatized, never re-explained" is good discipline wrapped around a bad instinct** — the instinct to have a fully coherent system at all. The plan's confidence that the rules work is the problem. **Nike's backstory is exposition-ready:** temples, Louvre, fountain coins, 1971 signing. Delivered via dream sequences (italicized — always italicized), it's lore-delivery infrastructure. A human might make the past resistant: Nike refuses to discuss it, or misremembers it, or Callie's account contradicts hers, and the reader must sit with conflicting versions. ## Cast **Imani is sympathy-engineered.** Quit track *because money*, hoards shoes *out of love for Mom*, wants to *save the household*. Her only real flaw in the plan is wanting money for excellent reasons. That's circumstance, not character. Where's her actual venality? Has she ever done something small and rotten for margin? If not, her arc toward generosity is a walk downhill. **Mom is a prop with a scheduled tearjerker.** Tired, night shifts, one late line of grandmother-wisdom delivered at maximum yield. Either she's a person or she should be reduced further and honestly so. **Callie is the Exposition Elder.** Old woman, inherited rites, delivers the rules, presumably exits gracefully after serving function. Charming, and completely architected. Her knowledge should be *partially wrong* — folk practice is inherited noise, garbled across generations — which would reintroduce doubt and make her human rather than oracular. **Bea is a vessel.** She exists to receive the gift and win the race. No stated wants of her own. What if she doesn't *want* charity? What if accepting shoes from the neighborhood flipper is humiliating, and trust has to be built on-page through awkwardness? **Hermes is the trope I literally named in the plan** — "antagonist-with-a-point." Charm + honesty + "deadlines are my favorite holiday": every trait is calibrated for sophistication. Worse, the plan gives him no real victories. He's stalled twice and spectates at the fence. An antagonist who never wins is a device, not a threat. ## Voice & Style **First-person wry teen, past tense, likable by design** is the safest possible container. The opening line announces theme in sentence one (*"I didn't believe in anything I couldn't resell"*), which is a mission statement, not an arrival. A human might open smaller and dumber — inside a physical complaint, a queue grievance — and let the worldview surface sideways. **The sensory ladder (myrrh-and-ozone → hum → rain-on-cinders)** is motif engineering. Pick one sensation, let it behave inconsistently, tie it to memory rather than metering it to divinity levels. **Emotionally, the prose risks being ornate in the wrong places.** Humans go plain when genuinely moved and ornate when performing. The plan's emotional summit (Ch. 7, full manifestation, visible wing-stumps) risks video-game-cutscene energy — the god rendered cinematically rather than encountered strangely. Withholding her — a reflection, a voice through leather, a shadow with the wrong silhouette — might land harder than showing her. ## Structure & Chapters **Every chapter ends with a button.** I wrote the word "Button:" seven times. That compulsion alone will date the piece as synthetic. **Uniform chapter shape and length.** Eight ~1000-word units, each with want→turn→button, is screenwriting architecture poured into prose. Variation — one long rambling conversation chapter, one very short one, one rendered as marketplace listings or group-chat fragments — is how humans breathe. **No rest chapters.** "Money-pressure and mystery advance simultaneously every chapter" is braid-maximalism. Slack is needed; a chapter that's mostly texture gives the stakes somewhere to live. **The rent resolves too well.** Selling her collection covers everything — a bailout by another name, laundered through effort. Real evictions don't arc cleanly. Options: partial payment plans (undignified, real); Mom having quietly handled it weeks ago (undercutting Imani's savior narrative — painful and true); or the deadline passing with consequences that aren't erased. **Bea winning her heat is the expected payoff.** And the gift-chain closing in perfect circulation — Imani gives to Bea, Bea dedicates to Nike, Nike releases Imani — is a closed economy. Something should leak out of the system. ## What the Plan Lacks Entirely - **Bodies.** For a story about sneakers, there's startlingly little foot: blisters, breaking shoes in, sweat, the ache of standing all day, shoes that don't fit right. Which points at a bigger missed reading of the prompt — - **"Wore."** The prompt's key verb is *wore*, and the plan treats sneakers mainly as commodity-relics. The stranger, fleshier reading: dead stock is unworn, and unworn is unalive. A god whose nature is exertion is preserved in virgin condition — that's not protection, it's embalming. Being *broken in* — molded by a mortal foot, creased, sweated in, worn out — could be the actual grace, reframing the climax from "feeding her glory" to "letting her be used up." Mortality as gift. This vein exists implicitly in the plan and deserves centrality. - **A wider divine ecology.** The prompt says *gods*, plural; the plan has essentially two. Minor gods glimpsed unremarked — a woman at the bus stop, something old in the laundromat — would make Nike's plight part of a lived-in world rather than a bespoke problem manufactured for the protagonist. - **Social world.** Reselling is communal — group chats, servers, mutuals, in-jokes. Imani is isolated by design for focus, which reads as artificial. - **Season and weather.** The story floats in timeless space. - **Genuine loss.** Nobody loses anything irreversibly. Hermes should take something that stays taken. # Brainstorm: Moves Toward the Human 1. **Kill the buttons.** End scenes flat, mid-dialogue, on a non-answer. Save any resonant closer for one or two chapters max. 2. **Break the rules' reliability.** Callie's lore is garbled inheritance; Nike contradicts her; the "given things can't be collected" rule works — or seems to — for reasons nobody understands. Keep deniability alive until it genuinely collapses, and even then withhold full explanation. 3. **Give Imani a real sin, small and specific.** E.g., in chapter one or two she talks a younger kid down from keeping his own raffle win and flips it. Forgotten by her, remembered by the reader. Her later generosity then costs credibility before it earns it. 4. **Make Nike hard to like.** Contemptuous, self-absorbed, bored by mortals, wrong about her own history. Her softening must visibly cost her pride. Let her say at least one thing that is truly *other* — not translatable into quip. 5. **Let Hermes win a round.** Mid-story, Imani witnesses an actual repossession — some minor god living in a beat-up pair of Converse, collected in broad daylight — and stands by, doing nothing. Stakes made flesh, plus guilt that compounds her later choice. 6. **Give Bea friction.** She suspects Imani's motives, resents the charity, maybe drives a bad bargain of her own to preserve dignity. The gift should pass through resistance. 7. **Unsolve the rent.** Partial payment plan, or Mom quietly already fixed it, or consequences that persist past chapter eight. Imani's sacrifice should not map one-to-one onto salvation. 8. **Consider Bea not winning.** If she loses the heat and offers the effort anyway — and that offering *counts* — the theme deepens past results. Caution: expectation-subversion is itself algorithmic; choose it only if it's true, not contrarian. 9. **Vary the containers.** One chapter as listings/messages/group-chat text. One very short. One long single conversation. Uneven lengths throughout. 10. **Re-center the body.** Wrong size, blisters, breaking-in pain, the run in Ch. 6 leaving her physically wrecked. Grace should cost calves. Possibly the entire theology pivots on worn-vs-unworn rather than bought-vs-given — or holds both tensions at once, untidily. 11. **Scatter unremarked divinity.** Background gods, never catalogued, never explained. Resist the urge to make them cute. 12. **Open dumber.** Inside the queue's physical misery, not inside a worldview. Theme surfaces later and sideways. 13. **Cut or relocate Mom

# Intention ## Premise (final) **Title: "Dead Stock."** Imani Brooks, 17, reseller in Philadelphia, wins a raffle for the "Apteros" — a 500-pair limited release named for the wingless Nike of Athens. The god is in the box, starving, because dead stock is embalming: a god whose whole nature is exertion, preserved unworn. The story's center of gravity is the prompt's verb — *wore*. Being broken in, creased, sweated through, used up: that is not damage to a sneaker-god. That is communion. The bought/given rule stays as plot engine (Hermes' law), but the deeper truth — surfaced late, never systematized — is worn/unworn. Both tensions held at once, untidily. ## Voice & narration - First person, past tense, Imani throughout. **Opens dumb**: inside the queue's physical misery (numb toes, hour six, somebody's speaker), not inside a worldview. Theme arrives sideways, late. - Humor from grievance and specificity, not quips. One deliberate register-clash: her **listing copy is purple, auction-house ornate** while her actual voice is plain — commerce makes her perform. - Dreams set off by line breaks only. No italics, no labels, no lore-delivery framing. Two dreams total, fragmentary, contradictory, refusing to explain. - Plainness when moved; ornament only when a character is performing. The emotional summit (Ch. 7) is the plainest writing in the piece. ## Cast (final adjustments) - **Imani**: given a real, small, unredeemed sin — in Ch. 1 she talks a younger kid (Deon) out of his raffle win and flips it. Never punished, never referenced again. Reader remembers; she doesn't. Her generosity later must survive that memory. - **Nike**: hard to like. Contemptuous, vain, bored by mortals, wrong about her own history, dismissive of Callie's rites ("that's a Roman reading"). Says at least one genuinely *other* thing. Will not curse the brand — they fed her when her own people forgot her face. Softening visibly costs her pride. Manifestation restrained: a reflection, a silhouette with the wrong shape, a voice through leather. Never a full cinematic reveal. Her big moments are tiny: "Oh." Saying Imani's name correctly. - **Hermes**: runs the authentication/courier infrastructure every reseller depends on — which is how he kills her listing and freezes her account. **He wins twice**: the account freeze costs Imani her crucial selling week, permanently; and Imani stands by, complicit, while he repossesses **Elias** — the humming corner-store man whose ancient New Balances carry something old. Elias isn't killed, just flattened; the store loses its luck; nobody knows why. That loss persists past the last page. Hermes remains half-right: he did save Nike. His offer is legitimately attractive and honestly described. - **Callie Stavros**: outlet returns-desk priestess, but her lore is **garbled inheritance** — wrong islands, conflated saints and gods, rites mixed with diner English, phone buzzing with corporate training she ignores. Her central rule is family folklore, possibly about Catholic saints. Nike contradicts parts of it. One full scene of functional waste: coffee cake, folding hoodies, complaint about management. - **Bea**: freshman sprinter, seeded early (Ch. 3, glimpsed from a bus — great form, hole in her shoe). **Friction**: resents Imani for quitting the team, refuses charity outright. The gift passes through resistance via a face-saving reframe: *"They don't fit me. Do me a favor — wear them out."* The gift disguised as a request. Bea forces a crumpled twenty into Imani's hand; **Imani keeps it**, feels strange, never mentions it. No redemption of the twenty. - **Mom**: light-touch. No scheduled wisdom line. Her one beat is flat and unceremonious: covering the rent gap Imani's sales don't reach — *"Don't ask where"* — plus making her eat. That's the whole aria. ## Plot mechanics (final) - Rent math stays concrete but **doesn't resolve cleanly**: selling her entire collection covers most of the arrears; Mom patches the rest; consequences (the frozen account, the lost selling week, the emptied shelf of grails) persist. - **The Apteros runs small** — Imani's grown-out feet can't wear them properly; they fit Bea. Quiet providence via sizing, not magic. - The private sale fails because the shoes have gone **inert** — a collector rejects them as fakes precisely because they feel dead. The market itself diagnoses the starvation. - Climax requires both laws at once: given (uncollectable) *and* worn (fed). Neither alone suffices. Nobody explains this fully. - Bea **takes second by half a step and is furious** — not noble-loss, not triumph. Her rage is the offering; Nike feeds on the reaching, not the result. That morning, inexplicably, the whole field runs personal bests. Nike eating wide, unremarked. - Ending: no bow. Imani tempted toward next season, bends, tightens her laces. Cut on action. ## World texture - Late winter into early spring; rain on the Ch. 6 night run earns the cinders smell naturally. - Background divinity scattered, unexplained, uncute: a woman at the bus stop whose umbrella never drips; the depot's rows of humming locked cages; Elias. Never catalogued. - Sensory economy reduced to **one recurring signal** — the leather's warmth, behaving inconsistently, tied to memory rather than metered to divinity levels. Myrrh appears exactly once (Ch. 1) and never returns as a gauge. ## Structure - Eight chapters, uneven lengths (~850–1150 words). Containers varied: Ch. 3 textured with listings/texts/forum fragments; Ch. 4 one long rambling conversation; Ch. 6 short and kinetic. - **Buttons rationed to three total**, spaced: Ch. 3's closing grip ("Who tied those laces?"), Ch. 6's closing question ("How do I give a god away?"), and nothing after Ch. 7. All other scenes end flat, mid-air, or on non-answers. ## Aim for - The prompt's verb made theological: unworn = embalmed, worn = alive, worn out = fulfilled. - Ambivalence without lecture: the brand kept her alive; Hermes isn't wrong; Imani's hustle is love before it's greed. - Bodies: blisters, sizing, wrecked calves, the taste of blood at the end of the run. Grace costs calves. - Loss that stays lost: Elias, the account, the collection, the twenty. - Understatement at the summit: a god surprised, a name spoken correctly, an empty idling van at the fence instead of an antagonist cameo. ## Avoid - Thesis-statement openings; motif metering; full divine reveals; karmic payback; closed gift-economies; villainous or fully-stalled Hermes; Bea as vessel; Mom as tearjerker prop; Callie as oracle; tidy rent arithmetic; quippy grief; expectation-subversion for its own sake. # Chapter Planning **Ch. 1 — The Drop (~1100).** Hour six of the queue, told from the toes inward: cold, speaker guy, porta-potty line, Deon panicking beside her about his own win — Imani talks him down to $300 and flips it in her head before he's stopped talking. # Imani Brooks ## Background Seventeen, junior year, North Philly — a rowhouse near Erie Avenue with the hospital laundry two bus transfers away. Her mother Renee works nights; the house runs on opposite schedules, and Imani learned to be quiet in her own home early. She started selling at thirteen without knowing it was a business: her feet grew, her mom bagged the outgrown Jordans for Goodwill, and Imani — who'd checked StockX first, because checking is free — pulled them back out of the bag. Kids' sizes, she learned, are a real market: little feet grow fast and parents hate paying full price for eighteen months of use. She reinvested. By fifteen she had a system; by sixteen she had a wall of boxes she refused to wear, because wearing is depreciation and a worn grail is just a used shoe. The track history: she ran a 59-flat 400 as a sophomore, which at her school is a rumor-level number. Quit mid-season. The official version — repeated so many times it's smooth — is that track ate her afternoons. The real version is uglier and smaller: spikes, meet fees, the team dinner ritual where everyone throws in fifteen dollars, and her stomach learning to knot at the phrase "split the bill." She couldn't stand being the girl who needed the waiver form. Coach believed the lie, or pretended to. ## Personality & flaws Money-brained as a native language, not a pose — she converts instinctively ("that's forty percent off," she says of a car crash she witnesses, and hates herself for it). Generous in emergencies, stingy in inches: makes friends cover shipping, splits a two-dollar fry order to the cent, once didn't speak to her cousin for a month over eleven dollars. She'd give someone her last fifty in a crisis and invoice them for the bus fare home. The sins are small and unredeemed. She sold a pair with reglued sole separation and never disclosed it — everyone does it, she tells herself, and mostly believes it. And there's Deon, fourteen, first raffle win of his life, holding the confirmation email with shaking hands outside the Foot Locker — Imani talked him down to $300 in under four minutes, flipped the pair for $700 that weekend, gave him a fist bump for his trouble. She hasn't thought about it since. That's the flaw: not cruelty — an inability to see a person and a margin at the same time. Her hoard isn't greed. It's insurance against the specific terror of her childhood: the lights going off, the tone her mom's voice gets on the phone with the gas company. Every sealed box is a door out. She likes owning them more than she'd ever admit — likes the wall they make. ## Idiosyncrasies - Presses her thumb into the midsole of any shoe within reach, including display models and strangers' feet-adjacent floor space. Has been yelled at in three stores. - Rates buyers in her notes app like horses: "pays fast, whines much"; "ghost"; "good egg, broke." - Can spot fakes from a photo in seconds — stitch count, tag font, the way counterfeit suede photographs *flat*. - Won't eat while counting money. Rubber bands by denomination, bills facing the same way. - Phone volume maxed forever; drop alerts outrank sleep. - Gum only when negotiating. She read it lowers the other person's guard. Never verified. Still does it. - Waste-detail: irrationally afraid of escalators since age nine, will not discuss it. ## Physicality Compact, quick, always scanning — she checks out strangers' shoes before their faces, a professional deformity. Sits with one foot tucked under her. Hands never idle: folding, banding, re-lacing something that didn't need it. Rotates one battered pair of dailies, laces triple-knotted; dresses in hoodie-seasons. Her braids get redone every six weeks, Sunday nights, sitting on the floor between her mom's knees while Renee watches cooking videos she never cooks from — the closest thing the household has to church. ## Motives & relationships Wants, in order: the arrears paid, the wall of boxes intact, her mother sleeping past seven someday. Loyalty runs entirely through Renee; the world beyond the house is counterparties. She trusts Callie before she trusts the shoes. Toward Bea she carries a debt she hasn't admitted exists — she knows Bea watched her quit, and has avoided the track end of Fairmount Park for a year and a half to avoid the knowing. ## Voice *"Hour six. My toes checked out around hour three and left no forwarding address."* Listing voice (ornate, auction-house): *"An opportunity such as this presents itself once in a lifetime — a sealed piece of history, untouched by mortal feet—"* Actual internal monologue, same object: *"It's a shoe. It's a shoe that smells like church."* On Deon: *"His face did something complicated. I bumped his fist. Deal's a deal."* # Nike ## Background Daughter of Styx — the river, the oath, the cold — sister to Kratos, Bia, and Zelos. Her siblings got jobs: they stand beside Zeus's throne and are *named* doing it. She got statuary. That's her whole biography and she knows it: carried onto ten thousand fields, present at every triumph, the protagonist of no story ever told. The Greeks carved her on everything and wrote about her almost not at all. She was the most visible god in the pantheon and a footnote in its literature, and she has had centuries to be bitter about it in a dignified way. Athens clipped her wings — built her wingless so victory couldn't fly away. She has two accounts of this and uses whichever suits: the flattering one (they loved her too much to risk losing her) and the true one (they caged her). Samoth

# Dead Stock — Chapter 1: The Drop By hour six the cold had gotten into my toes and filed for residency. I did what you do, which is nothing. You stand in a line on Germantown Avenue at five in the morning in February because a shoe company decided five hundred people on Earth deserve a certain shoe and the rest of us deserve to learn our place. The metal gate was still down over the storefront. Behind me a man's Bluetooth speaker had been playing Meek Mill since midnight, at a volume where the bass stopped being sound and became weather. Nobody told him to turn it down. That's the social contract of a queue. Everybody's miserable in their own sleeping bag. There was one porta-potty for thirty-one people. At four a.m. the line for it was longer than the line would be for the shoes themselves, which felt like a parable, though about what I couldn't say. A woman two rows up had brought her man a duvet and he'd stretched out across three camping chairs like a king. A guy worked the line with a thermos, two dollars a cup, no sign, just eye contact. Two bucks. I respected it more than I respected the entire company whose shoe we were freezing for. I checked my banking app out of habit. $212 and change. The number on the notice taped to our door Tuesday was $1,860 by the first. PAY OR QUIT, in letters meant for somebody who hadn't read it ten times already. I know both numbers the way you know your locker combination, without looking, without wanting to. The Apteros. Five hundred pairs, two hundred retail, projected resale north of nine hundred if you believed the pages and I believed the pages. Named after some statue in Athens where they took the wings off the victory lady so she couldn't fly home. The app draw had closed at forty thousand entries. I'd done the math in the shower a week ago: one in eighty. Worse odds than the school lottery and the prize was less useful, but the prize converted to cash in under seventy-two hours, so. Deon was three spots ahead of me, fourteen years old in a puffer zipped to his chin, showing everybody his confirmation screen like it was a birth certificate. First raffle he'd ever won. He had braces with green bands and a way of reading his phone out loud to himself without noticing. "Some dude offered me two-fifty outside the Wawa," he said, mostly to me, mostly to his phone. I had gum in, the cinnamon kind, because I read somewhere it makes people trust you faster and I never checked whether it was true. "Two-five-oh," I said. "For a nine-hundred-dollar shoe." "They said that's the number." "That's a disrespect number. That's what you give somebody who looks like they don't know." I clicked my gum. The math was already done, had been done since he said *dude*, running in the background like a download: two hundred retail, three hundred out, six-forty back easy, maybe seven. "Look. I'm not gonna insult you either. Three hundred, right now, Cash App, and you don't have to stand out here hoping the Wawa guy comes back. He's not coming back, by the way. Guys like that circle the block till the crowd thins and then they're gone." He looked at the gate. He looked at his screen. He made a face like a word he couldn't pronounce yet. "My moms is gonna kill me regardless." "Your moms is gonna kill you slower with three hundred extra dollars in the house. That's just physics." He bumped my fist. Deal's a deal. I sent it before he could grow a conscience, and he watched the notification land on his phone like it was something alive. I'd have it listed before his bus cleared the corner. Gone by Monday, $640 after fees, buyer paid insured shipping. I felt fine about it. Mostly. At eight the gate rattled up and a guy in a vest came out with a clipboard and a laser pointer energy, calling wristband numbers for purchase windows. Mine was in the second group. Inside smelled like new carpet and ambition. The display pair sat on a pedestal under a glass dome, and while the vest counted somebody's bills I pressed my thumb into the display model's midsole — you check the foam density, everyone does it — and the vest coughed like a lawyer. I bought mine at $204.19. The card went through. I didn't celebrate until I was outside, and then only internally. On the 4 bus I kept the bag upright on my lap with one hand the whole way, which I never do, and told myself it was because of the potholes on Erie. The house was empty. Mom's on nights at the laundry, so mornings belong to the radiators and the dishes from Wednesday. There was a text from her sent at 5:51 a.m.: *eat something.* I ate Cheerios over the sink and carried the box upstairs. My room is half bed, half wall. The wall goes floor to shoulder, boxes stacked in load-bearing columns, each one dated and sized on painter's tape, the good ones marked DO NOT OPEN in marker. People see the wall and think greed. It's not greed. Greed spends. This is a fire escape. Every box on that wall is a month the lights stay on, a month I don't hear my mother do the voice she does on the phone with the gas company, the one that goes polite and then younger. I like the wall. I've never pretended otherwise to myself. I opened the Apteros on the bed. The tissue was heavy-stock, the kind that crackles like it costs extra. When I lifted the first sheet there was a smell — resin and something sweeter underneath, incense-adjacent, the smell of the front pews of my grandmother's church. Myrrh, maybe. I'd know myrrh if I knew anything. One breath of it and then the second sheet was just paper, dry and neutral, like the smell had gotten bored. The shoe itself was sail-colored, gum-soled, and almost blank. No logo on the lateral. None on the medial. Nothing on the tongue but a size tag. For two hundred dollars of hype, blankness is a flex — collectors lose their minds over clean. The heel swept back into nothing, smooth as a bar of soap. I turned it over. The insole had a tiny stamped mark, a laurel sprig or a feather, worn-down looking, like the stamp had run low on ink halfway through five hundred shoes. I tried the right one on. My toes kissed the front seam. Not painful, but honest — these run half a size small, minimum. I'm a nine. These were built for somebody still growing. I wrote *RUNS SMALL — SIZE UP* in my head for the listing and took it off careful, by the heel, the way you're supposed to and nobody does. The laces were the strange part. They weren't knotted. They were *tied* — flat, woven-looking, tight against the eyelets, a pattern I didn't know and couldn't name. Factory laces come in a loose bow you snip and replace on day one. This looked deliberate. This looked practiced. I picked at the top loop with a fingernail and got nothing, tried the crossing strands, got less. Ten minutes of that and my thumbnail ached. Scissors would fix it in a second, but cut laces are disclosed laces, and disclosed laces are discounted laces, so the knot stayed. It sat there in the streetlight, neat as handwriting. When I stacked the box on the wall, between the Dunks and a Jordan 4 I'll never forgive myself for selling, the cardboard was warm under my palms. Radiator's on the far wall. It was February. I filed it under nothing and set my alarm for nine, because listing photos need daylight.

Let me work through the key elements. **Voice and Character** The first-person narration is genuinely distinctive. Imani's voice has the quality the plan called for — "opens dumb," inside physical misery, not inside a worldview. The line "By hour six the cold had gotten into my toes and filed for residency" is a strong opener that earns its slight whimsy through the deadpan follow-up ("I did what you do, which is nothing"). The voice is consistent throughout: money-brained, observational, dry. The banking app check ($212 against $1,860) is delivered without sentimentality, exactly as planned. The Deon scene is the chapter's moral center and it's handled with real skill. The plan called for Imani to talk a younger kid out of his raffle win and flip it — this is executed with uncomfortable precision. "He made a face like a word he couldn't pronounce yet" is excellent. The transaction is rendered without authorial judgment, which is harder than it sounds. "I felt fine about it. Mostly." — that "Mostly" is doing exactly the right amount of work. The plan specified she never thinks about it again; the chapter honors this by moving on immediately. **Sensory and World-Building Details** The queue scene is richly textured: the Meek Mill speaker as weather, the porta-potty parable, the thermos guy at two dollars a cup. These feel observed rather than invented. The myrrh smell — appearing exactly once as planned — is handled with appropriate restraint: "One breath of it and then the second sheet was just paper, dry and neutral, like the smell had gotten bored." This is good. The smell doesn't announce itself as supernatural; it just is, and then isn't. The wall of boxes as "fire escape" rather than greed is the chapter's thematic statement, and it's earned through context rather than declared. The explanation of why she keeps the wall is the closest the chapter comes to over-explaining, but it's brief and in-character. **The Laces** The chapter's closing mystery — the impossibly tied laces — is introduced with appropriate restraint. The detail is strange without being announced as strange. The warmth of the cardboard at the end is similarly underplayed: "I filed it under nothing and set my alarm for nine, because listing photos need daylight." This is exactly the right note — the supernatural intrudes and Imani's practical mind files it away. The plan called for the knot to be something she "can't" undo, and this is delivered. **Dialogue** The dialogue is functional and character-revealing. The Deon exchange is the main dialogue scene, and it works: Imani's sales patter ("That's a disrespect number. That's what you give somebody who looks like they don't know") feels authentic. The gum detail — "I read somewhere it makes people trust you faster and I never checked whether it was true. Still does it" — is a nice character beat delivered efficiently. **Weaknesses** The "parable" observation about the porta-potty line ("which felt like a parable, though about what I couldn't say") is slightly self-conscious — the narrator gesturing at her own profundity. It's minor but noticeable. The vest-as-lawyer cough is a slightly strained simile. "Ambition" as a smell alongside new carpet is a bit of a cliché. The listing voice contrast (ornate vs. plain) promised in the plan doesn't appear in this chapter, which is fine — it's presumably coming — but the chapter plan mentions it as a feature. The chapter follows its plan faithfully: the queue, Deon, the purchase, the box opening, the myrrh (once), the strange laces, the warm cardboard. The plan's instruction to end on the laces being unknottable is honored, though the chapter continues slightly past that beat to the warm cardboard, which is actually a better ending. **Overall** This is confident, controlled literary fiction. The voice is distinctive and consistent, the character is rendered with moral complexity without authorial hand-wringing, the supernatural is introduced with appropriate restraint, and the prose earns its occasional flourishes. It's not a masterpiece — some metaphors are slightly strained, and the chapter is doing mostly setup work — but it's genuinely good work that honors its ambitious plan. # Dead Stock — Chapter 2: Dead Stock The light in my room only cooperates from nine to eleven, so at nine I was wiping the mirror with Windex and lint-rolling the shoebox like it was going to a job interview. There's a routine to it. You dust the box, you smooth the tissue, you kill every speck on the lid because the camera sees everything and buyers read dust like handwriting. I shot the box closed, the box open, the tissue peeled back, both shoes angled on the white poster board I keep for exactly this. Sail-colored leather eats shadow, so I bounced the flash off the ceiling till my arms burned. Here's the thing nobody tells you about dead stock: the letters stand for *deadstock*, and dead means never worn, not even once, not even for a second. Creases are sins. Sole dirt is testimony against you. A grail with a crease is just a used shoe with a good story, and stories don't convert to cash. But listings with on-feet shots close forty percent higher. That's not vanity, that's data. So I wore them. Once. Strictly professional. Socks stayed in the box the whole time as evidence of innocence. They ran small the way I knew they would. My right pinky toe filed a complaint within the first half block and stayed on it. I did the loop around the corner — Germantown to Susquehanna and back — taking the shots at angles that made it look like I wasn't standing in front of a boarded-up check-cashing place. Five green lights in a row on Susquehanna. I counted, because counting is what I do instead of praying. Five isn't luck, it's a clerical error. I walked faster anyway. Outside the barbershop a man getting out of a chair looked down at my feet and said "clean." People say clean about shoes constantly, usually at your feet, not to your face. He said it to my face. Inside the Chinese takeout the lady gave me extra crab Rangoon I hadn't ordered and wouldn't take back. At the bus stop an old woman with a furled umbrella looked at my shoes too long, then at me like she was checking my face against a description, and missed her bus on purpose to keep looking. I turned around and walked the other way. Halfway down the block, a twenty, folded tight, dry, the way money gets folded when it's been living in a pocket doing a job. I picked it up. You pick it up. Twenty dollars doesn't come with questions attached. I put it in my sock, which sounds crazy until you've had a twenty lifted out of your jacket on the 4. Back upstairs I took them off by the heel, careful, and they were warm. My feet are warm. Feet are warm, that's the whole job of feet. But it was warm like a seat stays warm after somebody gets up, and I stood there holding a sail-colored shoe in February daylight letting myself think exactly one thought about that, and then putting the thought back where I keep Deon's fist bump and the reglued soles, in the drawer that doesn't open. The listing took forty minutes because I write those different. I don't know whose voice that is. It shows up when the post button's involved, some auction-house ghost that lives in my thumbs: *"Offered: the Apterоs, size 9, deadstock, complete with box, tissue, spare laces, untouched. Five hundred pairs exist worldwide. This silhouette strips victory to its essentials — no branding, no ornament, nothing left but the shape of forward motion. The ancients built their goddess wingless so she could never leave them. A rare chance to hold what cannot be held. This pair will not stay long."* I typed "what cannot be held" with a completely straight face and hit post. Asking $2,400 or best offer. Everybody knows or-best-offer means the offer is the point. You anchor at robbery and negotiate down to felony. In the Apteros flip channel, Trey posted his pair on a glass table with LED lights behind it like a car ad. Kev asked if mine was DS. I said box-fresh. I left out the block, the greens, the twenty in my sock. Some information costs more than it pays. Mom's shift started at seven, so the house went quiet the way it does when she's on nights — dishes moved a quarter inch, TV off by six-forty-five. Before she left she stood in my doorway for a second looking at the wall of boxes with her coat already on. "That's a lot of rent sitting on one wall," she said. Not a fight. Not a lecture. Just a woman doing arithmetic on her way to work. Then the door, then the stairs, then the bus. Around midnight the channel started popping — somebody's cousin got a pair authenticated at 1.9, somebody else swore a store in Jersey broke their allocation early. I watched the numbers climb with my phone on the pillow next to my head, volume maxed, the way it always is, because in this house a drop alert outranks sleep. I don't remember getting to sleep. I remember this: Cold stone under my cheek. Salt in the air. Rigging knocking somewhere, or chains, hard to tell them apart in the dark. Steps going down into water that had no business being there, black and flat as poured tar. Weight across my shoulders — not heavy, exactly. More like being remembered by somebody who won't say your name right. Gulls. The sound a crowd makes right before it decides what it came for. Somebody spoke a language I've never studied and I understood every word of it, and I couldn't repeat one syllable now if you paid me. Then close, closer than a person, in plain English, patient, like it had said it before and would say it again: *Take me outside.* I woke up at 3:12 with my heart going and the radiator clanking its one joke. Checked the phone out of reflex. Sale notification? No. Better: a gray banner where my listing used to be. *Item removed — under review.* Support had opened a ticket with a number longer than some zip codes. I typed *why*, considered adding punctuation, sent it bare. Nobody answers why at three in the morning. Including me. The box was on the wall where I'd left it, between the Dunks and the Jordan 4. I lay back down and told myself it was a glitch, a keyword flag, a bot sweep — things with causes, things that fix themselves by nine. The twenty was still in my sock. I fell asleep doing the math on what 1.9 meant for a 2.4 anchor, which is the most normal thing I do.

My pair wasn't special. Apparently the whole run shipped tied. Somebody's cousin worked freight at the distro center and swore the pallet smelled like a funeral home, and the thread laughed, and locked, and stayed locked. Here's the part I kept to myself. Tuesday morning my dailies were tied in the weave too. Same flat crossing, same tight spine down the eyelets. Hands copy what eyes stare at — I'd been studying that knot for photos, that's all, muscle memory, whatever. I retied them normal. By Thursday they were back in the weave. I stopped fighting it the way you stop arguing with a dream about work. The 4 driver chin-nodded me on without tapping. The takeout lady comped my order again and then wouldn't look at me while she did it, like the generosity embarrassed us both. And Mom texted a picture of a scratcher — *played ur bday numbers, won $40, ur my lucky charm* — with three exclamation points, which for her is fireworks. Forty dollars. I sat with that feeling you're not supposed to say out loud: winning feels great right up until you wonder who's paying. Every green light, every comped crab Rangoon, started tasting like a tab running up somewhere under my name. You don't get comped forever. I know comps. Comps are marketing. Wednesday the certified letter came through the slot. Municipal Court, Landlord-Tenant Division, hearing date March 14th, 9:30 a.m., Room whatever. Under it, in pencil, on the back of an envelope: *filed tuesday. sorry imani. bring yr paperwork — Mr. Landis.* Mr. Landis owns six rowhouses and apologizes to everybody, including the water company. It somehow made it worse. A slumlord you could hate. A sorry doesn't cover March. Thursday I took the Apteros out to reshoot — the restored listing was dead in the algorithm, and dead listings need fresh blood. Nine, close, silent, which is already wrong; pigeons travel with commentary. They dipped. All together, once, like a congregation getting the cue. Then they stayed down. Birds don't hold bows. Birds are transactional — bread for presence, gone in a wingbeat. This one in front held his head at his toes for four full seconds, and I counted, because counting is what I do instead of praying, and then I went inside with my photos and let them have the fire escape. Friday afternoon, the 4 along the park edge, and I saw a girl doing hill repeats. In February. Somebody grinding uphill past the reservoir when the team's official practice ended an hour ago is either training for something or running from something, and the form said training — arms driving straight, shoulders level, landing quiet even from across the road. Then she turned at the top and I saw the left shoe: split wide at the pinky knuckle, sock showing, gray with road salt. Bea. Freshman. The one who used to watch me at practice with her arms crossed like she was taking notes for later. I looked at my phone until the bus moved. Screen black, mirror-glass, my own face doing something complicated. Filed it. Saturday I ran errands for the hustle: mailers in bulk, a tape gun, tissue. Philadelphia Mills, because the outlet packs cost half what the post office rapes you for. Escalators and I settled our differences years ago, permanently, in their favor — I took the ramp the long way around, past the pretzel place. The rumor I was chasing: a guy had returned an Apteros at the factory store last week. Claimed it was defective. Returns desk, one woman working, seventies maybe, reading glasses on a beaded chain, folding a mountain of returned hoodies into squares so precise it looked liturgical. Name tag said CALLIE. # Dead Stock — Chapter 4: Callie "Nobody," I said. "They came tied." She looked at my shoes a long time. Then she crossed herself right to left, fast, like scratching an itch, and came around the counter with her walkie crackling about a zipper dispute she clearly intended never to resolve. "Come on. Not here." The break room smelled like burnt coffee and laminated schedules. She poured two cups without asking and cut me a slab of coffee cake off a foil tray, wax paper, no napkin. "Friday cake," she said. "Saint Phanourios. You bake for him when you've lost something, he finds it. I bake Tuesdays, work Fridays, so I buy from the bakery on Cottman. He understands overtime." She sat down like furniture being placed. "Sit. You're making the room nervous." Her name tag had CALLIE and under it, in marker gone gray, *returns only*. Taped inside her locker door, visible whenever it swung: a paper icon of a saint with a lamp, curling at the corners. "You win these shoes or buy them?" "Won the draw. Bought them. Two hundred four dollars." "So you paid." She nodded like that confirmed paperwork. "Sign anything? Name, email, the little boxes?" "Everything. There's always everything." "Mm." Coffee. "My yiayia kept an icon of the Panagia through the famine years. Men offered her silver — real men, with coats. She fed it to the stove instead of selling it. You know what she told me? Sold things have chains on them. Given things, nobody touches. A thing given walks free." She shrugged. "Could be saints. With us it was saints. Saints and gods, same landlord sometimes." "That's not — okay." I put the cake down because my hands wanted to gesture. "It's a shoe. It's a limited shoe. Five hundred of them exist. I have people offering me real money—" "How much you owe?" She said it like she already knew there was a number. I didn't answer, which answered it. "I do returns twenty-two years," she said. "Everybody who sits in that chair owes something. The shoe is not the problem. The wall of shoes you won't wear is the problem." I hadn't told her about the wall. I made a note of not telling her. "You're hungry sitting next to a wall of dead men, and you want to sell the living one because she's worth more. Sell the corpses first." "They're inventory." "They're shoes you're keeping from feet." She refolded a hoodie that was already folded. "You know what dead stock means, child? Never worn. A bed nobody sleeps in. A meal nobody eats. My papou worked freight, he said the new pallets come off the truck smelling like a wake, and everybody laughs, and he's right. That boy brought his pair back Tuesday — the one from the rumor — said it smelled like a funeral. Wasn't haunted. Was *lonely*. There's a difference." She looked at me over the glasses. "Shoes are for walking. That's the whole mystery. You want the deep part, there isn't one." "And the returned pair? Is it on the rack? Because I'd take it as-is, damaged box, whatever—" "It's gone." "Gone where?" She told me with her chin: the salvage bin by the loading dock. Tuesday night, before corporate's new policy memo, she'd blessed it and snapped the insole over her knee and broken the pair down for salvage, because it had stopped. "It had *stopped*?" "Like a clock. Cold all the way through. The little stamp on the insole — you seen it, the feather — hers had faded clean out. Whatever rode in that shoe had gotten off or died aboard, and either way I'm not putting a body back on the rack past the funeral." She sipped. "New policy says everything sells. Corporate would've sold him his empty shoe twice." Her phone buzzed on the table, screen up: MODULE 7 OF 9: DE-ESCALATION ESSENTIALS. She turned it face-down without looking, the way you swat a fly you've stopped hating. Two hundred dollars, snapped over a knee. I did the math on it anyway — salvage insole, dead pair, story discount — caught myself doing it, and ate my cake. "Who is she?" I asked. "The shoe." Callie wiped crumbs with the side of her hand, unhurried, deciding how much of the inheritance she trusted me with. "My yiayia's people came from an island — Samos. No. Samothrace, that was the other side, my papou. Never mind, they're all the same water." She counted on her fingers like beads. "There's a lady in Paris, marble, big wings, no head — they pulled her out of the ground and she's been headless ever since and nobody embarrassed about it. And there's a little temple in Athens, no wings at all, because the city took them off her so victory couldn't fly home to somebody else." She pointed her cake fork at me. "Same lady. Yiayia said they loved her too much to risk it. Papou said jail. Both of them crossed themselves and kissed their fingers after, so make of that what you make of it." "Nike," I said. "Victory." "Victory herself, if the old ones are right." Against my hip, through canvas, the tote went warm. Not radiator-warm. Seat-still-holding-somebody warm. I didn't look down. Looking felt like agreeing to something. "She's a saint to us," Callie went on, "a goddess to the books, a logo to the children, and none of those are insults, whatever she thinks. But she's not *merchandise*, and that's what you've got her filed under." She stood, joints reporting in order, and gathered the foil tray. "You don't sell a god, child. Not because of punishment. Because of what it makes you. I watched men who sold holy things live long lives with a hole in them shaped like the transaction. Nobody warns you the hole doesn't spend." "So what do I do? I can't wear them, they run small, they're not even my size—" "That's above my floor." She was already moving, tray under her arm, phone buzzing Module 7 against the table edge. At the door she paused, back to me. "Don't sell on a Sunday either. Just in case." Then she pushed through into the fluorescents, where a man was waiting to dispute his zipper again, and I sat alone with two cups of terrible coffee and a slab of Friday cake for a saint who finds things, wondering what it costs to lose something on purpose.

# Dead Stock — Chapter 5: Pickup Window Saturday night my whole account locked. Not the listing — the account. Balance held pending review, all $212 of it hostage, a banner explaining that resolution times vary. My money went to escrow. That's what Callie would've called it, anyway. Sunday, 3:07 a.m., a text from a number with no country code: *YOUR PICKUP WINDOW IS 3:00–3:15 AM. REPLY R TO RESCHEDULE. THIS WINDOW DOES NOT RESCHEDULE.* I'd found the card Thursday, reshuffling tissue for photos. Black, heavy stock, no phone number, no website. HERMES LOGISTICS. Under it, smaller: *We deliver everything eventually.* An address out by the air cargo terminals, past where the buses quit. Mom was at work. I left a note saying the library opened early. Put in the cinnamon gum out of ritual, then took it back out, then put it back in. Outside, a white van idled at the curb with its hazards off, which somehow read as more polite than hazards on. The side said LAST MILE SOLUTIONS. The driver door was open. Nobody in it. "You press your thumb into everything," Hermes said from the passenger seat, not looking up from a tablet. "Displays, mostly. Store fixtures. We have footage. It's excellent footage." He gestured at the other seat with a stylus. "Buckle up. Cargo rules." I checked his feet before I checked his face — occupational deformity — and immediately wished I hadn't. Low-tops in a colorway I couldn't place, and I can place anything. No tag I knew. No SKU my brain could pull. Samples of something that hadn't decided to exist yet. My palms sweated. Not fear. Appetite. That scared me worse. The depot was rows of steel cages under sodium lights, stacked to the ceiling, each shelf labeled in a font that hurt to read. The whole building hummed, low and uneven, like a fridge in every apartment of a building you can't leave. Some cages hummed in a different key than others. One had fresh tape across the front and nothing inside. I stopped cataloguing after that. "One pickup first," he said. "Routine. You can wait in the van." "I'll come." Elias & Son Groceries sits on Susquehanna between a church that's been renovating since Obama and a nail spot. There is no son anybody's met. Elias opens at five, hums tuneless behind the register, sells me a honey bun most mornings and pretends the register shorted himself on purpose. His luck is local knowledge: scratchers pay out near his machine, the ice never melts wrong in July, fights step outside before they start if they start in his doorway. At ten to five the lights were on and Elias was in his chair, humming, wearing New Balances the color of oatmeal. Older than my mother. Soles worn round as river stones, laces double-knotted the way old men tie, against funerals. Hermes knelt like a fitter at a nice store. Held a phone under the tongue. Read something off it and said a name — not Greek, not anything, too many consonants, gravel poured slow — and the humming stopped mid-note like a dropped call. Elias didn't wake up. That was the worst part. He stayed in the chair, eyes open, breathing, hands still resting on the counter like a man waiting for a bus he'd stopped believing in. Hermes boxed the shoes with foam and tape, neat, respectful, the way you pack somebody else's china. "Hold this," he said, and handed me the lid. I held it. "You can look away," he said, taping. "Most people do." I looked. The store got quieter than physics allows. When we left, Elias rang up a sale for nobody — scanned air, bagged nothing, set it on the counter. His eyes worked. They were just turned down to a pilot light. In the van I wiped my hands on my jeans four times. Hermes watched the road and let me. "Now," he said. "Business." He laid it out like a rate card. Option one: he buys the Apteros today. Twelve-five, wire, account thawed within the hour. Above anchor, above sanity. Nobody pays twelve-five for a two-four shoe, and we both sat there knowing what the extra ten thousand was priced for. Option two slid across the seat as a tablet. FIRST ATHLETE PROGRAM. Forty thousand signing. Thirty-two hundred monthly through graduation. "Penn, Temple, wherever admits you — we have relationships." Mom's arrears cleared tonight, medical covered if she ever needs it. Photoshoot in April. "All we ask," he said, "is that nothing you give, you give alone. Gifts route through us. Fulfillment, packaging, documentation. Generosity scales, Imani. Charity needs a logistics partner. You'd be her first priestess with a salary." "You killed my listing." "I paused your listing. You had a keyword problem." He turned a page with the stylus. "You've sold holy things before. Reglued soles, undisclosed. You bought a kid's first raffle win for three hundred dollars outside a Wawa — he'd have gotten nine hundred easy. I'm not shaming you. I'm establishing precedent. You already work in my industry." The gum clicked against my teeth. "Cinnamon," he noted. "For trust. It doesn't work. Keep going, though." I wanted it. That's the confession of this whole chapter: I sat in a van at four in the morning wanting it, running the numbers with the good calculator, the one where March 14th dissolves and Mom sleeps past seven and the wall comes down box by box into a life. My thumb hovered over the signature field. Hovered. The glass fogged under it. "If I sign," I said. "What happens to her?" "Nothing," Hermes said. "That's not —" "Nothing happens to her. Forever. That's the product." He said it kindly, which is the version I still hear at night. "No more Louvres. No more clipped wings. No more starving decades in a fountain, eating coins. Victory without risk, preserved perfectly. She will never lose anything again." He smiled with real warmth. "Including you." I thought about my wall. Five years of sealed boxes, each one a month the lights stay on, and how much of my life I'd spent keeping things exactly safe enough to never be used. A climate-controlled nothing is still nothing. I grew up next door to that math. I *was* that math. "I need until the first," I said. "Of course you do." He tapped the tablet and everything folded away, unhurt, unhurried. "Deadlines are my favorite holiday. Rent's due the first. Your hearing's the fourteenth. I'll see you at one of them." The van stopped. We were somehow outside my block. "Reply R to reschedule." Dawn came up gray over Susquehanna. I got a honey bun at Elias's because habits don't consult you. The coffee burner tasted scorched. The scratcher machine ate a dollar and gave nothing back, and the man ahead of me kicked it once, gently, like apologizing to a horse, and walked out. Elias scanned my honey bun and didn't hum, and didn't short the register on purpose, and I stood there chewing in the doorway trying to remember what tune it had even been.
