# Chapter One — In Order Everyone tells it the same way: they came, the fish died, then the fish spoke. Order matters to people. It makes a thing seem like it happened for reasons. Here's my version, which is also in order, but longer. They came first — that part's true. Three of them, standing past the shelf edge in three kilometers of water, black against the water the way a chimney is black against a sky, except there was no smoke and no fire and nothing moved. The official name is Structures. The Task Force sends bulletins with capitalized names in them. Locals called them the Pylons by the second morning and the name stuck because it sounded like something you'd already known about. Other coasts got theirs too — eleven confirmed as of this month, none closer to shore than ours — but nobody has visited one and come back with anything except photographs that look like photographs of nothing. They don't transmit. They don't reflect radar in any way that makes sense to the people paid to understand radar. A month now. They just stand there. My neighbor Denny, who manages the dock and has not changed his expression about any of this, said: came all this way and they just stand there like my ex. Then the fish died. That part everyone gets wrong, so let me get it wrong properly first, the way I did in print. Four days after arrival the beaches started silvering — herring first, then dogfish, then things with no common name. I published an interpretation inside two weeks. Storm scatter, seasonal hypoxia, a die-off consistent with the warm blob sitting offshore since spring. I was confident. I was quoted. I was wrong, and the correction came from Nanaimo using my own hydrophone data, because our array feeds an open consortium, so the proof arrived through my own front door wearing my own coat. Dr. Brandt's rebuttal was polite in the way that costs more than rudeness. I walked it back in a follow-up that eleven people read. There's a version of me that would have kept arguing if the fish had let me. The beach itself I won't prettify, because I did that too, once, in a grant report — *a biomass deposition event* — and a drone tech quit partly over that sentence. What it actually was: a kilometer of Port Anselm's west beach under ten centimeters of dead fish, warming. The smell got into the station's air intake and stayed for nine days; we drank coffee that tasted of it and stopped remarking on it, which tells you something about us faster than any testimony could. Gulls so gorged they couldn't lift off, standing in the wrack like drunk spectators. A bulldozer working the tide line dawn to dark, pushing the mass into windrows above the high-water mark, where it steamed. A seal pup that should have been weaned and wasn't, crying along the berm for its mother in a register that went through the dozer operator worse than the smell did — he gave it his lunch, which was wrong biologically and correct otherwise. The red-tide people had a point about the dinoflagellate blooms; the denialists built their whole story out of half of it. The counts never agreed. They still don't. Nanaimo says four hundred tonnes for our stretch of coast in the first week. The Task Force says two hundred and change. Both numbers are printed in the same briefing document, facing each other across a page, neither footnoted to the other. You learn to make decisions anyway. That turns out to be the whole skill. My brother Cole didn't publish anything. He sat at his kitchen table with tide tables and the die-off dates and drew lines, and a week before anyone with a peer-review process caught it he'd mapped the kills against the ebb of the big springs and against a shelf-current eddy that doesn't have a name, and he took it to the Legion, where the room laughed, and then, two nights later, stopped laughing when the eddy showed up in a university preprint with somebody else's name on it. He doesn't bring it up. He brings everything else up. The *June B.* is tied at the co-op float with her gear flaked down and her tanks full, which is its own kind of grief — a boat ready for a season that isn't coming. His crew went to Alberta in the second week. The cannery ran two shifts in April for the last of the frozen inventory and then went cold, and the cold is the thing people mention when they talk about it, not the layoffs. Cold carries farther. And the orcas were gone. That's what I knew best and said least. The A-clans pass through in May like clockwork — I have nine thousand hours of them on disk going back to my doctorate — and this May the passes came back empty. Rubbing beaches unused. Hydrophones hearing weather and ship noise and nothing else. Residents starve quietly; transients move on; you can't tell from a distance which you're watching, and the distance was all anybody had. Which brings me to the night part, and why order matters less than everyone wants. It was the twelfth of May. I'd done my rounds — swapped batteries on the outer moorings that morning, argued with the co-op's invoice system, smoked one Du Maurier on the observation deck where my doctor believes I've quit — and I couldn't sleep, so I went into the analysis room and did the thing insomniac acousticians do, which is listen to the floor of the sea at three in the morning for no fundable reason. The deep-channel feed runs to a hydrophone at ninety meters off Kessler Point. Strip out the ship traffic, strip the swell, strip the current rumble, and you get the noise floor — a flat brown carpet of sound, thermal agitation, the planet's own hum. I've looked at that carpet thousands of nights. It's how I know the difference between the sea being quiet and the sea being empty, which is a difference most people will never need. That night there was a pulse in the floor. Below everything. Not loud — you'd never hear it, you'd never see it on a normal spectrogram, it lived under the threshold the way fin whale song lives there, which is a sentence Gus Merrill used to say until people's eyes glazed. A pulse, evenly spaced, and between pulses a silence of exactly the same duration, and every pulse-and-silence pair added one to something. I'm going to say it plainly even though plainly sounds crazy: it was counting. I ran it back through the archive to find where it started. April 19th. Arrival plus six days. It counted without pause for twenty-three days, and then, somewhere around midnight while I sat there with cold coffee, it reached a number and stopped. Not faded. Stopped. Complete. The way you stop when you've said a number out loud to someone and are waiting to be told whether it's right. I sat in the dark until the window went grey, and I did not call anyone, because there was no one left awake who wouldn't have told me to sleep, and because some part of me already knew that whatever happened next, I'd been present for the beginning of it, alone, which is how I seem to arrive everywhere.

# Chapter Two — Calligraphy Gus Merrill lives five minutes from the station in a house that smells of coffee nobody finished. The jars are labeled — FLOUR, SUGAR (REAL) — in grease pencil gone amber with age. CBC murmurs on the TV with captions and no sound, the way other houses run clocks. Me, apparently, now. "SOSUS," he said, "was listening for boats by how they counted. Screw turns. You couldn't hide a submarine's arithmetic — blade rate, we called it. You could tell a Charlie from a Victor by its rhythm through the floor of the ocean, a thousand miles out." He tapped the spectrogram printout. "Somebody's running blade rate at you. Only thing is, there's no boat." "You said once there's a tone under the noise floor. Fin whale song. You chased it for years." "I filed a love song as a threat for thirty years." He said it the way you'd read a shipping manifest. "So forgive me if I hold off deciding what these ones want till they're done talking." My first instinct — and I'm recording it here because I'm trying to be accurate about myself — was aesthetic. I wanted to say beautiful. It's made of four hundred tonnes of dead animals, give or take two hundred depending which agency you believe. Any beauty in it belongs to whoever finds it beautiful, and I've decided that isn't me. Structure, though. Structure I'll swear to. The overlay took us two days because I made Gus check everything twice. After the correction came through my own front door wearing my own coat, I don't publish a comma without three passes. Here's the shape of it: the count ran twenty-three days. Every mortality cluster along the coast has a start time. Plot the clusters against the count and each increment lands on a site — not randomly. Sequentially. The count was indexing. Pulse one, site one. Pulse nine hundred and change, site nine hundred and change. And the sites, taken in count order, trace the strokes. The windrows weren't drift. The drift was the medium. Whatever was written got written in bodies because bodies were what moved with the current, the way you'd write in water with anything that floats. I drafted an email to Brandt with the overlay attached. Subject line, one line of text, deleted it, sat there feeling pathetic about it, deleted the subject line too. There'll be time. There turned out to be time. What we had was structure without meaning. I ran the glyph inventory the way you would for any unknown script: frequency distributions. The recurring forms obeyed a rank-order curve — few forms very common, most rare, the long tail you get in every human language ever counted and in no random deposit ever measured. Zipf's law, if you want the term. It doesn't prove language. It proves the opposite of noise, which at that point was enough to ruin my week. "We should send it back," Gus said. "Send what?" "The count. As received." He shrugged, a small careful motion, like the shrug might spill. "You knock on a door, you expect somebody to say who's there. We haven't knocked." The station keeps a calibrated projector on the outer mooring — playback experiments, play an orca call, measure who answers. Standard kit. I routed the archived pulse train through it at source level and let it run the full twenty-three-day sequence compressed into six hours, which is either rude or efficient, and then we waited, and nothing happened, and Gus made tea from the REAL sugar, and I went out to the porch to lie to myself about having one cigarette only. The answer came at slack water the next morning, on every hydrophone in the array at once. An A-clan call. Not a live animal — the acoustic geometry was wrong for anything swimming, it arrived phase-locked across all eight receivers like a voice pressed against the whole coastline. G30, if you want the catalogue number, the one the A-matriline uses coming onto the rubbing beaches. I have nine thousand hours of it. I know it the way you know your mother's footsteps on stairs. Except the intervals were wrong. The contour was theirs, note for note, and the timing between notes was the count's spacing — our spacing, the pulse-and-silence arithmetic we'd played back, grafted into the middle of a family's greeting like a borrowed word used slightly wrong. Then it ended. Mid-phrase. It stopped where a pause should have opened and didn't resume, and the sea went back to weather and ship noise, and Gus sat looking at the spectrogram with his pen uncapped, not writing. "It didn't finish," he said. I played it forty times that night. On the forty-first I closed the file and did my rounds and did not sleep, and in the morning I emailed the overlay to Brandt after all, because whatever was out there had just said hello in my whales' voices, and I'd spent four years not playing two voicemails, and I am apparently someone who does things late.

# Chapter Three — The Chorus After the G30 answer, the mimicry went through the coastline like a rumor. Gray whale moans with the count's spacing inside them. Sea lion barks answering each other slightly wrong. Gulls screaming phrases no gull ever taught them. And then, nine days after our knock, the choruses started, and I have to describe them carefully because everything you've seen on television gets them wrong. There is no single mouth. That's the thing nobody believed at first. A chorus fires along the whole shelf at once — thousands of animals, herring and rockfish and lingcod and things we never did identify, all holding the same pitch at the same instant, phase-locked across ninety kilometers. On a spectrogram it looks like one voice. Underlying it, if you decompose the arrivals, you can see the swarm: individual signatures stacked into agreement, the way a chord isn't any one string. At the edges of each chorus, on every event, a percentage of the singers went belly-up while they fired. I noted it. I didn't compute it yet. There's a version of me that computed it immediately, and she's the one who slept. The voice learned English the way a crow learns your garbage routine — by theft, opportunistically, without shame. We started catching scavenged audio in the choruses. Fragments of the overnight marine forecast, the ten o'clock man, with his pause before *winds light*. A verse of *Shall We Gather at the River*, looped for six hours straight one Tuesday for reasons nobody established; a theologian on the national broadcast called it selection bias, which is what theologians say instead of *we don't know*. Mayday recordings, Coast Guard relays, weather buoys. Each word arrived wearing its origin — *river* carried church reverb, *becoming* carried radio compression, some words had a gymnasium in them somewhere, a school PA. You could hear the seams if you listened like me, and I listened like me whether I wanted to or not. At the fuel dock they were bottling water from the seaward side, ten dollars, calling it structured. Denny rented them the table space and never changed expression. On the second of June I was in the analysis room at 0300 doing nothing fundable when every hydrophone on the coast spoke at once. Not the array — the coast. Every recorder, every ship's hull, every phone pressed to a tide pool. The sentence landed globally; that part's documented, time-stamped to within a millisecond by three separate agencies who otherwise agree on nothing. *WE READ THE SEA.* *We* out of the church. *Read* in the ten o'clock man's cadence, pause and all. *Sea* carrying a gymnasium I've never located. Four words, if you count it right, and the seams showing, and underneath the whole assembly a bass note I now know was the swarm holding pitch, ten thousand small bodies agreeing to be one throat for four seconds. What happened next happened everywhere at once and I only saw our slice of it. The Legion put the sentence on above the till, laminated. Services on the beach, folding chairs, a guitar. Markets did whatever markets do — I'm told the word for it is *repriced*. The Task Force issued a bulletin assigning it a capitalized name, THE VOICE, as if naming it were a procedure. The red-tide people pivoted to hoax, then quietly unpivoted. Tourists came to photograph the Pylons standing in fog and got photographs of nothing, and bought the water, and went home. And at the bar, on the TV above the taps, during a replay of the sentence, Cole went still with his glass halfway down. The voice had spliced in a sign-off between iterations — *clear on this side* — in an intonation I didn't recognize and every man in that room did. Nine years gone off Cape Caution. Nobody said anything. The game came back on. Cole finished his beer facing the good ear toward the screen, and walked home the long way, past the co-op float, and stood on it a while. I know because I followed him at a distance like a coward, and then drove home, and did not sleep, and wrote in my own notebook: *it has our dead in it too.* Underlined once. The tank at the station holds what the DFO monitoring crew saved from the second die-off — five herring, then four, then one, the losses logged as *environmental stressors* in a report I signed because the alternative words hadn't been invented. On the fourth of June, doing a night check, I heard the last one. One small body in forty liters, firing alone. The phase geometry of a single animal — no swarm under it, no chord, just the one throat. It couldn't make the big voice. What it made was a whisper with church reverb shrunk down to nothing, and the word it had kept was the pronoun. *We. We. We.* A choir of one, holding the plural. I sat on the tank shed floor with the recorder against my chest for an hour. I want to tell you I thought something large. Mostly I thought about how the other four had died, and whether they'd been part of the chorus when they did, and whether that was worse or better, and I still haven't sorted it. Last coffee with Gus was the fifth. CBC muted, captions on, crossword in pen. He timestamped my visit in the green book, hydrophone hours, my name between a Sunday call from Calgary and a pressure reading. Near the end he tapped the spectrogram of the sentence, the way he tapped things. "Every one of them quits like a man waiting for you to interrupt. Nobody lands home. Listen long enough, you start holding your breath for them." He capped his pen. "They keep stopping like they're waiting for permission, kid. Somebody ought to try giving it to them." He sounded fine. He sounded like always. Three days later Renata's Sunday call went to the machine, and Monday Denny let himself in with his spare key and found him in the analysis chair with the headphones on and the archive running and the Folgers cold beside him, and the crossword open to a page with blanks in it. Forty years I knew the man, he never left a blank. The funeral was Thursday. Eleven of us, Renata flown in, Ada's plot up the hill. The same morning every station on earth was replaying the third sentence, and his obituary ran below the fold under a translation of it. I spoke about the fin whale he'd filed as a threat for thirty years — a love song catalogued as a warhead. Wrong story. Right one. Afterward I stopped at the co-op for bread and stood in aisle three crying over the shelf tag for kippers, price unchanged, stock never coming, and the clerk restocking around me with the tact of people who live where everyone's grief shares a shoreline. Then I went home and did my rounds and logged the hours.

# Chapter Four — Arithmetic Here is the thing I did that I keep not saying plainly, so let me say it plainly: nobody assigned me the exchange rate. I built it myself, at 0300, alone, before any agency asked and while the sentences were still coming. I decomposed the chorus arrivals — twelve thousand individual signatures agreeing per event, give or take — and matched each firing against the mortality clusters that followed it along the coast by morning, and I put the two series in one spreadsheet because I wanted to know what I was buying. Between the fourth of June and the fourteenth the coast fired eleven choruses and delivered sixty-one words. Coastwide mortality for the same ten days runs, depending whose number you hold, between five hundred and nine hundred tonnes. Take the low figure. It's still eight tonnes of fish per word. A herring weighs two hundred grams. Forty thousand bodies a word, and the words were *RIVER* and *BECOMING* and *LIGHT WINDS*. I looked at that column for a long time. Then I saved the file under a name with no meaning in it and did my rounds, and when the next chorus came up the shelf that night I listened to every second of it, and I want that in the record too. Knowing the price changed nothing about the wanting. That's the honest version. The version where I weighed lives in a balance and chose — that version came later and wore better. On the twelfth, the voice named its own invoice. It had been building something long for two days, clause by clause, the way the ten o'clock man reads a gale warning, subclauses hanging off subclauses, and then it set that aside and said, everywhere at once: *THE READING COSTS.* *Costs* arrived wearing a payday-loan commercial. I checked that seam four times. Then, after a pause the length of a tide: *SAY STOP AND WE STOP.* They told us the price and offered the door. Both sentences in under a minute, no negotiation, no asterisks. I have since heard economists, ethicists, admirals, and one very confident podcast host explain what the offer really meant, and I'll tell you what I heard, standing wet-footed in my own analysis room: a landlord offering to stop renovating. Governments moved faster than they do for wars. Compliance directives, contact moratoriums, the Task Force issuing bulletins with capitalized names in them. Our liaison arrived the next morning to walk the stations through it — Cmdr. Priya Nair, RCN, twenty-three years, a woman who chews quitting-smoking gum to plastic during briefings and folds every paper into quarters, including mine, including the directive she'd come to deliver. Politeness is her gauge. The politer she gets, the worse it is, and she was extremely polite. "You'll hear I'm a bureaucrat," she said, "so before you decide that, look." She opened her notebook to the inside cover. A team photo, taped, creased from refolding. Eleven people in coveralls around an animal on a trailer. "Active sonar, exercise off the Brooks Peninsula, years ago. Two Cuvier's beaked whales came up floating after. I helped open one of them. Denny sold out of structured water the day the Voice announced its prices — demand was elastic, he said, first economics lesson the sea ever gave anybody. Nobody had written the form for a herring in forty liters. The relief I felt was real, and I'm recording it accurately: relief, and grief under it, and shame about the relief, in that stratigraphic order. Humanity chose silence. # Chapter Five — Dead Calm Dead calm is a technical term. Sea state zero, no wind waves, no swell worth naming — the sea going glassy the way a room goes quiet when the argument leaves it. We got a week of it after the order took effect, weather conspiring with policy, and I want to report that the coast rested. It didn't. Quiet, in my trade, is data. This was absence. Ships still ran the shipping lanes, generators still hummed, the world hadn't stopped making noise. The A3s came through on the twenty-second. Four of them, up the channel at dawn, traveling slow the way animals travel when they're checking behind themselves for food that isn't there. She tried six times over forty minutes. Standing in the analysis room after, I caught myself reaching for my phone. Not to call Cole. The mailbox with two files in it, 0:47 and 0:11, four years unchanged. I looked at the lengths. Cole left two drums of diesel inside my gate sometime Thursday, no note, no knock. We'd fought; that's how Vosses say it. I paid the account he has at the co-op down by four hundred dollars and neither of us mentioned that either. We are people who conduct entire reconciliations in ledger entries. Listening, it turns out, was never prohibited — the order covered transmission, and whoever drafted it didn't include ears, possibly because the drafters were the kind of people whose ears are assumed to be instruments of the state anyway. The launch smoke, then nothing for a while — the weapon's run is silent to the eye at that distance — then a white feather of water standing up off the black flank, absurdly small. And the Voice said nothing. That's the part I keep turning over. We broke the spirit of the thing within fourteen days and they held the letter — no answer, no reprisal, no flicker. The structured water found a second life as *vintage batch*, ten dollars became fifteen, Denny's expression remained uncharged. Talk of ramming the research vessel surfaced at the Legion, circulated, and sank — nobody owns a boat that floats well enough to ram with. Young people keep leaving for Alberta in cars packed past the windows. At the bar, watching the test replay on the news, a deckhand I won't name said, "Two million bucks to make a splash. My ex-wife does that for free." The room laughed the way rooms laugh when the alternative is not laughing. And the residue. Since the order, six to ten fish a week, dead, at three coves south of the point. Small bodies, fresh, arranged in nothing — I've checked them against the full glyph inventory twice. They match nothing. They're not drift, they're not gear damage, they're not bloom. The Voice has not acknowledged them. There is no form to report them on. I log them in the green notebook Gus's daughter gave me, in his column format, because someone should, and because starting a new notebook felt like agreeing the old record was finished. Renata flew through between Calgary and Victoria the week after the funeral and left me two green logbooks and a biscuit tin of tape reels marked, in masking tape, MISC, and one marked simply 1974. The 1974 material is the wrong-frequency hunt, decades of it — and one entry, June, this June: *18 Hz again? no. checked twice. not it.* Even now, even with everything, he refused himself a coincidence he couldn't verify. I sat with that page a while. In MISC, pages of chorus timings, kept since the first week, before anyone asked him, before I knew to ask myself. Each chorus annotated: duration, participants, and a column headed END, where he wrote, over and over, variants of the same note. *Quits early.* *Same spot.* *Not random.* Beside the last entry: *waiting.* I'd been hearing it for days without having the term for it. Every chorus stops on the same unresolved interval — think of a chord that leans and never arrives, a phrase that quits mid-breath, a man pausing because he assumes you'll interrupt. Gus said nobody lands home. He was right. They don't resolve. And now, with nothing else in the water, the missing resolution rings in my ears like the note after an organ stops — invented by my own cochlea, persistent, unbearable. You can't listen your way out of an unresolved cadence. There's exactly one cure for it, and it's supplying the tonic. Sending the interval that comes next. Finishing the phrase for them. # Chapter Six — The Ask The morning of the seventh I found the grammar in my own archive, which is the correct punishment for nine thousand hours of hoarding. It was the MISC tin that did it — Gus's chorus timings, his END column, *waiting* in grease pencil — and I did what I'd been avoiding since the funeral: I went back through the old A-clan recordings looking for the interval every phrase quits on. Dissertation tapes, 2013. DFO copies from the seventies, hiss and all. And there it was, underneath the greeting calls like a bone under skin: the pulse-and-silence spacing. The count's arithmetic, living inside the notes. Not everywhere. In the resting places between phrases, in the gaps the way you hear a person's breathing pattern inside how they talk. I measured it four times across four decades of tape and the ratio held. Pulse to silence, silence to pulse, generation after generation of grandmothers carrying it in how they paused. I don't know what that means. I've heard every theory and I believe none of them completely — that the structures seeded it, that the whales taught them, that both learned it from whatever the sea says to itself down where nobody's ever put a microphone. What I know is that the Pylons have been listening to this coast longer than I've been alive, and when they finally knocked, they knocked in the oldest grammar they knew here. You learn patience from grandmothers or you don't learn it at all. So the held note wasn't a message waiting to be found. It was a phrase left hanging in a family's front room, and somebody had to walk over and finish it. Nair called at dusk. Politeness off every chart her staff keep. "Dr. Voss. The window opens at 0600 tomorrow. Strike package, both structures, weather holding." Paper folding, down the line. "I've filed what I file. I'll be reading bulletins until late tonight, and after that I sleep like a civil servant." A pause you could park a truck in. "Whatever anyone chooses to do with the hours in between, I trust it will be quiet." She hung up. Twenty-three years of service, and that was her desertion, and I'll testify to it if anyone ever asks. Cole came at ten with jumper cables coiled over his shoulder like a bandolier. "You're going out to the mooring," he said. Not a question. Denny had seen me loading the skiff; Denny reports to everyone. "I'm finishing a phrase," I said, which sounded insane, so I played him the chorus endings, six of them back to back, each one quitting on the lean. He listened with his whole head turned, good ear forward. "That's a man stopping so someone else can talk," he said. Then, jaw working: "Fine. You're asking. Mine goes first." He said it like a contract clause, because contracts are the only scripture he trusts. "Ask them when the herring are coming home. Not science. Home. Can you carry that?" "I can carry it." He tapped the doorframe twice on his way out, which is leaving-port behavior, and stood on the porch a second facing the water like it owed him money. Midnight. The tag on item nine cut easier than it had any right to — one snip, side cutters, a crime with a serial number. Shore power stayed isolated; we weren't idiots. The *June B.*'s battery bank sat in my skiff, cables running to the projector element on the outer mooring, ninety meters off the point. Cole ran the boat, unasked and unargued. Cold enough to see breath. The array console glowed green in the wheelhouse, every receiver on the coast open behind us, and I want it recorded that my hands shook so badly on the gain that he took over the fader without comment, the way you'd take scissors from a child. What we transmitted, in order: the chorus-ending interval, six times, each one completed with the tonic that comes next — the phrase finished, resolved, landed home. Then my voice. "Station Kessler — this is — okay." Breath. "My name is Dr. Mara Voss, I run the array at Kessler Point, I'm not authorized to say any of this, and I've already cut a government lock, so. Two things. One: when the herring come home." Cole's eyes on me from the helm. "Two: tell us what we broke. We will listen. That's — that's the whole message. Please. Sorry." And then, because I am who I am, apologizing again into an open ocean channel at one in the morning: "Sorry." We let the element cool and ran in dark, and tied up, and walked up the slope, and nothing anywhere made a sound, and I remember thinking, with a shame I still haven't filed correctly: *well.* At 0312 the sea inhaled. Every hydrophone on the shelf caught it at once — a broadband rise under everything, not a chorus, not a voice, more like the room-tone before an orchestra lifts its bows. Pressure more than sound. I felt it through the station floor, through the soles of my feet, a swell coming up from below the noise carpet that Gus spent forty years sitting on top of. It rose for eleven minutes. On the spectrograms afterward it looks like a hill growing. Then it crested, held — held the way a held breath holds — and began, very slowly, to come down. I sat on the analysis room floor with the recorder against my chest, the same spot I'd taken the choir-of-one from, and waited for words. They didn't come. Not that night. What came instead, at dawn, when I finally did the rounds and pulled the deep-channel feed to log the hours properly: a pulse in the floor. Evenly spaced. Pulse, silence, pulse. Counting. I ran the archive back to find the start time and the timestamp is the thing I keep returning to, the splinter under the skin of the whole story. The sixth of July. 2200. Three days before I asked. It had been counting for three days — through Nair's call, through the jumper cables, through Cole's contract clause, through every word I transmitted into the black water — steady, patient, incrementing, needing nothing from me at all. Maybe it was answering. Maybe it was a new count for a new message. Maybe nobody was ever waiting, and the door was already opening while I stood outside cutting locks and apologizing to the dark. I don't know. I've stopped pretending the knowing matters. The window opened at 0600. At 0615, per the evening bulletin, the strike package returned to base. No reason given.

# Chapter Seven — The Long Sentence The count ran four more days and stopped on the tenth at 0940, complete, the way you stop when you've said your number out loud and someone finally nods. I logged it, did my rounds, made coffee I forgot to drink. Waiting, it turns out, is physical labor. You carry it in the shoulders. It began at 1312. The inhale came back first — shorter than the first time, a breath drawn to speak instead of held — and then the voice opened its mouth, and the first thing out of the mouth of the world was Cole's question. *THE HERRING WILL COME HOME.* A beat, tide-length. *THE SEA WILL CARRY WHAT IT CAN CARRY. IT WILL NOT BE WHAT YOU REMEMBER.* No church in it. No forecast man. Plain assembly, almost flat, and I understood the flatness as mercy. Denny told me later the co-op radio played it to a full store and nobody moved, and Cole stood at the counter with his account book open and said, "That's a maybe," and closed the book, and that was his entire commentary, then and since. A maybe. From him it reads as hope. Then: *WE WILL SHOW YOU WHAT WE BROKE. THIS ALSO COSTS. WE PAY FROM OUR OWN SIDE.* And the long sentence started. It ran twenty-six hours. I know because I never stopped logging. Within two hours my consortium feed was on the open channel and every station on earth was carrying it, which means the world listened through a projector powered by a fisherman's battery bank, cut loose past a government lock, and I have stopped expecting anyone to find that as strange as it is. What it showed was one morning. One dawn on this shelf, played again and again, and each time it played, things were missing. First dawn: the sea hearing itself. That's the only way I can put it. Every sound answered — whale to whale across twenty miles of water, the reply arriving clean, no hull between them to shred it. A herring school moving through it like weather with a million small throats, and the school singing, which nobody knew, which we'd have sworn wasn't true, herring don't sing — and the recordings say otherwise at three a.m. in deep water where nothing has ever dropped a microphone. Glaciers calving at the head of the inlet, the boom rolling down the channel and coming back off the far wall twice. Cold water, loud water, crowded with conversation. Nobody in it was lonely. You could hear that. Loneliness has a texture and this wasn't it. Fourth dawn, or fifth — the dawns blurred; I stopped marking time properly somewhere in the second night: nets. Nets arriving like weather fronts, like squalls you could set a watch by, and the school learning the shape of them the way coastal trees learn wind. Not evil. Just enormous, and everywhere, and always angled the same way. Engines underneath everything now, the floor of the sea going dull under propellers. The voice gave us the engines the way you'd hand someone a burn scar — *noise like fire* is my phrase, not theirs, theirs was worse: it simply played the water as it became, and let us hear the conversation radius shrink year over year, a family's call range collapsing from twenty miles to six to one, the replies arriving later and more broken until they didn't arrive. Airguns. Ten seconds apart, months at a stretch, mapped surveys crawling the shelf like artillery barrages laid end to end. On the spectrogram they print as vertical stripes, and the voice printed them that way deliberately, thousands of them, a fence built through the middle of every song the coast had. Sonar pings inside that. The beaked whales leaving the banks — Nair's animals, the ones she's helped open up on trailers. She watched the whole thing from Ottawa on the task force feed. She sent me one message, 0400 our time: *I was wrong about wanting the lecture. This isn't a lecture.* No punctuation after. I've kept it. And each dawn the school came back smaller. That was the sentence's grammar, once I saw it: the same morning, iterated, subtracting. By the last repetitions the school was a remnant moving through a loud gray noon, and the answering voices around it were gone, and the morning was all machinery and one thin line of herring holding together out of what I can only call habit, and then even the habit thinned. The last dawn had almost nothing in it. Quiet, yes. Our quiet. Dead-calm quiet. The voice held that emptiness up for a long time, unedited, and it was unbearable in a way the loud dawns weren't, because the loud ones had grief in them and this one had just — space. Then, near hour twenty-five, three words, spaced like stones: *SLOW. WIDE. QUIET.* Not commandments. Conclusions. The terms had been in the images the whole time — the bays where ships had passed slow and far out, and the calls had crossed the water whole. That was the entire treaty. Three adjectives. We've built longer documents and meant less. While it spoke, the coast paid. The biggest deposition of the summer ran concurrent with the telling — south coves first, then the west beach again, dozers working night shift under floodlights, gulls standing gorged in the lights like an audience that wouldn't go home. Nanaimo's number and the Task Force's number faced each other across the briefing page again, unreconciled, both terrible, neither footnoted. I started to build the column — words against tonnes, the old spreadsheet — and closed the file without entering anything. I'm not saying that was principle. Partly it was that I couldn't have stood watching a price tick upward in real time against sentences I wanted. Both things are true and I've decided to leave them tangled. At 1520 on the eleventh, the last phrase ended — and landed. Resolved. Came down on the tonic and stayed there, finished, home, the way no chorus ever had, the way Gus spent his last weeks pointing at and never got to hear. *Nobody lands home*, he said. This one did. I sat on the floor of the analysis room with my hand flat on the deck plating and felt the resolution come apart slowly into ordinary sea, weather, swell, the tug two miles out, and underneath it all a stillness that was different from June's stillness. Attended. Like a room where the talking has stopped because everyone present has agreed. At dusk the Pylons dimmed. Not out — down. Radar return softened for the first time since April; the evening bulletin confirmed it with visible reluctance; photographs finally show something, which is that they are slightly less there than they were. Eleven coasts reported the same change inside the same hour. They're still standing tonight. Smaller-seeming. Listening, I'd swear to it, the way the grandmothers listen. I did my rounds at dawn. Nothing new on the sand.

# Chapter Eight — Sea State Zero It's October now. Here's how it stands, in order, or near enough. The Pylons are still standing, dimmed to whatever counts as idle in a thing like that. Eleven coasts, eleven structures, none closer than they ever were, all of them slightly less there than physics says anything standing in water has a right to be. The Task Force bulletin last month ran to forty pages and concluded, in essence, that further study is required, which is the sound institutions make instead of *we don't know*. Nobody knows what they're waiting for or whether they're waiting at all. Renata visited in September and stood on the west beach looking at them a long time, and then asked me to timestamp her visit in the green notebook, which I did, because it seemed right. They never dimmed back up. They also never left. Both facts get reported monthly, side by side, unreconciled, like everything else on this coast. The quiet held — by custom, not law, which was always going to be the case, because there's no form to sign for a habit. Slow ships, wide turns, engines eased down through the passes. The noise charts are dimming like a city at bedtime, district by district, and the A-clans' call range has come back up from six miles to somewhere past twelve, measured, checked twice, real. Ferries run quiet protocols now; the crews complain and comply. And every Tuesday night the *Corviglia* comes down the outside passage at full speed, twenty knots of disregard, hull thunder rolling across the water like a door slammed in a church. Nobody stops her. There's no mechanism. I log her transit each week in the green book under RESIDUE, same column where I logged the unexplained fish, and I've decided the logging matters even though I couldn't defend that decision at a hearing. Some things you do because someone should, and being someone is the entire qualification. The residue fish stopped, by the way. After the long sentence, nothing new on any cove, all summer, and I still walk the tide line every morning looking. The checking is the point. Ask my dissertation committee. September brought the herring. Spawn on the kelp off the point, miles of it, the water gone white with milt along the shallows — the old-timers call it the glitter, and I'll admit the word is correct, which annoys me. Cole stood on the co-op float watching it with his arms folded like it might be trying something. "That's a maybe coming due," he said. His account book stayed shut. He's taken work running hydrophone shifts for the consortium — my shifts, half of them, since I finally admitted one pair of ears can't stand watches alone — and he's good at it, patient in the way of men who've spent decades waiting on weather. He still runs the diesel up the inlet sometimes, out of spite or habit, windows down, and nobody says anything to him, partly because of his face and partly because the covenant was never going to survive on purity. It survives on most days being better than the alternative. So far, most days have been. The A3s came home in August. Full family, up the channel at dawn, and this time when the old female hung at the mouth of the bay and called, the bay gave her back an answer — another family two miles north, clean across open water, no hull between them to shred it. I sat on the dock with headphones on crying in front of Denny, who pretended to inventory cleats until I was finished. Tact, again. This town runs on it the way other towns run on power. Now the part I keep starting and deleting, so I'm just going to say it. In August I played the short voicemail. Four years, and I did it in the station parking lot, sitting in the truck, phone against my ear like a normal person receiving a normal message. Eleven seconds. "Mara. It's Dad. Nothing wrong. Just wanted to hear your machine. Call when you can." Click. That's all. He called to hear my answering machine pick up. Nine thousand hours of archive and the man just wanted the click. I sat there while the parking lot went on existing around me, and then I went inside and did the rounds. The long one — 0:47 — I still haven't played. I keep meaning to and I keep not, and I've stopped calling that avoidance. Some signals you sample when you have the bandwidth to hold them true. The mailbox isn't going anywhere. Neither, apparently, am I. The world's version of events has settled into something usable. Brandt's lab published the decode framework in August and made me second author, which stung for exactly as long as it took me to notice they'd put Gus in the acknowledgments — *chorus timing records, personal communication* — and then it didn't sting at all. Forty years he chased one tone and filed it wrong, and his marginalia cracked the cadence. I think he'd have labeled that SUGAR (REAL). As for the lock, and the battery bank, and the transmission: Nair's incident report describes connector fatigue on item nine. Her handwriting folds the sentence into quarters. The inquiry closed in September for want of a culprit, and she has been transferred to a posting she almost certainly requested, and we have exchanged one email since, subject line only: *bulletin attached.* Twenty-three years of service. I owe her more than a subject line and haven't found the currency yet. When I do, I suspect it will be quiet. Last thing, because the rounds are done and the kettle's on and this account should end where the work ends, which is 3 a.m. at the console. Thursday night, on the deep-channel feed, a young orca — A3 calf, second summer, the one they call the tag-along — came up the channel practicing. Calves do this; they rehearse their family's phrases for years, getting them wrong, getting them less wrong. Except this phrase had the count in it. Pulse-and-silence arithmetic living in the rests between notes, the way it lives in the grandmothers' pauses, except this calf wasn't born when any of this started, and the spacing in its rehearsal matches the April count to within measurement error. I've listened to the file maybe sixty times. Healing or inheritance or infection — I genuinely cannot tell you which word applies, and neither can Nanaimo, and neither can anybody. Both will have to sit in the same briefing document, facing each other across the page, footnoted to nothing. I saved it the way I save everything now. Plain filename, today's date, and one line in the notes field, because someone should: *anomaly? — probably not. checking tomorrow.* Out past the point the sea kept on talking to itself, quiet, wide, unhurried, the conversation radius growing back like grass through a dozed track. Somebody ought to be listening. That's the job description I wrote myself, anyway. Kettle's on.

# Brainstorming **First, interrogate the prompt itself.** Three blood emojis at midnight is deliciously ambiguous. Who sends only emojis? Someone who can't type (injured, hiding, sobbing), someone who *won't* type (shame, fear, a code), or something that isn't a person at all (a glitch, a scam, an automated system, the dead). Each interpretation implies a completely different story. Wide-net meanings: - Literal blood: injury, accident, violence, first period, nosebleed, medical crisis - A private code between friends — an old pact suddenly activated - An automated message: blood donation appointment, period-tracking app, health alert - A hoax or wind-up — the sender is pranking, or the number is spoofed - A message from beyond: the sender is dead, or the phone is - A cry for help disguised as nothing — the sender can't say the real thing in words - Marketing/stunt nonsense — a "vampire experience" escape room booking confirmation That last one is funnier than it sounds — imagine a teen getting a midnight promo text from a goth-themed cocktail bar shaped like a crisis. --- **Premise options (casting wide):** 1. **The Pact.** Years ago, a group of friends invented an emergency code: 🩸 = minor, 🩸🩸 = serious, 🩸🩸🩸 = *come now, no questions*. It was born in childhood and retired years ago. Then, just after midnight, it arrives from the friend everyone's lost touch with — and the horrible catch is that the code failed once before, the night it mattered most. A one-night quest to not repeat the same mistake. 2. **The Ghost Texter.** Eight months after Danny died, his number lights up the group chat. Is it a hacked account, his grieving mum with his SIM, a cruel hoax — or something worse/better? A grief story dressed as a mystery, fuelled by gallows humour: arguing over who inherits his Xbox, a disastrous memorial bench ceremony, a "séance" party that's really just six teens drinking Aldi cider in a graveyard because it's somewhere warm. 3. **Cold Storage.** Narrator works Saturdays at the family butcher's. Dad texts 🩸🩸🩸: *get to the shop.* Nan has died at home, the funeral costs are obscene, the relatives can't fly over for three weeks, and the shop's cold store is — inconveniently — empty. A *Weekend at Bernie's* with a beloved Nan, satirising the price of dying in modern Britain. Nan, of course, planned ahead, and her instructions are hidden in the freezer among the pork pies. 4. **The Vampire of Brackton.** The crush texts 🩸🩸🩸 and announces she's turning. Narrator humours her — garlic from Aldi, SPF 50, a "turning" party — until it curdles into something real underneath (illness, or a controlling boyfriend the "vampire" story is a cover for). Gothic parody with a dark centre. 5. **Three Drops, the Ritual.** There's a school legend: do the Three Drops ritual and the marks appear. A girl goes missing after the emojis circulate, and the town loses its mind — TikTok sleuths, a true-crime podcaster, safeguarding theatre from the headteacher. Narrator knows the truth is messier and sadder, and must find her before the panic consumes her. Escalating caper: sell blood, sell hair, enter a clinical trial for a hangover cure, uncover the "clinic" is one man funding his daughter's treatment. 7. **The Walk.** The sender is the best mate who self-harms; the emojis are the only vocabulary she

# Intention **Core concept:** Fuse *The Pact* with the emotional residue of *The Ghost Texter*, minus the supernatural. Five friends invented an emergency code at eleven — one drop = warn me, two drops = worry with me, three drops = *come now, no questions*. The code was retired as childish. Three years ago, Danny — the boy who needed it most — typed 🩸🩸🩸 and never sent it. He survived the worst night of his life, but the group didn't survive the silence after. Now, at 17, scattered and estranged, they receive a live 🩸🩸🩸 just after midnight — from Danny. It is the first successful deployment in the code's history, and the story is the chaotic, funny, frightened night it takes to answer it. **Why this version:** The prompt's menace is preserved (the text *means* something terrible) without a fake-out death or a hoax. The dramatic question isn't "is he alive?" — the reader learns early that he is — it's "what could possibly make *him* of all people send it now?", which lets dread and comedy coexist. The dark centre is grief and survivor guilt; the comic surface is five teenagers attempting a rescue mission with no money, one illegal Corsa, and a SatNav named Margaret. The thesis earns its sentiment: the code was designed for catastrophes, so everyone learned to hide anything smaller until small things became catastrophic. The fix isn't a bigger code — it's a lower threshold. **Key decisions:** - **Narrator:** Nas, 17, first person, present tense. Dry, deflecting, self-aware — the one who officially "retired" the code, so she carries specific guilt. Comedy is her defence mechanism, and the story is structured so she (and the prose) gradually runs out of deflection around Chapter 5. - **Cast:** tight quartet — Nas, Priya (organised, anxious, sole licensed driver of a dying Corsa), Callum (food-delivery e-bike outlaw, phones when he should text), and Danny (deadpan, works at a garden centre, lives with his gran, therapy on Thursdays). Adults exist at the edges: Gran Brenda (unflappable), Mr Hedges the PE teacher (recurring petrol-station cameo), the mums who secretly stayed in touch and hold the plot's key address. - **Setting:** Brackton, a fading British seaside town — off-season seafront, nightworks road closures, one chip shop with irregular hours. The final act happens on the sea wall at dawn with chips. - **Structure:** one continuous night, midnight to dawn, then a short time-jump coda. Each chapter ends on a hook. - **The reveal object:** Danny's old phone, found in a box, still holding the unsent draft — *"To: Blood Club. 🩸🩸🩸. Not sent — 3 Nov, 21:47."* Tonight is the anniversary. Nothing huge happened today; a hundred small things stacked (his mum wants to visit, a breakup-by-text, a missed therapy session, insomnia at 11:47pm). He fired the flare early instead of riding it down. The system worked — for the first time ever. - **Ending:** the code is recalibrated. One drop = "not okay, no questions, response mandatory, thumbs-up reactions banned." Coda proves it working, then mirrors the opening line: a triple-blood arrives just after midnight — and it's a trifle emergency requiring custard. Fear, one beat of it, then laughter. That's the tonal contract of the whole piece. **Things I intend to aim for:** laugh-and-gut-punch alternation at sentence level; the unsent draft, the ketchup pact, and the chips as recurring motifs; British texture that's specific but timeless (leaves-on-the-line energy, not slang-dated); a tonal dip in Chapter 5 where the jokes genuinely stop, so the return of humour in Chapter 6 feels like recovery, not evasion; circularity (midnight text opens and closes the story). **Things I will avoid:** any graphic depiction of self-harm or method detail — Danny's "bad night" stays oblique (*"the night he ended up in hospital"*); no ghost, hoax, or twist-villain resolutions — the antagonist is distance, time, and their own silence; no PSA monologues or therapist-speak — emotional breakthroughs happen sideways, over chips; no quirky-prop overload (Margaret the SatNav is the single whimsy allowance); no neat closure on the harder arcs — Danny's mum visit begins, it doesn't resolve; no Americanisms, no prom, no dollars. # Chapter Planning **Chapter One — 🩸🩸🩸 (~1,000 words)** Midnight. Nas, awake and doomscrolling, gets the text from Danny — a contact she'd renamed "DO NOT TEXT" and never blocked. Establish the group chat's fossil record ("Blood Club," dormant three years). Interleave the origin memory: age 11, Priya's conservatory, a nosebleed, a ketchup-bottle pact with recited rules. Crucially, establish early that Danny is *alive* (liked Nas's post last week; bag-packing at the garden centre) — so the dread is historical, not gimmick. Callum does the unthinkable and *phones*. Priya says: "I've got the keys to the Corsa. Ten minutes." Hook: they haven't all been in one room since the hospital. **Chapter Two — The Retired Code (~1,000 words)** Assembly at Nas's. Flashback proper: Bonfire Night, three years ago — the fight that fractured them, the night Danny ended up in hospital, the discovery that he'd typed the message and deleted it, and how the group quietly dissolved afterwards (Priya changed schools; nobody archived the chat; nobody left it either). Nas's guilt: she formally retired the code ("we're not kids anymore"). Priya arrives in the Corsa; comedy of the car's ailments; realisation that nobody has Danny's new address — solved by the detail that Priya's mum still sends Christmas cards to his gran, Brenda. Hook: pulling away, Danny's typing indicator appears… then stops. **Chapter Three — Recalculating (~1,000 words)** The drive. Peak comedy chapter: Margaret the SatNav's hostile rerouting; the gang debates whether 🩸🩸🩸 could be innocent ("he donates blood now, he's insufferable about it" — hope as coping mechanism); nightworks close the ring road ("Diversions" sign pointing in circles); wrong turn, a fox standoff on an estate. Underneath, Nas admits she rehearsed apologies for years and never sent them. Hook: engine warning light; the Corsa dies at the closed retail park by the B&Q. Margaret pronounces it 2.4 miles on foot. **Chapter Four — Nightwalking (~1,000 words)** On foot through sleeping suburbia; confessions come easier at walking pace. Callum reveals he still marks Danny's birthday on every calendar. Priya's confession — the big one: Danny asked her for a lift home that night, three years ago, and she said she was busy revising. Cut across the golf course; a security guard on a buggy mistakes them for joyriders; brief farce. Hook: they reach the bungalow street — Danny's window dark, curtains shut. And the front door is standing open. **Chapter Five — The Draft (~1,000 words)** Tonal dip: the comedy drains out entirely. The quiet house; the terror of the hallway; then the shed light — Danny on a deck chair with Gran's lurcher, Nelson, and a torch, mid-repair on Brenda's mobility scooter. Relief curdles straight into the real conversation. The anniversary; the stacked small things; his mum's letter; the insomnia. Then he shows them the old phone: the unsent draft, timestamped 21:47, three years ago. Hook: nobody speaks. Nas looks at the words she retired, glowing on a cracked screen. **Chapter Six — Chips at 4am (~1,000 words)** Recovery begins. Gran wakes, entirely unbothered, puts chips on. Tea at 4am; Danny's dry humour resurfaces ("downgrade me, it was three drops' worth of small things"). The reframe: tonight he chose to fire the flare *early* — first successful deployment in the code's history. Priya proposes the recalibration: one drop = bad day, no questions, mandatory response, thumbs-ups banned. Amends begin, clumsily, incompletely — Priya for the lift, Nas for the retirement. Hook: dawn breaking; the walk to the seafront; is the chip shop even open? **Chapter Seven — One Drop (~1,000 words)** Sea wall, dawn, gulls, paper cones. Quiet landing-pad chapter. Danny talks about the hospital months from his side — lightly, without detail. Callum admits he's been at one-drop level for years, performing fine. Mr Hedges jogs past, second cameo: "Don't tell anyone about the scratchcards." Nas applies the theme personally: she sends a single 🩸 to someone she's gone quiet on (her dad). Hook: the reply comes fast — proof the low threshold works. **Chapter Eight — Just After Midnight (~1,000 words)** Coda, weeks later, montage-flavoured: the new code in action (Callum's 🩸 during double maths, answered within a minute); Danny's mum visit happening — awkward, survivable, unresolved; the Corsa passes its MOT ("statistically impossible"). Group chat renamed. Final image mirrors the opening: just after midnight, Nas's phone lights — 🩸🩸🩸 from Priya. One paragraph of pure fear. Then: "*Dropped the trifle. Emergency dessert situation. Bring custard.*" Closing lines land the thesis: nobody has to earn a catastrophe to ask for help — and you always, always come.
With a view to making the writing more human, discuss how a human might approach this particular piece (given the original prompt). Discuss telltale LLM approaches to writing (generally) and ways they might not serve this particular piece. For example, common LLM failings are to write safely, or to always wrap things up with a bow, or trying to write impressively at the expense of readability. Then do a deep dive on the intention & plan, critiquing ways it might be falling into typical LLM tropes & pitfalls. Brainstorm ideas to make it more human. Be comprehensive. We aren't doing any rewriting of the plan yet, just critique & brainstorming.
Model Output:
# How a Human Would Approach This Prompt Start with the honest difference in process. A human writer given "Darkly Comic British YA Fiction" and a midnight triple-blood-emoji text wouldn't begin with a systematised plan — they'd begin with an obsession. Something personal would snag them: maybe they were the friend who once didn't reply in time; maybe they've sat in a hospital corridor inventing jokes to survive it; maybe they just find the emoji itself funny — three little droplets, the most melodramatic unit of digital communication ever devised, and therefore irresistible. The story would grow from that snag outward, and the plan would be partial, superstitious, full of "I'll figure out the middle when I get there." Human drafts are also discovery-heavy in a way my plan isn't. Motifs get stumbled into — a character grabs a bag of frozen peas during an emotional scene and suddenly frozen peas *mean* something, so the writer retrofits them backwards. Half the planned material dies in draft one because it reads fine in outline and dead on the page. And crucially, a human writing eight thousand words of fiction rarely knows their ending until they're two-thirds through; the ending is found, not engineered. My plan contains a fully specified thesis ("the fix isn't a bigger code — it's a lower threshold"), a designated reveal-object, a scheduled tonal dip, and a mirrored closing image. That's not how discovered stories look. That's how *pitched* stories look — and readers can smell a pitch executing itself. There's also a commitment issue. The prompt is ambiguous on purpose — 🩸🩸🩸 could be death, a prank, a period, a code, a marketing stunt. A human writer picks their interpretation fast and *commits with relish*, often choosing the option that embarrasses them slightly. An LLM tends to hedge: acknowledge multiple readings, pick the safest emotionally-resonant one, and neutralise the others with a wink. My plan picked the code interpretation (good) but then spent effort inoculating against the other readings ("establish early that Danny is alive") — which is smart plotting but also a hedge. A human might let the reader sit in genuine "is he dead?" terror for two full chapters and trust them to forgive the misdirection, precisely because the misdirection *is* the experience of receiving that text at midnight. # Telltale LLM Approaches, Generally, and Why They Don't Serve This Piece **The designed-feeling story.** Everything pays off; every motif has a job; the structure is legible from orbit. Readers experience this as a faint hum of machinery. In a piece about how real emotional life refuses to be systematised — which is literally my thesis — a hyper-systematised story contradicts itself. **Equilibrium banter.** All characters equally witty, exchanges perfectly balanced, no one dominating, no jokes that bomb. Real friend groups have asymmetric comedy economies: one person who is funny *at* people, one whose humour is pure deflection that everyone politely ignores, one who kills a mood without meaning to. **The scheduled emotional arc.** Dip here, recovery there, integration, coda. Grief on a chapter grid. Real crisis-nights are jagged: laughter at the graveside, tears in the kebab queue, forty minutes of nothing while someone fixes a scooter. **The bow, disguised.** My plan explicitly bans "wrapping things up with a bow" — and then delivers a coda where the Corsa passes its MOT ("statistically impossible"), the group chat gets renamed, the new code demonstrably works, and the story closes on a cute trifle emergency mirroring the opening. That's a bow. It's a bow shaped like a chip cone, but it's a bow. The tell is that every thread terminates in either resolution or *flagged* non-resolution ("begins, doesn't resolve" — even the unfinished business is finished neatly as unfinished business). **Impressive at the expense of readable.** Aphoristic narration, clever interchangeable metaphors, every paragraph landing on a wry beat, prose polished to a single uniform register. The human alternative has ugly sentences, flat stretches, jokes that don't land, and rhythm that varies because the *writer's attention* varied. **Safety.** No one behaves badly in an unredeemed way; all conflicts are guilt-shaped and internally held; adults are benign; the worst thing anyone does is retire a code. For a story tagged *darkly* comic, my plan is remarkably gentle. The darkness has been relocated into backstory (hospital, oblique) and forward into worry, leaving the present-tense night itself almost conflict-free. Five estranged seventeen-year-olds thrown together at 1am after three years of silence would not form a smooth rescue squad. They'd be prickly, rusty, embarrassed, occasionally cruel. That friction is where both the darkness and the best comedy live. **Theme stated, then restated.** "Closing lines land the thesis." If a reader can quote your theme back to you after finishing, the story has become an essay wearing a narrative costume. The strongest version of this material keeps the thesis *implicit* — shown in behaviour, never articulated — and lets the final image do quiet work instead of summarising. # Deep Dive: Critiquing the Intention **The narrator.** "Dry, deflecting, self-aware, first person, present tense" is the default setting for contemporary YA voice and doubly the default for LLM output. Worse, the plan *assigns* comedy as her defence mechanism and then schedules when the defence fails (Chapter 5). That's a good idea executed mechanically: the reader will feel the switch being flipped. A human version would let Nas's humour fail *mid-scene, badly* — a joke that lands wrong, that Danny doesn't react to, that makes Priya flinch — so the collapse of deflection is dramatised rather than announced. Also worth questioning present tense itself: a retrospective past-tense Nas, telling this years later, unlocks hindsight irony and self-indictment ("I retired the code because retiring things was the closest I came to courage") — a darker, funnier register that present-tense quippiness can't reach. **The cast.** Four teens, each allocated exactly one confession and one amend, distributed evenly across chapters like a duty roster: Callum's calendar (Ch4), Priya's lift (Ch4), Priya's amend (Ch6), Nas's amend (Ch6), Callum's one-drop admission (Ch7), Nas's dad (Ch7). Nobody is allowed to stay opaque; everybody completes their arc. Humans let characters resist the story. Danny especially: the plan casts him purely as the wounded party everyone failed. That makes the reunion *charity*. If Danny was also complicit in the estrangement — went silent first, said one unforgivable thing that night, chose the closed door — the reunion becomes *negotiation*, which is tenser, sadder, and funnier. **Gran Brenda, "entirely unbothered."** The unflappable wise elder dispensing calm at 4am is a stock unit. Mr Hedges as a recurring petrol-station cameo is a sitcom runner. Both are charming; both are pre-packaged. If Brenda stays, she should be allowed to be odd in a less functional way — genuinely alarming, or briefly and unexpectedly fragile — rather than a comfort dispenser with a chip fryer. **The reveal-object.** The old phone with the unsent draft, timestamped 21:47, is almost too perfect — a workshop-darling prop, presented ceremonially ("he shows them the old phone"). Two problems: plausibility (phones die, get wiped, get sold) and gracefulness (being *handed* the symbol is the opposite of how discovery feels). More human: Nas finds it transgressively — rooting through a box for a phone charger, snooping in a way she'll be ashamed of — so the revelation carries guilt of its own. And consider whether the draft needs to exist as an object at all versus arriving through memory or argument; the physical artefact risks turning grief into a museum piece. **The origin and death of the code.** Ketchup-bottle pact with recited rules is cute but sits in a long lineage (blood-oath childhood pacts, *IT*, *Stand By Me*) and tips toward whimsy. More importantly, the code's death is currently administrative: "retired as childish" by decree. Far darker and funnier: the code died of *embarrassment*. Someone once cried wolf — three drops over nothing, everyone converged in pyjamas, it became a legend they got mocked for — and the lesson the group absorbed was to under-use it. That mechanism explains the fatal silence better than maturity does, and it's painfully true to how kids actually learn to stop asking for help: not by growing up, but by being laughed at once. **The recalibration.** Priya formally proposing new rules in Chapter 6, demonstrated twice in the coda, is emotion-as-policy. The banned-thumbs-ups rule is genuinely good — funny and true — but it should be born messily *during* the night (someone thumbs-ups the 🩸🩸🩸 message in the group chat and nearly gets murdered for it), not decreed at a kitchen table. Systems that emerge from live friction feel human; systems that get ratified feel like a committee. **Nas's dad.** Introduced in Chapter 7 solely to demonstrate the theme. That's a construct: a character deployed at the exact moment the story needs proof-of-concept. Either seed him from Chapter 1 (an unanswered message thread visible on her phone; a custody-adjacent tension humming underneath) or cut him and find the demonstration elsewhere. **Texture spec.** "British texture that's specific but timeless (leaves-on-the-line energy, not slang-dated)" — that's a design brief for focus-grouped Britain. Lived-in specificity ages fine and feels real; sanitised timelessness feels like a set. Commit to a real year's worth of texture: Snapchat versus WhatsApp class markers, voice notes, screenshot paranoia, UCAS deadlines if it's autumn of Year 13, the specific shame of a part-time job lanyard. **Missing darkness audit.** Current comedy inventory: SatNav, Corsa ailments, fox standoff, security guard, PE teacher, trifle. All external, all situational, all safe. Missing: comedy of embarrassment (the Inbetweeners register — shame is the great British engine), comedy of inappropriate timing (laughing at the wrong thing *on the page*, not just narrated), and the gallows humour that actual teenagers in crisis deploy — the hospital-era jokes Danny told that nobody laughed at then and everyone remembers now. Also unused: it's a Bonfire Night anniversary. Fireworks going off all night during a tense drive and walk — every bang a small heart attack, jump-scares provided free by the local council — is a gift the plan leaves wrapped. # Deep Dive: Critiquing the Chapter Plan **Chapter 1.** Solid, but "calm doomscroll → text arrives" is the polite version. More human: the text arrived twenty minutes ago and Nas has been paralysed staring at it — start *in* the panic, mid-paralysis, with the contact name "DO NOT TEXT" doing silent work. Also, the plan defuses the death-question early (liked her post last week, seen bag-packing). Defensible, but consider letting Chapters 1–2 breathe in genuine uncertainty; the reader's spike of "oh no" is the prompt's whole engine, and pre-neutralising it is hedging. **Chapter 2.** The Bonfire Night flashback delivered as a discrete block is tidy. Consider braiding past into present by traffic-light stops, or better, withholding the full flashback and letting it arrive *broken* — different characters remember that night differently and contradict each other, which is both truer and a comedy engine ("that's not what happened, Priya, you were on the trampoline"). The typing-indicator-appears-then-stops hook is excellent; keep. **Chapter 3.** Peak comedy chapter built entirely from situational gags (SatNav, diversions, fox). Fine, but it's also where the group's interpersonal rust should start showing — the car is a pressure cooker, someone wants to turn back, someone's managing the mission like a group project and annoying everyone. Hope-as-coping ("he donates blood now, he's insufferable about it") is the best idea in the chapter; protect it. **Chapter 4.** Walking-pace confessions: good principle, but the rostered distribution (Callum's calendar, then Priya's lift-guilt) feels scheduled. Priya's confession is strong — keep it, but let it *cost*: Nas's reaction shouldn't be graceful. And the golf-course security-guard farce currently costs nothing; either cut it or make it cost thirty crucial minutes, so the farce has stakes. **Chapter 5.** The engineered tonal dip — "the comedy drains out entirely" — announced in advance, will feel announced on the page. The open front door is a strong hook. But the scene as planned runs: terror → relief → real conversation → artefact. Real nights include botched hugging, displacement activity (four teenagers aggressively offering to make tea), someone crying and someone else laughing and it somehow being okay, and Danny initially being *annoyed* — "I'm fine, go home" — and meaning it for a painful stretch. His embarrassment at having sent the code is barely addressed in the plan; it should be the scene's live wire. He fired a flare he'd sworn never to use, in front of the people he least wanted to see him do it. **Chapter 6.** Recovery-on-schedule, amendments exchanged like diplomatic communiqués. Let the amends fail on first attempt. Let Priya's apology not be absolved same-night — Danny accepts it the way people actually accept apologies at 4am: with a shrug that settles nothing. Chips are good; consider whether the sea wall at dawn is too cinematic — a kitchen table with a plastic tablecloth might be the truer altar. **Chapter 7.** Landing-pad chapter, and it shows

At twelve, Callum cried wolf (three drops over a spider; the whole year group laughed about it for a term), and the lesson everyone absorbed was to never pull the lever. So on Bonfire Night, aged fourteen, when Danny needed it most, he typed 🩸🩸🩸 and deleted it. He survived; the friendship didn't — partly because the group dissolved in guilt, and partly because **Danny burned it down himself**: one cryptic, cruel message to Nas (*"tell priya i know what she did"*), then silence. Now seventeen, scattered and estranged, they receive a live 🩸🩸🩸 just after midnight — on the anniversary. # Character 1: Nas (Anisa) Rahman — Narrator **Background & personality.** Seventeen at the story's present, narrating from nineteen. Lives with her mum in a semi near the rec; her dad left for Leeds two years ago with a new partner named Sue whose name Nas refuses to say aloud. The text came just after midnight: 🩸🩸🩸. From DO NOT TEXT. I'd like it noted that I didn't scream. I want that on some kind of permanent record, because everything I did afterwards suggests otherwise. What I did was sit very still on my bed with my thumb hovering an inch above the screen like the phone might go off if I touched it. Twenty minutes, that gap. I've measured it since, against the timestamps: 12:04 the blood, 12:26 my first movement. Twenty-two minutes of being seventeen years old and completely paralysed by three small red droplets sent by a boy I hadn't spoken to in three years. Outside, someone set off a rocket early. Bonfire Night. The sky over the rec went green, then orange, and I remember thinking, distantly, that the timing was almost too neat, like the universe had hired a production designer. Here's what you need to know about DO NOT TEXT. His actual name is Daniel Whitmore. At fourteen he messaged me exactly once — *tell priya i know what she did* — and then made himself a ghost, and instead of blocking him I renamed him, which is a form of keeping him, and I've never once examined that. The chat between us contains two bubbles. His sentence. And nothing from me, because you can't send to someone who's blocked you. Not that I tried. Well. Once. And the code — because I have to explain the code or none of this makes sense — was ours. Invented age eleven, in Priya's conservatory, while Danny pinched his own nosebleed shut through a sock he'd found somewhere. One drop meant warn me. Two drops meant worry with me. Three drops meant come now, come fast, no questions asked. We demonstrated it with a ketchup bottle because we were eleven and dramatic, and we recited the rules so often that other kids started calling us Blood Club, taking the mick, and we reclaimed it like armour. It worked, is the thing people forget. It worked for years. Until it became embarrassing to be seen carrying it, which — I'll get to. That's not tonight's problem. Tonight's problem was that the flare was up. Three drops. First live deployment in the history of the code, and I mean that literally: in five years of ownership, nobody had ever fired it for real. I called Callum. Not because I decided to — my hands decided, dialling while the rest of me was still buffering. He picked up on half a ring, which meant he'd been staring at his phone too. "You saw it," he said. "I saw it." "That's three." "I can count, Callum." There was a pause where a joke should've gone. I gave him one anyway — something about him finally having a legitimate reason to use his emergency hi-vis — and it dropped dead between us, no reaction, nothing, and for the first time that night I understood properly that this was real. Callum Okafor not laughing is the closest thing we have to a fire alarm. "We need Priya," he said. "Priya changed schools." "Priya has a car." Which was true, and also somehow the saddest sentence I'd ever heard, our entire friendship reduced to logistics: who still holds a licence, who still answers. Then Callum did the unthinkable. Callum phoned Danny. Nobody phones. Phoning is what adults do to deliver bad news about parking. But he rang him, speaker on, and we both sat listening to it connect and ring and ring, and every burst of static sounded like breathing, and it rang out. Voicemail. Danny's voicemail, which is still just the network lady saying the person you are calling — the person you are calling — because he never recorded one, even at eleven, even when we dared him. "He's dead," Callum said. Flat. Not hysterical. Worse than hysterical. "He liked your post last week," I said. "The one with the bike upside down." "People can die in a week, Nas." "Cheers, yes, thank you, very calming—" My phone buzzed against my ear. I pulled it away and there it was, a second bubble under three years of silence: **im fine. dont come.** I read it four times. I'm reading it still, honestly, at nineteen, and it hasn't got less strange. Because *im fine* is the most common lie in the English language, but *dont come* — *dont come* is work. You have to type that. You have to decide to type it. And Danny Whitmore knew better than anyone alive that we would come anyway, because he wrote the rule that said so. No questions. Come now. He'd built the trap himself and then stood inside it and told us not to enter, and both halves were true, and that's the whole of Danny for you. I put Callum on conference and added Priya, whose number I'd kept out of pure superstition. She answered mid-breath like she'd been holding it since 12:04. "Three drops," she said. "Yes." "From him?" "Yes." A pause. Somewhere behind her, faintly, I'd swear there was the click of a laptop closing. Six weeks untouched, that personal statement. But that's hindsight talking — I only know about the six weeks because she told me later, in the car, in the dark, in the way people confess things they think nobody's listening to. "I've got the keys to the Corsa," Priya said. "Ten minutes." "It might be nothing," I said. "He said he's fine. He said don't come. Legally speaking, those are his wishes—" "Nas." A breath. "We retired the code. We never retired each other. Ten minutes." Nobody said anything to that. There wasn't anything to say. I got off the phone and stood in my room while another rocket went up, and grabbed my charger off the desk, and my hand knocked my dad's thread open — nine messages from him since August, all grey ticks, all read, none answered, me doing to him exactly what had been done to Danny, and I looked at it for one second and shoved the phone in my pocket. Downstairs the telly murmured. Mum, asleep in front of some property programme. "Going to bed," I called, which was technically a forecast. And I went out into the smoke-smelling street, hood up, walking too fast, fireworks going off everywhere like the sky was sending its own emergency signal, towards a car full of people I used to love, to answer a message that told me not to.
