# Chapter 2 — Daylight Saturday we bought groceries, which is how we didn't talk about it. This is a skill we have. We can fill an entire cart around a subject. She wanted the cheap olive oil and I argued for the good one, and we stood in aisle six having a genuinely heated discussion about polyphenols, both of us leaning into it like a couple of firefighters leaning into a controlled burn, because it was better than the fire we weren't putting out. In the car she said the new cashier reminded her of a hamster, and I laughed, a real laugh, and for eleven minutes everything was normal, and I want it on the record that those eleven minutes happened. Monday, at my desk between claims, I typed into the search bar: *wife sits up at night stares at husband counts numbers.* You feel stupid typing a sentence like that into Google, like the machine will judge you. The machine judged me with results. Parasomnias, it turns out, are a whole country. Confusional arousals. Sleep terrors. REM behavior disorder, where people act out dreams, sometimes violently, sometimes for years. There are forums. There are people whose spouses have entire second lives between midnight and four — cooking, driving, folding laundry with great care. Everyone in these threads sounds so tired. Everyone's advice is *see a sleep specialist*, which is advice the way *have you tried being rich* is financial planning. I bookmarked four pages. Then I noticed what I was doing — building the case file, assembling exhibits — and closed the laptop, and felt briefly insane, and went to a meeting about hail damage in Cedar Falls, where a man showed me his roof with the pride of a man showing me a newborn. Twice that week I drafted the conversation on my legal pad, the way you draft a difficult email. *Elena — weird question, and I'm not worried, I'm just—* Crossed out. *When you're counting at night, what are—* Crossed out so hard the pen tore through. Wednesday I came home early and cleaned the gutters instead. Two hours on a ladder, hauling wet maple helicopters out of the trough, and I came down feeling like a good husband, which is the closest I get to saying anything. The closet I found on Thursday, looking for the good tape. Hall closet, top shelf, behind the Christmas lights: a paper sack from Fenwick's Hardware, rolled shut. Inside — a box of cut nails, iron, the old kind. Two pounds of coarse salt in a zip-top bag. A stub of white chalk. And a spiral notepad, which I opened, and immediately wished I hadn't, because it wasn't notes. It was a chart. Columns ruled in pen. Times down the left side. Little tidy entries, dose-like: *11:58 — settled. 12:40 — stirring, held. 1:15 — count started, reached 60.* It looked exactly like the recovery boards at Elena's clinic, the ones she fills in every twenty minutes for a dog coming out of anesthesia. Except the patient column at the top said, in her square nurse handwriting, my name. I put everything back exactly as I'd found it, including the roll of the sack. Here's what I decided, and I believed it about sixty percent, which was enough to function: her grandmother. Elena used to tell stories about the woman — iron over doorframes, mirrors draped when somebody died so nobody's reflection got caught lingering. Old-country stuff Elena claimed to find embarrassing and performed flawlessly whenever it came up. And somebody *had* died. My father. Two years ago. So the sheet over the hall mirror — I dated that sheet, mentally, to the funeral season, and the salt, and the nails, to grief working on a delay, to rituals that keep their own calendars. People mourn sideways. My wife was mourning my father with hardware. What I couldn't date, no matter how I turned it, was the sheet itself. I stood in front of that mirror trying to remember it bare and couldn't. It was like trying to remember the ceiling white before you paint it. I reached for the edge of the sheet once. Just to check. Just to be a man who checks. Then I let it fall back and went and made tea, because apparently that's who I am. Friday night I charged the little black band Elena gave me for Christmas — I wear it for the step-count bragging rights, mostly — and in the morning there was my night, laid out in blue bars. Asleep, asleep, asleep, and then, most nights this month, a spike of *restless* or *awake* starting around three. 3:04. 3:12. 3:09. Night after night, like a bus schedule. Glitches, obviously. Bands misread everything. Mine logged a spin class I attended from my couch. But Elena asked about it. Sunday, drying her hair, too casual, eyes on the mirror — on the sheet — she said, "Can I see your sleep thing sometime?" So that night I handed her my phone and watched my wife study a graph of me. She didn't skim. She scrolled back through weeks, thumb slow, and stopped on the 3:12 spike and tapped it, twice, like taking a pulse. "Huh," she said, and gave the phone back, and thanked me, and I didn't ask her why she wanted it, because not asking is the house style. Thursday I woke at dawn standing in the upstairs hallway. No transition. One minute the inside of a dream — something about the barn, my father's voice, gone before I could grab it — and then I was upright, cold, gray light coming through the hall window, and my feet hurt. My feet were *dirty*. Actual soil, dried in the cracks, crumbling off my toes onto the floorboards, smelling like the bed under the kitchen window. And my fingernails ached, deep, that bruised-root ache you get after digging, and when I looked, there was dark packed under every one of them, ten little crescents of the garden. I don't know how long I stood there. Long enough to hear myself breathing. Down at the bottom of the stairs sat Blue, tail flat, watching me with an expression I've only ever seen on him and once on a horse — not fear, exactly. Appraisal. He looked at my feet, then at my face, then walked off and put his head in his bowl. I showered until the water ran clear and told the mirror — the sheet — sleepwalking. People drive cars in their sleep. People eat entire meals. My father used to walk the fence line at all hours; farmers do; probably it's genetic, probably it's nothing, probably I'd been out checking on tomatoes I don't grow. I bookmarked another page. Saturday morning she woke first, so by law she got the dream report. "Go on," she said, chin on my chest, game face on, our oldest bit. "Badly. No editing." "Nothing," I said. She waited. "Nothing what?" "No dream. Black. Straight through." "You always say that lately." She smiled when she said it, but she looked at me a long time after, the way you look at a gauge that's reading wrong. That night, going under — that warm slide, the last handhold letting go — I heard her voice beside me, barely air, not the counting: "Not tonight. Please." I lay there deciding what a person does with that. Whether it was prayer. Whether it was aimed at me. Whether I was the tonight. Then sleep took me like a trapdoor.

# Chapter 3 — The Ledger The study was my father's room, and I hadn't been inside it since moving in except to dust, which tells you something. Elena cleaned around it too. We had a silent treaty: the house was ours except for one locked door, and neither of us signed anything, and both of us kept it. I broke the treaty on a Tuesday. Not for any good reason. That's the honest version. I'd come home early, she was at the clinic, and the question I wasn't asking had gotten so loud that doing *anything* felt better than carrying it. My father used to hide the key to that desk in the doorframe's crack above the hinge — childhood knowledge, forty years stale — and my fingers went up there without consulting me, and found it, still wedged in the old paint groove. He never changed its hiding place. There's a metaphor in there I refuse to look at directly. Bottom drawer, left side, under warranty folders and seed catalogs: a green ledger book, cloth-bound, spine gone furry with age. And beside it an envelope, sealed, with my father's blocky carpenter letters on the front: *FOR ELENA. WHEN IT STARTS.* When what starts. I sat on his old office chair — it still knew my weight somehow — and opened the ledger, and the first thing I understood was that I was holding years. Decades. Different inks, different hands, page after page of columns and dates going back further than paper should. The oldest hand called itself Margaret, slanted and severe. Then Ada, round and patient. Then Ruth, cramped, hurrying. Then — and this is the part I keep coming back to — a hand I knew. Loops I'd seen on a hundred school permission slips, on the flour tin, on the note she left on the kitchen counter the morning she drove away. My mother had kept this book for forty years. The entries argued with each other. That's the only word. Margaret, 1958: *Wake him, always. Better a bad minute than a lost hour.* Ada, beneath her decades later, in fresher ink: *Never wake him past the third hour. Margaret woke him once and we paid for a year.* Salt, Margaret insisted, was everything: *renewed the line, held till dawn.* Ruth, further down: *Salt is comfort. It does nothing. Do it anyway if it helps you sleep.* In the margins, things that weren't protocol at all. *It learned the bell. Moved the bell.* *Took six weeks to stop answering when I spoke.* One line, unsigned: *Do not let it hear you cry. It keeps what it hears.* And every few pages, a day count. *Day 214. Quiet.* *Day 891.* Numbers climbing like rings in a tree. Then the last section. Fresh ink. Blue ballpoint. My wife's square nurse hand, and the columns she ruled looked exactly like the chart in her closet, because they were the same chart, promoted. *Day 41. Count reached 60. New record.* *Day 47. Salt swept again. Third time this week.* *Day 52. He smiled in his sleep at 3:19. I did not smile back.* *Day 55. Bought the nails. He didn't ask.* *Day 58. Called M. She hung up. Called again. Got four sentences. Green book. Count his breaths. Don't believe anything she told anyone in 2009. Whoever M is, she's angry enough to chew through wire.* And the newest entry, dated nine days ago: *Day 61. He suspects nothing.* I want to describe what that sentence did to me accurately, because my first feeling — before fear, before confusion — was relief. Someone was keeping records. Someone had it handled. I remember thinking, with my father's desk dust on my sleeves, *oh good,* and hating myself for it about four seconds later, when the rest arrived. Because the rest was this: my wife was running a surveillance operation on me out of a locked room. Sixty-one days of logged nights. Times, counts, movements. *He suspects nothing* — written with the flat satisfaction of a case going well. And my mother's handwriting underneath it all like a foundation, forty years of it, until the year she left. Until the book stopped being hers. I did what I do. I went downstairs, got my work notebook, and started a file. Date, time, observed behavior. Her new supplies — nails, chalk, two pounds of salt bought Saturday while I pumped gas, I checked the receipt. The mirror sheet, undated, unverifiable. Sleep-app spikes at 3:12. The hallway, the dirt, the fingernails. Two columns now: *her symptoms*, *mine*, and I told myself the second column was for balance and knew it was for evidence. Somewhere around eleven p.m. I caught myself drafting, under *prognosis*, the phrase *escalating pattern of paranoid ideation, possibly substance-related,* and put the pen down, and picked it back up, because the alternative was knocking on her door and saying *Elena, what is the green book,* and apparently I would rather document my marriage's death than interrupt it. The drugging theory came to me in the shower Thursday, whole and horrible. How tired she looked. How tired *I* felt, sleeping twelve hours and waking filthy. Something in food or drink, slow, deniable — a wife managing a husband into compliance. I stood under the water assembling the case, and the case assembled itself beautifully, which should have warned me. Beautiful cases are what you build when you already know the verdict. Friday I put the ledger back exactly as found, key returned to its paint groove, and stood a moment in the doorway of my father's study like a man leaving a bank he'd robbed politely. But I took one thing. The envelope stayed — sealed, addressed to her, none of my business, that's the line I drew and it cost me — but on the way out I copied three entries into my notebook. *Wake him, always. Never past the third hour. Do not let it hear you cry.* Evidence. Exhibits A through C of a woman unraveling, starting with my mother, forty years of unraveling preserved in ink for the next one to inherit like a casserole dish. That night I lay facing Elena's back and made my resolution: watch the watcher. Let her have her little log. I'd be awake behind my closed eyes taking mental notes, the world's worst-adjusted adjuster, and I'd catch whatever it was she did in there, counting, and I would finally have the thing on tape, so to speak. She started at midnight. *One, two, three.* Slow. Patient. The house ticked. Blue sighed at the foot of the stairs, unwilling even in sleep. *Forty. Forty-one.* Past the forties, where she usually exhaled and settled. On into the fifties, and my heart began keeping its own count alongside hers. *Fifty-eight. Fifty-nine.* She passed sixty — the new record, day forty-one's record — and did not stop. I lay rigid in the dark listening to my wife climb, number by number, somewhere no entry in that book had ever gone, and the itch came on my nose and I didn't move, because for the first time I wasn't pretending to sleep. I was afraid to.

# Chapter 4 — Vigil I lasted eleven minutes. Not for lack of effort. I came armed. Ice chips in a jelly glass to bite when drowsiness pulled. A safety pin through my waistband for the inside of my thigh. Mental alarms set at every quarter hour. Elena started her count at midnight, and I lay there watching her profile the way I'd watched a thousand policyholders' roofs, documenting, and at *sixty-eight* I remember thinking I'd stay up all night if that's what it took, and then it was morning. No slide, no drift, no decision. Just a gap, clean as spliced tape. Eleven minutes of vigilance and then six hours gone, and whatever took me hadn't even bothered to knock. So I stopped trying to out-stubborn it and went to the barn. Dad's trail cam was on the top shelf in a Ziploc, strapped to a bent post, still half-charged. Nineteen photographs on the card: a raccoon, living enormous, plus forty deer and one blurred coyote. I mounted it on the bookshelf facing the bed, tucked behind the row of paperbacks nobody read, and told myself it was a reasonable step. People film their homes. People film their *dogs*. Wednesday morning: dead. Not low — zero, clock reset, the whole unit amnesiac. Thursday: dead again. I ran it three days on my desk at work, pointed at my stapler, and it purred along like a kitten. Full charge, bedroom, night — flatline. A forum man blamed geomagnetic activity. Another blamed mice. I wanted very much to blame mice. Friday I found the salt line broken. Not scattered — swept. A gap at the bedroom threshold you could step through, the grains gathered into a neat crescent, arranged the way water arranges itself around a stone. Deliberate. Elena was already crouched there pouring a new line, measuring by eye, and she didn't look up, and I stood on the landing holding two explanations, hers and mine, and preferred mine, because mine didn't require the dark to have hands. I checked my own fingernails anyway. Clean. I checked under the bed. Dust, a quarter, a dog toy. I put the quarter in my pocket like evidence and hated myself in a new register. That night I kept the vigil again, out of spite, and she caught me. Her count had reached the forties when her head turned — not gradually, not the slow drift of someone checking a sound. All the way around, immediate, like she'd known the exact moment. In the dark her eyes found mine, open, guilty, wide. "Your breathing's wrong," she said. I did the thing. The old thing. Slack face, slow blink, the whole furniture act. "Danny. Nobody sleeps that evenly. You breathe like a man being graded." "Were you awake?" she asked. Direct, level, a nurse taking report. "No," I said, and heard it catch — *n-no* — the stammer I've carried since third grade arriving right on schedule, and Elena closed her eyes the way you close a door on a room you can't deal with tonight. "Say it properly or don't say it." Silence. The house ticked. Downstairs, Blue sighed against the stair rail, unwilling even in sleep. "Whatever you think I'm doing at night," she said finally, barely above the count's volume, "stop watching me do it." And she turned to the wall, and her shoulders moved once, a single suppressed shudder, held the way you'd hold a door shut against weather — and I thought of my notebook, Exhibit C, copied out of the green book in my own handwriting: *Do not let it hear you cry.* I had no reason to connect those. I connected them. My scalp crawled and I couldn't have told you why, and I lay there listening to my wife not-cry until the ice in my glass melted, and this time I didn't fight the dark when it came. I was grateful for it. Saturday I bought lithium batteries at Fenwick's, the same aisle her paper sack had come from, and felt like a man shopping in his wife's medicine cabinet. That night the camera lived. I watched the footage Sunday in my truck outside a storm claim in Marshfield, engine off, doors shut, like a man watching something illegal. Green-gray infrared. Date stamp. 3:04:11 — Elena sits up. Precise. I'd have called it choreographed except I'd seen her do it live; it was more like a shift starting. She sat with her hands loose, watching me, lips moving, and from outside — from the camera's cold distance — she looked exactly like what she is, a nurse starting rounds. At 3:26 I got up. No hesitation, no confusion, none of the groggy stagger of the hallway morning. I swung my legs out, slid down, and settled on the floor against the side of the bed, back to the mattress, arms at my sides, facing the wall. The posture was familiar in a way I couldn't place, and then I could, and wished I hadn't: it was how I'd slept as a boy. Straight, contained, furniture. The audio caught it. Two streams of numbers, whisper-thin. Hers, steady, patient. And mine — running one ahead. She'd say *forty-one* and my voice, flat and unhurried, already had *forty-two* out. Forty minutes of it. Two liturgies in one room, mine leading hers, and hers never wavering, never following, professional to the last syllable. Then I rose, got back in bed, lay down, and at some number in the seventies Elena exhaled and settled, and the footage ran on to dawn recording nothing but two people breathing. I sat in the truck a long time. Here's the version I built, and I want credit for its craftsmanship: dreams eat sounds. An alarm becomes church bells; a lawnmower becomes surf. My brain had been lying next to her count for two months, of course it absorbed the material, of course it staged a replay. REM behavior disorder — I'd bookmarked it weeks ago; people act out their dreams, sometimes violently, sometimes for years. I called a sleep clinic from the truck and left a message with my insurance group number, feeling efficient, feeling handled, and hung up before the receptionist asked what the problem was, because there was no field on the form for it. Two things I couldn't file. The batteries — four dead charges, one survivor, no pattern a man could write down. And the cadence. The way I counted in that footage, the spacing of it, the little hitch before the forties — it wasn't Elena's rhythm. It was older than ours. Familiar the way a smell is familiar, a kitchen you haven't stood in for thirty years. I knew it from somewhere, and the somewhere had a locked study and a woman counting in it, and I drove back to the office and worked late on purpose. Monday night — Tuesday, technically, somewhere past three — I woke to cold. My right hand throbbed. Ring finger: the nail torn to the quick, crusted black, tender as a burn. I lay still, cataloguing, and heard the house breathing wrong — a draft where no draft lives. Downstairs the front door stood wide open to the June dark, moths stuttering against the hall light, and Blue stood at the threshold with his head low, making a sound I'd never heard from him, refusing the doorway like it was a cliff edge. Beyond the porch, out on the gravel, Elena stood barefoot in her pajamas, phone light shaking in her hand, calling my name into the tree line. "Danny," she said. "Danny." She turned when the screen door cried. The light hit me full in the face, and I watched her take inventory — fast, triage-fast, my face, my hands, my feet, the dark behind me — hope and horror fighting for the same ground. "Where were you?" she said. "I don't know," I said. And meant it. Completely, for the first time in weeks, all the way through.

# Chapter 5 — Confession She didn't sleep either. We sat at the kitchen table while the sky went from black to pewter, the front door still standing open behind us because neither of us wanted to be the one to close it, and the milk sat out going warm, and at some point I got up and put it away, mid-nothing, mid-the-end-of-everything, because my hands needed a job. Elena watched me do it with an expression I'll be seeing on the inside of my eyelids for years. Then I ruined us properly. I want that on the record too. I put my notebook on the table between us, squared it up like a deposition exhibit, and read to her. *Day forty-one. Count reached sixty.* *Day fifty-two. He smiled in his sleep. I did not smile back.* *Day sixty-one. He suspects nothing.* My voice came out level, professional, the voice I use to tell a man his barn is totaled, and it was the cruelest thing I own. Then I asked the question I'd assembled in the shower, the beautiful case, and I watched it land. "What are you giving me? At night. In my food." Elena went very still. Then she laughed — one syllable, no air in it, a sound like a stitch popping — and I understood too late that it wasn't madness arriving, it was relief, horrible relief, the pressure dropping before the storm wall. Because I had finally asked *something*. Sixty-one days of waiting for me to ask anything at all, and my one question accused her of poisoning me. "I rehearsed this," she said. "In the shower, at red lights. Every version where you finally turn around and look at me. You know what I never rehearsed?" She pushed her sleeves up. The wrist bruise had faded to old yellow. "Defending myself. To you. Get the other notebook." "There's no—" "Danny." I got it. The green book's little brother, my two columns, *her symptoms, mine.* She flipped through it fast, nurse-quick, not reading so much as triaging, and stopped at the drugging entry and stared at it the way you'd stare at a tumor on a scan. "Week two," she said. "You stood up out of a dead sleep and I took your arm and you didn't stop. Until sunrise. You want to know where the bruise came from? Not the gate. I lied about the gate *for you*, because the truth was worse and you weren't ready and apparently you're still not, so." She closed the notebook. "Here's your evidence." She set her phone on the table and played a recording. Sheet sounds first. Then her voice, low, careful, the rounding-a-patient voice: *"Danny? Are you in there?"* And then mine. I'd know my voice anywhere — that's what I'd have said yesterday. This wasn't it. Same instrument, different player. Flat, unhurried, almost courteous. *"He's resting."* *"Don't lie to me. Who's talking?"* A pause long enough to have texture. *"The patient one."* *"What do you want?"* *"To finish the count."* She killed it there. Forty minutes of breathing followed on the file, she said. She'd never listened to the end. Neither had I, obviously, since I'd been the performance. The kitchen ticked. Moths bumped the hall light through the open door. I cleaned my reading glasses on my shirt, slow circles, though they were clean, though I wasn't reading anything, and Elena let me have the gesture and waited, the way she waits for animals to come out of it. "When I go under," I said finally. "Something—" "When you go *all* the way under," she said, "it gets up. I watch. The count is a monitor — your breathing changes when it rises, I can hear it come to the surface of you. Waking breaks its grip, early on, mostly. Past a certain point I don't test it." She rubbed her eyes. "Salt, nails, mirror — half of it's probably superstition. I don't know which half. So I do all of it. Ask me anything else tomorrow. Tonight I need your hands, not your understanding." "That's not an explanation." "No," she agreed. "It's a shift report. Explanations are for people who slept." And there it was, the ugliest thing she gave me that night, offered flat and then instantly paid for: "Some nights I hated you. You dreamed, Danny. You smiled at things in there while I sat on a cold floor doing arithmetic. I hated you for getting to leave." Her voice cracked on *leave* and she turned to the sink and gripped the counter, and I thought of the bathroom fan, all those nights, and couldn't decide whether knowing had been better than suspecting, and understood suddenly that it hadn't been either. Knowing and suspecting were the same marriage. We'd just been keeping separate files. I told her about the camera. All of it — the trail cam, the dead batteries, the footage of me on the floor against the bed, whispering along with her count one number ahead. She took that better than I deserved. She nodded slowly, like a symptom confirming itself. "One ahead," she repeated. "It counts with me." Something crossed her face that I'd learn later was fear wearing a nurse's blankness. "It's been learning the liturgy." "The batteries die whenever it—" "I don't know. Nobody knows. That's the job." She pulled a fresh sheet of paper toward her and ruled columns down it, two columns, and wrote a name atop each. Hers. Mine. First time the chart had ever been joint. "There's one more thing," I said. "In the study. An envelope. *For Elena, when it starts* — his writing. I found it weeks ago. I should have—" "Three weeks," she said, and closed her eyes, and I watched her decide not to fight about it, filing it somewhere I'd pay for later. "Morning. It'll keep." Then, softer, almost to herself: "He told me there'd be a book. He never said anything about a letter." Dawn came up gray at the windows. She got up, took the salt canister down, and refilled the jar, and measured out the threshold line fresh, both of us stepping over it carefully like it was a patient, and when she finished she stood there a second in the early light, tiny and wrung out and absolutely steady. "New rule," she said. "If you wake up tonight and I'm counting — you count too. Out loud, in your head, I don't care. You join the count." "What happens if I—" "Never ahead," Elena said. "*With me.*" Outside, the trash truck ground down our road, right on schedule, obscene in its normality, and I lay down beside my wife in the daylight and tried to learn the numbers all the way to sleep.

His handwriting, the carpenter block letters gone loose and shaky at the edges: *Elena. If you're reading this, it started, and Danny never asked me a single question, which I counted on and am ashamed of.* *It comes down the men of my line like height. You'll have worked that out. No salutation to me, no goodbye. I read it four times and got angrier each time — at him, at the burned pages, at the word *silences*, which meant he'd known I'd be the one calling. I called her that night. She picked up on the second ring, game shows murmuring behind her at volume seven, exactly like home. "You sound terrible," Marion said. "Good." A pause with approval in it. Then, when I told her: "No. Whatever you're about to ask me. No." "He left pages out, Mom. We're improvising off a torn—" "I did my forty." Flat as a form rejection. "Last time cost me eleven years of sleep, and I was forty-one years old with a farm to run. You want to do the math on what I've got left? I have. Every night. With the lights on." "You could at least—" "Here's what I'll give you, free." Something shifted against her receiver; ice in a glass. "It never bills the same way twice. That's the only rule that's held across every hand in that book. Margaret paid blood. Ada paid years. Ruth—" The ice clinked. "Ask the book. There's a page with no name on it." "There's a lot of pages with no—" "And Danny. Salt is for amateurs. Use it anyway." Click. Tuesday we stopped being subtle and started being engineers. Trip-lines of chalk-dusted twine across the doorsills, a cowbell off the barn on the hall door, iron nails in a jam jar rigged to rattle at a breath's disturbance. Elena measured angles; I tied knots from claims-inspection training. We worked all day with the windows open, ordinary as people putting up storm shutters, and went to bed feeling, for the first time in two months, armed. In the morning the twine hung slack and untouched. The salt crescents stood perfect. And the cowbell — the cowbell hung on the *closet* door across the room, dusted, adjusted, level, as if it had always lived there. *I learned the bell,* Margaret wrote, decades back. *Moved the bell.* I'd copied that into my notebook as Exhibit whatever and filed it under her paranoia. Standing there in my pajamas looking at our bell, relocated overnight with a craftsman's eye for stud placement, I understood two things. First, that Margaret hadn't been unraveling. Second, worse: the bell didn't need finding at night. It had spent all day in the house. *Through me.* I drank coffee in front of every trap we built. She didn't scream. She went still — triage-still, nurse-still — and her eyes were flat, and the flatness was terror with everything stripped off it, and somewhere below us Blue came up the stairs. First time in six months. Past the glass wall, whatever it was, barking like the house was burning. Her knee found my ribs. Not a blow — a technique, precise, twice — and the grip let go all at once, like a coat sliding off a hook, and I was flung backward onto the floor with no memory of having leaned in, gasping, while above me my wife sat up massaging her throat with both hands and breathing in controlled fours, the way they teach you. Marks came up dark by morning. Five of them. My hand, printed on her. I don't remember most of that day. Fragments: me kneeling at the sink being sick. Me packing a bag. Me saying *chain me in the barn, padlock it, I mean it, I'll sleep in a dog run* — and her, hoarse, standing in the doorway with a scarf already on in June, saying no with an arithmetic I couldn't argue: *"A watcher who leaves loses. "I stood over you three weeks ago with a pillow." She said it fast, to get it out. "Middle of the night, it had smiled at me one time too many. # Chapter 7 — The Fourth Hour Elena wouldn't tell me what she built that day. She worked out in the garage with the door down, radio on, and my only assigned task was nothing. "You're bad at nothing," she said, handing me coffee like a medal. "Be bad at it indoors." I lasted until ten a.m., then picked up the screwdriver to tighten the hinge on nothing in particular, looked at it, and put it back in the drawer. Small victory. Nobody clapped. At nine that night the bedroom was ready. I won't describe the geometry; I only half understood it, chalk and salt and iron set in patterns older than the house, finished and waiting before I crossed the threshold, because that's the rule now — nothing gets built in front of him. Elena checked everything twice, made me walk the line with her, then stood me at the side of the bed like a nurse positioning a patient. "How do I do it?" I asked. "Sleep. Honestly. I've spent two months faking it. I think I've lost the real one." "You stop doing the other thing," she said. "I'll be right here. Whatever you hear in there — however it sounds — it isn't me unless it's counting." Then: "Lie down, Danny." For the first time since this started, I didn't fight it. There was a floor. I want to say barn wood, worn soft, but it gave nothing back when I looked at it directly. It was warm. That was the worst part, right away — the warmth, the specific warmth of the couch at two p.m. when you've decided not to nap and lose. Somewhere far off, figures sat the way furniture sits. Straight-backed, arms at their sides, facing nothing. Men, I think, though I couldn't have said how I knew. None of them turned around. One did. Big through the shoulders. Hands hanging like tools. He turned with the easy slowness Dad had, unhurried the way big kind men are unhurried, and he had Dad's face — not the funeral face, the other one, the pancake-morning one, creased and ready to be amused. "Hey, Danny," he said. My father's voice, down to the grain of it. And the courteous flat voice underneath, everywhere, patient as weather: *Nothing here needs fixing.* *No one asks you anything here. No conversations at three a.m. No forms with no field for it. Everything settles.* *You've been practicing your whole life.* I want to be honest, since honesty is the whole point of this account: I almost stayed. Not because it threatened me. Because it *offered*, and the offer fit me like my own coat. A place where the hard question never has to get asked. A father with a face. Rest that wasn't a performance. Sixteen years of assessing damage, and here was damage-free country, and all I had to do was stop climbing toward the sound of numbers. "Dad—" I started, and caught myself. Answering. Engaging. *Do not answer anything it says.* That rule was for Elena, but standing in the warm dark I understood it was really for me, because answering was my native language, my whole fluency, the not-fighting, the fine. The figure smiled wider. It had been waiting for exactly that syllable. Then, thin, from very far above: counting. *…thirty-nine, forty…* Not the counterfeit's cadence. Hers — the little hitch before the forties, the patience. The thing in the dark had never once joined her. It only ever led, one number ahead, conducting. This was following. This was *with*. I stopped answering and started counting. *Forty-one. Forty-two.* Each number a handhold, plain as rungs. The warmth pulled. The figure's face began to come apart at the edges, patiently, like frost leaving glass, and I counted anyway, forty-five, fifty, and the dark tilted and became effort, became climbing— *Sixty-eight* — and somewhere above us a knot let go. I felt it from underneath. The rope going slack. Cold coming in sideways through a gap the size of a step, and the last things I carried up were her numbers and the sound, distant, of my own voice begging. I woke at dawn with my whole body ringing, honest exhaustion for once, the good kind, earned. The bedroom looked burgled by someone polite. Every photograph in the room lay face-down — wedding picture, the one of Mom at the county fair, Dad on the tractor, all of them turned neatly over, frames aligned. The salt line at the threshold ran gray along one stretch, grains gone dull as burnt match heads. The cowbell hung crooked on the hall doorframe, mid-relocation, abandoned. Elena sat at the foot of the bed, back against the post, gray as the light. Her fingertips were crusted brown. She held her hands palms-up, an old habit, showing me. "Started 11:58," she said. Nurse-flat, reading her own chart. "Trip-line knot let go at 3:47. Your knot, for the record. Whipped the threshold when it slipped." She turned her hand over. "I couldn't leave position, so I crawled the line and repoured. Three minutes. Whole time, it talked. It used your voice. It begged me, Danny. Said please. Said it was cold." She swallowed. "I didn't answer." "I heard it in there too." "I know. Your breathing changed when you climbed. That's how I knew you were still ours." She exhaled, long, setting something heavy down. "Dawn closed it at 5:41. That's three hours fifty minutes of true sleep inside the wards." "Four hours," I said. "Eleven minutes short." Her eyes came up. They were red-rimmed and absolutely level. "So it's held, not bound. Pinned, not paid. And it is *furious* — see the photographs? It doesn't like being looked at right now. Doesn't like reminders." She nodded at the face-down wedding picture. "We do it again tonight, while it's weak and hurting. Full four hours. Nothing slips." "The knots—" "We retie everything. Both of us. You watch my hands, I watch yours." She got up stiffly, knees cracking like the house, and stood over me, small and wrung-out and steady, and gave me the orders I'd carry around all day like stones: "Tonight, while it's weak. And Danny — you have to actually sleep. All the way under. No pretending." Downstairs, Blue was asleep against the bedroom door. First time in six months. I stepped over him and didn't wake him either.

# Chapter 8 — Again We rebuilt the wards in daylight, together, both sets of eyes on both pairs of hands. She retied my knots and I retied hers. At dusk we sat on the edge of the bed like kids at a dock, and she taught me the count out loud, all the way up, including the hitch before forty. "Why the pause?" I asked. "Habit," she said, which meant it wasn't. "One rule tonight," she added, chin up, game face. "You come back and report your dream. Badly. No editing." "Even if it's nothing?" "*Especially* if it's nothing." I lay down inside the chalk and salt and iron, and for the first time since June, I didn't brace at the edge of sleep. I went down the stairs like a man going home. The dark place was colder than before. The warm figures were gone from their chairs. I found the floor and stood in it, counting toward her voice far above, and that's when the fourth hour opened and the thing spent everything it had left. First it begged in my voice. *Please. Please, it's cold down here.* I'd have believed me. Then it tried Dad's cadence, easy, reasonable, the tone for livestock and broken machinery: *Just checking the fence line, son. Go back to bed.* My chest cracked open at that one. I answered it — one syllable, *Dad* — before the rule caught me. Answering was the old language. I switched languages. Numbers. Then, from the doorway above, her voice. "Danny. Wake up. You're trapped in there — Danny, please, wake up." Every wire in me pulled toward it. That voice was the reason for climbing; that voice was the whole climb. Except the rule was simple enough to survive panic: *unless it's counting, it isn't her.* And this one wasn't counting. It was asking me to stop. Above, her count stumbled — one number skipped, fifty-one gone missing — the only time in ninety-three days. Then it resumed, steady, furious, hers. "It had my voice ready," she told me at dawn, nurse-flat, palms-up. "Day thirty-four. I fell asleep on watch. Twenty minutes. It lay there counting my breathing back to me the whole time." She looked at her hands. "I never told anyone. It's been wearing me since spring." Near the end, the warmth made its last offer — rest, the couch at two p.m., the country with no hard questions — and I felt how little it had left, how thin the heat ran. I stopped climbing and let go instead. There's a difference. Climbing is fear. Letting go is trust, and it turns out trust feels exactly like the thing I'd been faking all those nights, minus the itch, minus the swallow, minus the performance. Sleep took me down the last stairs. I woke first. Gray light, birds, and beside me my wife sleeping like the dead — like the living, I mean, like an actual person at the bottom of actual honest sleep, and I lay there watching her breathe and understood from the inside what she'd been doing all those nights, and it was unbearable, and I didn't look away. The evidence was small and total. My app showed one clean blue bar, dusk to dawn, no spike, no bus schedule. My thumbnail was whole. The salt at the threshold glittered like new money. The cowbell hung straight on the hall door where it belonged. And Blue — six months at the foot of the stairs — was sprawled across my feet on the mattress, twitching through some dog dream, having come up sometime in the night to stand guard or collect overtime. The photographs were still face-down. We turned them up together before coffee. Wedding picture last. She woke enough to croak, "Report." "I dreamed about rain," I said. "That's it. Rain on the shop roof. You could barely call it a dream, it was more like—" and I reached for the rest, the part where Dad's radio sat on the bench, the part where he'd holler something, and the reach came back empty. Not sad-empty. Missing-empty. Like a word in a language you've spoken your whole life. "Elena." My voice did the thing it does. "What did my father keep on his workbench?" "Radio. Coffee can of bolts." She sat up slowly, watching my face become a form with no field for it. "Danny?" I went to the hallway. The tractor picture: Mom at the fair, grin like a struck match, sharp as yesterday. And Dad — a smear where a face went, features slid sideways like paint in rain. I knew the facts. Big through the shoulders, laughed easily except certain hours, hands like tools. I could list him forever. I couldn't see him. I stood there trying to hear him say my name and got static, and the static had a courteous patience to it, like something that had packed carefully and taken only its favorite thing. Marion picked up on the second ring. "It's done," I said. Ice clinked. A long silence, volume-seven game shows underneath. "What did it take?" she said, not gently. Verdict-shaped, even now. "We don't know yet." "You'll know by Friday. It itemizes." Pause. "Margaret lost blood. Ada lost years. Ruth lost names. Me, I lost—" The ice stopped moving. "Check your pockets, Danny." "They're checked," I said. "It took Dad. His face. His voice. Kept them." Another silence, longer, and when she spoke again the verdict was gone out of her voice entirely, which frightened me more than anything all summer. "It wore him longest," Marion said. "Of course it wanted him." A breath. "Come down in the fall. Both of you. Watchers compare notes." Click. Weeks pass. The house learns us again. Some nights Elena counts anyway, out of habit, out of liturgy, and I join in, not because anything needs holding down but because it's ours now, said together, low, like grace. The mirror sheet stays up. Some rules outlive their reasons. Blue takes the stairs freely but pauses one step from the top, every time, and always will. Tuesday the trash truck comes. Wednesday I refill the salt, because amateurs sleep better. Today I'm ninety-four days in. I woke at three — real waking, rested, no dirt under my nails — and caught her staring at me again across the dark, upright, hands loose, eyes on my face, and my heart did the old lurch before it remembered itself. "You were under," she said softly. "Real under. Hours. I just couldn't stop checking." "I know," I said. "I was there." No pretense. Sixty-two days late, but plain. Then I reached past her to the nightstand, took the green book off it, and uncapped the pen. Generations of women's handwriting in that cloth-bound spine, and mine went in beneath Elena's, the first man's hand the ledger ever held: *Day 94. Quiet. She thought I'd been sleeping.* I capped the pen. Lay back down. Found her hand in the dark, and when her lips started moving through the numbers — habit, liturgy, love — I followed along, one behind, all the way down. With her. Never ahead.

Watchers compare notes" is perfectly calibrated: practical, bleak, and oddly tender. The entity's final assault is well-staged. The ledger entry — "the first man's hand the ledger ever held" — is a genuinely moving detail that recontextualizes the entire story's gender dynamics without announcing itself. **Weaknesses:** Some metaphors strain. "Sleep took me down the last stairs" echoes it too closely, creating a repetition that feels less like deliberate rhythm and more like a limited metaphorical vocabulary for the liminal state. The passage "I woke first. The plan explicitly noted that "people at the worst moments go flat, not eloquent" — this moment is the opposite of worst, but the self-conscious correction still feels slightly performed. The entity's begging in Daniel's voice ("Please. Please, it's cold down here") is effective, but "I'd have believed me" is a slightly too-neat formulation — it's the kind of line that sounds good but, examined, is a bit of a non-sequitur (he's not the one being asked to believe it). The "ninety-three days" count stumble detail — Elena's count skipping fifty-one — is a strong specific, but the chapter has been counting "ninety-four days" at the end, which creates a slight arithmetic confusion (sixty-one days in the plan, ninety-three in the vigil, ninety-four at the end) that isn't fully resolved. The final image of following "one behind, all the way down" is a satisfying inversion of the title's "one number ahead," and it works. But "With her. Never ahead." as a standalone paragraph risks tipping into the kind of neat emotional bow the plan explicitly warned against. It's close to the line. **Dialogue assessment:** The dialogue is largely strong — Marion's lines especially. Elena's "Report" is perfect. The exchange about the dream game returning is well-handled. No line feels false. **Coherence:** The chapter is coherent and follows the plan closely. The reveal of Elena's Day 34 shame is delivered as planned. The photographs turning up, the ledger entry, Marion's call — all executed. **Overall:** This is high-quality literary horror writing. It has genuine emotional intelligence, disciplined craft, and mostly earns its effects. The weaknesses are real but minor — occasional over-cleverness, a few strained metaphors, one slightly too-neat closing beat. It falls just short of masterpiece territory but represents serious, accomplished work. The confession scene in Chapter 5 is the emotional core and it lands: "I rehearsed this. In the shower, at red lights. Every version where you finally turn around and look at me. You know what I never rehearsed? Defending myself. To you." The supernatural mechanics are inventive and internally consistent. The counting-as-monitor, the thing learning the bell, the photographs face-down, the thing wearing voices — these cohere into a mythology that feels genuinely original. The cost system (Margaret paid blood, Ada paid years, Ruth paid names, Danny pays his father's face and voice) is haunting and well-deployed. The ending is earned. The final ledger entry — "Day 94. WEAKNESSES: The piece occasionally tips into self-conscious lyricism that doesn't quite land. "The warmth pulled. The figure's face began to come apart at the edges, patiently, like frost leaving glass" — this is fine, but the dream-space sequences in Chapters 7 and 8 are the weakest sections, relying on somewhat generic horror-dream imagery (warm figures sitting straight-backed, the father's face) after the domestic horror of the earlier chapters has been so precisely rendered. The supernatural interior is less vivid than the supernatural domestic. Some metaphors are strained: "a sound like a stitch popping" for Elena's laugh is slightly off. "The case assembled itself beautifully, which should have warned me. + Planning Phase (5 Steps)
Pulp Revenge Tale Write a short story over several chapters to this prompt: They fucked with the wrong babysitter. -- Your task is to create a writing plan for this prompt. The scope will be a short story, written over {n_chapters} chapters. Each chapter will be approximately 1000 words so plan accordingly for this scope. Your plan should be comprehensive and in this format: # Brainstorming <Brainstorm ideas for characters, plot, tone, story beats, pacing over the {n_chapters} chapters. The purpose of brainstorming is to cast a wide net of ideas, not to settle on any specific direction. Think about various ways you could take the prompt.> # Reflection <Reflect out loud on what works and doesn't work in these ideas. Model Output:
# Brainstorming ## Deconstructing the Prompt "They fucked with the wrong babysitter" is a promise to the reader. It contains three implicit beats: (1) someone underestimates her, (2) they do something unforgivable, (3) she makes them regret it spectacularly. The phrase is inherently pulp — lurid, confident, a little funny. The story should honor that register: fast, violent, wry, with a moral compass simple enough to enjoy. Key question: what does "fucked with" mean, and how wrong were they? ## Who Is the Babysitter? - **Ex-combat medic / nursing student**: Army veteran working nights while finishing her EMT certification. Medical training justifies both tenderness (splinting a kid's wrist) and controlled brutality (knowing exactly how much a body can take and how to undo it). Built-in code: a healer who can hurt. - **Retired underworld fixer**: Once known in certain circles as "the Nanny" — a cleaner who made problems disappear. Now genuinely retired, genuinely likes kids. The nickname is the hook. - **Getaway driver / ex-con gone straight**: Knows crews from the inside; knows how they think, where they stash people, who they call. - **Total civilian**: Just a sharp, stubborn college kid. More grounded, but harder to sustain eight chapters of revenge without her feeling implausibly lethal. - **Gender-swap variant**: A huge, gentle "manny," ex-boxer. Fresh subversion, though the phrase culturally evokes the underestimated woman, which powers the fantasy. ## What Do "They" Do? - **Home invasion for a MacGuffin**: Crew hits the house believing it empty; the father secretly laundered money or owes a debt; the real target is a ledger/safe contents. They expect a soft target and find teeth. - **Kidnapping for leverage**: Escalation of the above — when the first attempt fails, they take the child. This converts "defense" into genuine "revenge" and fuels the back half. - **The employers are the villains**: The parents run something vile (trafficking, a cult, a murder) and the sitter finds out. "They" becomes the trusted adults. Delicious irony, heavier and grimier tone. - **Past comes calling**: Someone from her old life recognizes her and tries to blackmail/recruit her by threatening her new normal. Turns the story episodic: one lieutenant per chapter, climbing the ladder to the boss. - **Pure random predation**: They rob her, hurt her, humiliate her — no larger conspiracy. Simplest, but thin fuel for 8,000 words. ## Setting & Structure Options - **One long night**: Real-time-ish, dusk to dawn. Suburban house → city underside → waterfront/rail yard finale. Compressed clock creates momentum and lets dawn serve as natural thematic closure (darkness ends, kids get breakfast). - **Single-location siege**: Halloween-style, all eight chapters in the house, waves of attackers. Pressure-cooker intensity, but risks feeling like "defense," not "revenge." - **Episodic takedown ladder**: Each chapter eliminates one enemy. Clean pulp rhythm; risks repetition at this length. - **Geography**: Keep it tight — house, a pawnshop/contact den, one safehouse, one industrial finale location. Police stay offstage with a stated reason (crews watching schools/hospitals; or her own history makes badges dangerous). ## Tone & Voice - **Hardboiled first person**: Terse, wisecracking, simile-flavored. Maximum pulp flavor, fast characterization. ("The house smelled like crayons and fabric softener, which is how rich people say *safe*.") - **Grindhouse third person**: Cinematic, lurid, chapter titles like drive-in cards. - **Coen-esque dark comedy**: Incompetent crooks vs. hypercompetent sitter. Funny, but comedy can undercut catharsis. - Violence level: pulpy and decisive, not torture-porn. Villains earn it. Dog lives. ## Possible Chapter Skeleton (hybrid version) 1. Quiet night, routine, tells of hidden skill (clocks the parked car, go-bag in the closet). Hook: headlights, a knock. 2. Doorstep duel, forced entry, kitchen fight — she drops one, they flee with the child. Stakes detonate. 3. Triage and interrogation of the wounded invader; learns the debt, the crew, the boss, the deadline. Decides against cops. Legend begins to spread. 4. Gear-up, old contact, trace the plates, first safehouse raid, second prisoner. 5. **Midpoint reversal**: the meet is bait for *her* — the boss recognized the handiwork; personal history revealed (she put away/killed one of theirs years ago). She loses round one, gets hurt. 6. Low point → cold resolve. Patch-up scene, plan built on the crew's greed; fake-ransom gambit with a copied ledger. 7. Waterfront assault: fog, containers, floodlights; she disassembles the crew, rescues the kid mid-chaos, duels the psycho. 8. The boss offers a deal wrapped in the parents' dirty secret. Her choice. Dawn coda: pancakes, returning the kid, a warning delivered to the parents, last line echoing the title. ## Other Ingredients - **The kid**: One child, ~8, precocious, brave — hides, calls 911, throws car keys at a key moment. Not a prop; her small acts enable the rescue. Possibly a dog for heart. - **Villain roster**: The planner (grudge against the father), the psycho (loose cannon, personal vendetta against *her*), the driver, the muscle, and the boss appearing late. Distinct silhouettes allow per-chapter satisfaction. - **Motifs**: Baby monitors as surveillance tech; diaper bag as tactical kit; glitter glue, minivan, bedtime stories repurposed; "lights out" reframed from bedtime ritual to threat. - **Title candidates**: *Night Shift*, *Bedtime for Bastards*, *Milk Money*, *Sit Tight*, *The Wrong House*. - **Endings**: Burn the ledger (protect the kid, damn the parents), keep it as insurance, or mail it anonymously. Surviving crew member retelling her as a ghost story in prison makes a nice bookend. # Reflection The strongest version, I think, is the **hybrid**: home invasion gone wrong (chapters 1–3) converting into a one-night revenge hunt (chapters 4–8). Here's why, weighed against the alternatives. **On the inciting harm.** Mere theft can't carry 8,000 words; the revenge must be proportional and righteous. Kidnapping the child she's responsible for is the right magnitude — it attacks her *identity* (caretaker), not just her body or wallet. That's what makes "they fucked with the wrong babysitter" land as more than a tough-guy quip: they violated the exact thing she exists to protect. I'm wary of the rape-revenge route (too grim, drains the fun) and somewhat wary of the evil-parents route as the *primary* engine — it's a great twist ingredient but a bleak foundation, and it muddies the emotional math of the coda. Better used as seasoning: the father's secret debt explains why the wolves came, adding irony (the "nice family" summoned this) without hijacking the plot. **On structure.** The single-location siege fails the prompt's verb: a siege is endurance, not revenge. The episodic takedown-ladder is tempting for its clean rhythm but needs a wider canvas and more enemies than 8,000 words can individualize — it would collapse into repetitive brawls. The one-long-night structure compresses naturally into eight ~1,000-word chapters, each with one job, one turn, one hook. Crucially, it front-loads the violation (end of chapter 2) so the majority of the story is *proactive* — her hunting them — which is what "revenge tale" requires. **On the midpoint reversal.** Chapter 5 turning the hunt into a trap aimed at *her* solves several problems at once: it prevents "competence porn" monotony (she must lose something and bleed), it welds her hidden past into the plot instead of leaving it as decorative backstory, and it personalizes the villainy so the climax is mutual rather than lopsided. The psycho with a vendetta gives the finale a face. **On voice.** First-person hardboiled is the right register. The prompt itself is a first-person sentence — cocky, colloquial — and the narration should sound like the person who'd say it. Wry understatement also manages the violence: pulpy, decisive, never sadistic. Full parody (Coen mode) would undercut the catharsis; straight thriller would waste the prompt's inherent grin. The sweet spot is a narrator who cracks wise because she's scared and angry, not because nothing hurts. **Risks to manage.** (1) Invincibility fatigue — she needs real costs: injuries that persist, ammunition that runs dry, a plan that fails in chapter 5. (2) The kid as luggage — giving the child agency (and a personality beyond "asleep") pays off emotionally at the rescue and thematically: courage is the family resemblance between sitter and kid. (3) Police plausibility — needs one clean stated reason to stay offstage, ideally tied to the crew's threats or her own record, established early and cheaply. (4) The father's subplot must stay seasoning, never a second plot — it earns its keep as motive and final-chapter irony, nothing more. (5) The ending's ledger choice should stay ambiguous on paper but resolved emotionally: whatever she does with the evidence, the reader must feel she chose *the kid* over everyone's comfort, including her own. **What I'm still weighing.** Whether the protagonist is the combat medic or the retired fixer — the medic offers fresher texture (healing/violence duality) while the fixer offers the juicier nickname; possibly both flavors can merge into one woman with a medical past and an underworld reputation. Also unresolved: the precise nature of her history with the psycho's crew, and whether the final image is the dawn coda, the prison-yard legend bookend, or both stacked. Those are choices for the outline stage — but the spine above feels like the story this prompt is asking for.
Great now let's continue with planning the short story. Output in this format: # Intention <State your formulated intentions for the piece, synthesised from the the parts of the brainstorming session that worked, and avoiding the parts that didn't. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
