Gerald Fairfax occupied the blue bedroom in the guest wing, and Julian had known it for three days without once letting himself think about it directly, the way you don't look at a loose sash-cord until you're ready to climb. He went up the outside at half past one, after the last candles below stairs had gone out — up the ivy on the chapel gable, along the lead flat, boots wrapped in flannel against the slates. Below him the house breathed. Somewhere a gentleman snored in the rhythm of a man who'd lost heavily at cards and drunk evenly about it. Gerald was still down. Gerald always stayed down; it was cheaper than being alone with his accounts. Julian had learned houses from servants and windows, which meant he'd learned them backwards, and it occurred to him — swinging over the parapet into the dressing-room casement Nell would have found in four seconds flat — that she'd have had the dispatch-box open by now and been halfway to the sundial. He was getting slow. Or he was getting careful. With him it had always been difficult to tell the difference, and lately the difference seemed to matter less than the company he kept at this altitude. The box sat on the dressing-table where a gentleman keeps his collar-studs. Locked, of course. It defeated him for six bad minutes — his picks were honest work and nothing better, and every scrape sounded to his own ears like a fire bell — before the lock gave with a click he felt in his teeth. Letters. Nine years of letters, tied in bundles, and the topmost hand stopped his breath before he'd read a word. He knew that hand. Every birthday card of his childhood wore it. *Your mama requires rest, the doctors insist.* The same upright, thrifty script, pressing hard enough to emboss the paper beneath, and here it was writing to *H. Danvers, Esq.*, year upon year. *…the enclosed further testimonies complete the series you hold. I am sure I need not remind you of the value of discretion…* *…my account current, per agreement. To purchases through the stationer Q.: the Fernleigh parcel, incl. the medical paper — settled.* Fernleigh. The ninth of October. Julian sat down slowly on the lid of a cedar chest and read it three times, because the first two times the words rearranged themselves rather than mean what they meant. The Fernleigh commission had been his. Quill had taken Gerald's money to have the Fairfax papers gathered safely into Danvers's keeping, and then — because Quill was Quill, because Quill sold everything twice — had sold the same night's work to a locksmith's daughter with grey eyes and a crooked mend in her sleeve. And Nell, knowing none of it, had carried the certificate of his mother's lunacy straight back through Quill's hands and sold it *home*. Sight unseen. Fifty pounds the parcel. Three years of his own night-work lay itemised in those account pages. Stonecross. The Wetherby letters. Parcel upon parcel, purchased by Danvers at fifty pounds the lot — Danvers, who held everything, whose purse fed Quill, whose commissions fed him. He had been digging his mother's grave deeper all this time and calling it a livelihood, and the men who handed him the spade had never troubled to disguise their handwriting. There was more. There was always more; cruelty keeps excellent records. Renewal papers pending. Removal of the whole series to Wraye Court before Christmas — *before Christmas,* initialled in the margin, dated in another note in Quill's obsequious commercial fist: *Thursday next, if convenient, cart at the lodge.* Voices in the corridor. Julian was behind the screen before thought caught up with action, folded into the gap between it and the cold window, his bad shoulder wedged against the frame. The door opened on lamplight and brandy-warm air, and his uncle came in talking — to Lady Hartwell's brother, a pleasant, half-seen bulk — and the talk was of nothing, of drainage and pheasants, until it wasn't. "—and Danvers's charges go up again, mark you. Custody isn't cheap. Sometimes I think—" A pause; the clink of a decanter. "Sometimes I think it would be simpler to have done with the woman altogether. But no. Papers everywhere. One must do these things *thoroughly*, that's the whole art of it." A laugh, comfortable, signet rings knocking the glass decanter. "Margaret was never strong. She'd have cost me her portion one way or another. This way at least it's orderly." *It would be simpler to have done with the woman altogether.* Said in the voice that had read him fairy tales. Julian stood in the dark with his arm pressed to the window-frame and discovered that rage, fully arrived, is a very quiet thing — quieter than the decanter, quieter than the door closing — and that his hands were steady, and would stay steady, and that this was somehow the worst discovery of the night. Then the house slept, and he was out of the window and along the leads with the box's knowledge sitting in him like swallowed stones, and Nell Croft was crouched by the chimney stack in a shawl the colour of soot, watching him come with an expression he couldn't read at any distance. "You've been crying," she said. Not accusing. Not kind. Simply filing it. "I've been wind-blown." He reached the stack, sat, found the lead cold through his trousers and didn't care. "How long have you been up here?" "Since your candle showed under his door. I survey rooflines." A pause. "I also copied the still-room book on Thursday." She passed him a sheet of paper, folded small. Weekly entries, years of them, in the apothecary's round commercial hand: *Tinctura Opii, two drachms, charged to Mr. Gerald Fairfax.* "Somebody drinks that medicine every night. It isn't the somebody it's prescribed for, because it isn't prescribed at all. It's ordered." She looked out across the moonlit park. "I thought you should see it from the money side. You've been seeing it from the son's side alone, I expect. It reads worse both ways together." He looked at her then — really looked, the way she'd caught him looking at parapets — and understood how thoroughly he'd had her wrong. He had filed her as cold goods: competent, expensive, loyal to fees. And she had spent the week following a living woman through a laundry-book and an apothecary's ledger, quietly, without telling even herself, perhaps, that that was what she was doing. "They move everything to Wraye Court Thursday," he said. "After that it's his ground, walls he owns, servants he owns. Before Thursday, it's a cart on a road." "Before Thursday," Nell agreed. Between the chimney stacks there was a moment — the park silver below, her breath smoking, her hand flat on the lead between them not quite touching his — when something leaned forward in him like a man at a rail. She didn't move away. That was the whole of it, and it was enormous. From the orangery below, at the top of its small lungs, a peacock screamed like a murdered soul. They broke apart laughing — badly, helplessly, two professionals undone by poultry — and the laughter shook loose whatever had gone rigid in him since the screen, and when they could speak he heard his own voice come out level at last. "Together, then. Properly. No sundials." "No sundials," she said. "And Julian — we'll want Quill. Turned, or blindfolded. Nobody moves a cart past Quill's counter without his arithmetic." Below them the peacock screamed again, triumphant, having saved or ruined them, it was impossible to say which.

The chalk told her first. She hadn't meant to go to the lodge at all. Surveying was a sickness with her — count your exits twice, her father used to say, and mean it about doors, about men, about life — and on Thursday night, unable to sleep with the still-room copy folded under her mattress like a hot coal, she went out over the laundry-yard wall and along the frozen spinney to look at the lodge yard and count. Two carts. One was Rokeby's, lent. The other stood under canvas with its tailboard chalked in a clerk's tidy commercial fist: *FRIDAY. FIVE O'CLOCK. TWO HORSES. SEVEN PARCELS + ONE CRATE — W.C.* Tomorrow. Not Thursday-next, not some comfortable horizon — *tomorrow*, and Julian had read the date loose from a bundle of correspondence and she had built three days of certainty on his arithmetic. She stood in the black fern-shadow with her breath icing on her collar and felt the old familiar thing rise in her, the thing that had climbed out of a sold workshop and never gone back down: *then I'll do it myself.* His candle was out. The guest-wing stairs had a footman on them now, since Fernleigh, since the business at Stonecross got talked about in servants' halls she wasn't supposed to hear. She stood in the dark under his window a long moment, telling herself the practical reasons — waking him meant the footman, the footman meant questions, questions meant Mrs. Roper — and hearing underneath them the true reason, which wore her father's apron and had taught a boy called Sam Petch every wire and ward in the county because trusting him had seemed like the same thing as loving him. She had come home from market that last morning with herrings wrapped in newspaper, and read the empty racks, and understood that everything she had ever taught anybody was a weapon pointed at her back by the time she turned round. She knocked twice on the sill beneath Julian's dark window. For luck. Then she went to the lodge alone. The yard cat had got into the cart and objected violently to eviction, yowling like a soul in a sack, and she stood rigid in freezing straw for a full minute while lamplight crossed the lodge curtains. The deal box was iron-bound and padlocked, and her picks whispered on the shackle — too long, too loud, too many strokes. When the lodge door opened she flattened under the chassis between the axles and lay in the rut-ice looking at the underside of the world until boots crunched away again. She got the hasp half-turned. Not open. Half. Enough to leave bright metal showing through the padlock's patience where no file had any business being. Seven parcels, tied, labelled in the clerk's hand. One crate, longer, chalked across the lid with three heavy crosses — *XXX* — and beneath, smaller: *DANVERS — NOTHING KEEPS ITS VALUE PAST THE SEASON. BURN AT CHRISTMAS.* She lay with her cheek against frost-burnt oak and put the whole of it away behind her eyes, parcel by parcel, cross by cross, the way her father had put joint measurements away, and then the east went the colour of dirty pewter and she ran. Back over the wall the easy ways were bolted — scullery, coal-door, all the honest servants' mouths shut till six. So she went up, because going up was what she had instead of prayer: the laundry-court wall to the lead flat, along to the linen-store casement whose hinge she had oiled her first week out of sheer incurable decency, and it rose for her without a sound, and she was in bed with her boots drying in the fender before the yard bell rang. Mrs. Roper held her court at nine, in the housekeeper's room, with the keys laid out on a baize cloth like instruments before surgery. Every lock in the gift of the house had been walked round since dawn. The padlock at the lodge sat on the cloth now, scratched silver-bright at the shackle. And two women, said Mrs. Roderick the cook, two women had been abroad before the bell — a veiled figure on the drive in the mist, and Susan Ash, up from the still-room at five to fire the copper, as she did Thursdays, as she'd done all autumn. "She's quick," said Mrs. Roper, not unkindly, which was worse. "Quick girls get above the still-room. Keys walk when girls get above themselves." She looked down the line of them, starch and terror. "Susan Ash. Your books, please. You'll go up to the village this afternoon." It took Julian until noon to reach her — she saw him come down the back stair with his hat actually in his hand like a petition, and heard him spend himself in the housekeeper's room, gently, honourably, a gentleman's plain word that he had himself passed Miss Ash at her lawful work at five and could swear to her character. And she heard Mrs. Roper accept the word, and add a line of it to Susan's paper — *honest, if headstrong* — and dismiss her anyway, because a scratched lock wants a body, and bodies are cheapest at the bottom. He found her at the linen press at dusk, folding other women's tablecloths with hands that wanted breaking things. "We said together," he said. Quiet. The quiet was the frightening part. "Not together-when-you-decide. Together." "The cart was tomorrow. Your Thursday was wrong, and I wasn't going to stand in the dark watching your window while seven parcels rolled away to Wraye Court." "So you told me at breakfast?" Nothing. "Or you spent my shoulder's worth of trust and went, and got half a hasp, and cost a girl with no family her bread." He stopped. Started again, lower. "Do you know what you are to me in all this? Not a colleague. I laced my hands for you at Fernleigh and my shoulder sang for a fortnight and you never once asked after it, and I understood — I *understood*, Nell — that in your arithmetic I'm a ladder. Useful at a height. Left where it falls." "That's not—" "You stood in that room today and let them take her rather than say one inconvenient sentence." He put his hat on, carefully, correctly. "I've been bought and used by experts. I know the feel of it. I'd hoped you were different goods." Snow started as he went down the stair — the year's first, fat and idle, settling on the leads. From the dressing-room window Nell watched the second cart of the day come round for the village: one box, one bundle, one girl sitting very straight with her character-paper in her lap like a ticket for somewhere that didn't exist. *Windows is where the learning lives,* her father said, and she looked at the glass, at her own ghost laid over the drive, and knocked twice on the sill. For luck. It didn't feel like enough.

Finding Nell Croft in daylight proved harder than any window he'd ever taken. She wasn't at her lodgings — *engaged*, said her landlady, with the special firmness reserved for gentlemen callers — so he tried Mrs. Bagshaw's sewing premises, where he was mistaken for the new tailor's man within four minutes of arriving, handed a widow's grey skirt, and ordered to hold it steady and stop breathing on the pins. He held it. For ten minutes. There were men at Hartwell whose word moved markets, and he stood being glared at by a seventy-year-old widow over a hem, because putting the skirt down would have meant explaining himself, and explaining himself would have meant the widow fainting. "Not you," Nell said at last, taking the skirt off him. "The other tailor's lad. Though you've the wrists for it." In the yard, rain beginning, she heard him out with her arms folded. "I've placed Susan," he said. "My aunt keeps a laundry school near Harrogate — training situation, honest mistress, her own attic. I paid the premium myself, and I asked the matron to keep it quiet until—" "I know." He stopped. "Mrs. Bagshaw had it from the still-room girl by Saturday," Nell said. "Sideways. The way servants get everything." She looked at the middle button of his coat. "You did it kindly, and you did it quiet, and I grant you the quiet was meant well. But I stood in that yard and watched her cart go, and then a fortnight passed, and I learned what you'd done like a servant learns things. You bought her a situation the way you'd tip a groom, Julian. What you never did was turn round and spend one plain sentence on me." "I'm spending it now." "You are." She was quiet a moment. "I've written to her. I'll travel at Christmas and see her myself, and pay my own account, because it's mine to pay." She put her hand on the yard door. "So. We're colleagues again. Colleagues." The word was colder than the rain. He wore it out to the street. They gave Wraye Court three nights of watching, which was becoming liturgy. Sir Hugo Danvers kept a compact grey house behind park walls — new-built, mean-windowed, a strongbox pretending to be architecture — and came down to it for the season with two footmen imported from London and a housekeeper who signed for everything twice. The consignment had arrived the week before; Julian had it from the carrier's boy, who had it from everybody. Seven parcels and a crate, delivered to the long gallery. The south front was glass — a conservatory the width of the house, ridged and dripping, joined to the leads above by a parapet walk. Below it ran the only ivy on the estate, twenty years old, her father's catechism said trust old ivy, never young, and Nell went up it first because she always tested doctrine personally. Six feet up, a limb the thickness of her wrist came away in her hand like stewed celery. Frost in November, then three days of warm rain: the freeze had split every stem and the thaw had rotted what the splitting spared. She swung, caught the frame, hung by her fingers over black shrubbery, and felt Julian's grip close on her forearm — his bad shoulder taking her weight without complaint, the way it had at Fernleigh, the way she had never once asked after. "Cames, not panes," she said, when she could speak levelly. "We go over the glass. Weight on the metal joins, never the panes. Like ladder rungs." "On wet glass." "On wet glass," she agreed, and went first, felt soles squeaking, arms out, a spider on the roof of a lantern, rain Needling her neck. Every window he had ever entered had been somebody's grief, Julian thought, following her with his heart in his ears — his mother's most of all — and he laid his palm flat on the cold pane and told this one it was going to be different. Inside, the long gallery was a museum of other people's ruin. Map-cases, cabinets, framed letters under glass, albums labelled in a collector's copperplate. They found the crate in the corner, stencilled *W.C.*, and took the Fairfax series entire — and were still at it when the front door bell went below, deep and domestic and appalling. Lights bloomed through the house. Danvers, back early from London with guests; orders passing along corridors; shutters going up room by room like eyelids. Sealed in, they did the only professional thing available, which was nothing. They sat behind the screen of a marquetry cabinet for five hours while the household dreamed around them, and in the fifth hour, by shielded match-light, Julian read. His mother's last letter to Danvers was in the bundle. The writing started upright and finished looping off the page — the laudanum legible in every line — *…they tell me Brighton is very gay this year. Do the dogs remember me? Tell Julian the sea is nothing like…* It ended mid-word. He read it twice and set it back exactly square with its fellows, which was the only prayer he knew. Then the instruction — Gerald's standing letter, the keystone, custody and renewal and *burn at Christmas* — and Julian stopped, and smiled, and it was not a pleasant smile. "The crest is right," he whispered. "The wax is wrong. That's a wafer — machine-cut. My uncle seals in wax thick as a thumbprint and licks his thumb, the vulgarian. This is a fair copy. Clerk's hand, fresh ink, old envelope." He looked at her across the shielded light. "Quill sold us the commission twice. Of course he kept what can't be sold twice. The original never left him." Rain eased towards dawn. They went out over roofs slick as fish backs, down ivy that held this time — doctrine vindicated by spite, Nell said — and dropped into the kitchen garden, and stood in the doorway of the gardener's bothy, soaked, breath smoking, his palms scored red where the glass-cames had bitten. Without a word she tore a strip from her petticoat hem and bound his hands, knotting each turn, checking each knot twice — her habit, but gentled now into something else, or the same thing grown another face. "There," she said, meaning the bandage, meaning nothing of the kind. "Fernleigh," he said. "Quill winters there. We go back to the beginning." Above the hedges, grey light. Somewhere a wren started up, absurdly loud for its size, as if the whole morning belonged to it.

Frost had got into Fernleigh's ivy, and Nell did not trust it an inch. She went up the drainpipe instead, old cast iron, her father's generation of casting, solid as churchwork — and found the dressing-room casement changed. New catch. Bright brass among sixty years of weathered fittings, put in since October. He'd noticed, then. Somewhere in the county a locksmith had been paid three shillings, and somewhere above it a collector had walked his own corridors counting wear the way she counted exits. It didn't stop her. A sash was a sash: she eased the staff bead from the frame with her father's marking-knife, thin blade kissing the paint, took the cord off its pulley, and had the lower sash up and herself inside on the strength of her forearms alone, silent, the bead back in its groove behind her. *Any fool can use a door.* Her father's voice, faint, amused, from wherever dead joiners kept their shavings. She knocked twice on the sill. Old habit. It wasn't luck she wanted tonight; it was the feeling of finishing something. Below, on the ground floor, Mrs. Tice's candle burned in its usual window. Nell still knew its hours. Some knowledge you couldn't give back. The trouble was that the study was already lit. Voices — low, two of them, one wheedling. She signed to Julian and they folded themselves into the gallery's winter shrouds, behind a dust-sheeted frame that had hung over Lady somebody's spaniels, and listened through six feet of cold air. "—appreciates, sir, that's the point. Land depreciates, paper appreciates. You taught me that." Quill's voice, oiled and frayed at once, a man counting aloud to keep from screaming. "The original instruction — Mr. Gerald's own hand, witnessed, sealed — that's not stock, sir. That's the mould all the coin's struck from." "It is a liability," said a voice Nell hadn't heard before and knew at once. Dry, unhurried, old. A voice like paper kept too long in a good drawer. "I am offering you eighty pounds for a document that hangs us both, and you are quoting me appreciation." "A hundred and twenty, sir, and I'll winter easy." A pause. When the old voice came again it was worse for the pause. "You have been drinking my sherry, Quill, and lying to me for a decade, and I have permitted both, because you were useful and because I collect. But I do not pay twice for one thing. You taught me *that*." A rustle — kid gloves, Nell thought, spotting the sound. "We conclude at eighty, or we conclude differently." "And the — other parties, sir." Quill again, quick now, frightened, selling the only goods he had left. "Because there's been enquiry. After the Wraye business. Certain persons asking after certain parcels, and a man in my position must consider—" Nell looked at Julian. Julian stepped out from behind the spaniels as if the gallery had invited him, and she went with him, because the whole architecture of the evening had just changed shape and the only way through was forward. "Gentlemen," he said. What happened next took eleven minutes, and Nell spent most of them watching Sir Hugo Danvers decide not to be afraid. He was smaller than his voice. Old, neat, spotted hands folded on the desk, a jeweller's glass hanging round his neck on a ribbon like a schoolboy's medal. He looked at Julian for a long moment, then at her, then back, and something in the look priced them both to the shilling. "You are the son," he said to Julian. Not a question. "Margaret's boy. You favour her round the eyes." And to Nell, mildly: "And you are the tradeswoman. Sit down, both of you. My legs are seventy-one years old and I don't rise for burglars." They didn't sit. Julian laid it out levelly — the copies taken at Wraye, the still-room book, the chemist's direction in a gentleman's hand — and the insurance beneath it: papers lodged with Mr. Pell, the barrister, and sealed summaries sitting with two London weeklies that fed on peers the way Goliath fed on ham. Harm or hindrance, and it printed. All of it. The certificates, the dosing, the custody fees, Gerald's comfortable voice saying *one must do these things thoroughly.* "I'd ask you to verify the copies," Julian finished. "You'll want to." Danvers did want to. He read with the glass screwed into his eye, turning pages with one gloved fingertip, and Nell watched a lifetime of collecting look itself over and find the work honest. Something moved in his face that was not admiration exactly. Inventory, maybe. An acquisition he hadn't planned on. "Pell drafts tightly," he said at last. "Who chose him?" "He came with the family," Julian said. "Like the lunacy." Silence. The candle spat. And Danvers set the pages square, drew a memorandum-book towards him, and wrote — unhurried, copperplate — a draft. Fifty pounds. He blotted it and slid it across with two fingers. "For your trouble," he said. "An ending, neatly done. Take it and the matter closes tonight, and you may think well of yourselves at Christmas." Nell picked it up. Fifty pounds. Forty-one pounds ten sat under a loose brick in her lodgings, and past it, a room of her own with a south-facing window, and past that a life where nobody's word was mortgage on her. She could feel the number in her hands like heat. She tore it. Once, twice, four times, her fingers steadier than she'd any right to expect, and let the pieces fall on his blotter. "No," she said. Something flickered behind the old eyes — she never learned what, and suspected it wasn't respect. He gathered the pieces, squared their edges out of pure habit, and consigned them to the grate. "Then we understand the position," he said. "No harm, no printing. Your mother goes to her sister's by spring, Fairfax, on medical recommendation I shall be pleased to arrange, since I arrange such things. My trade continues. Yours does not." He rose, joints cracking like green wood, and paused beside Nell on his way to the door. His glance fell, precisely, to her left sleeve. "The mend's better than October's," he said. "Still badly. A craftsman signs her work, madam, whether she means to or not. I never forget a customer." And he went, gloves creaking, up the corridor, and they heard Mrs. Tice's door, and the stair, and nothing more. "There's sherry," said Quill desperately, into the ringing quiet. "It's the vicar's. He won't miss one glass." Nobody had any. Quill unlocked the front door for them himself at dawn — the first time either of them had left Fernleigh like Christians — and stood wringing his shiny cuffs in the grey light, promising reform in the tones of a man promising it hourly. The lawn was silvered stiff. Rooks argued in the elms. At the bottom of the steps Nell stopped, and turned, and knocked twice on the doorpost — knuckle on painted oak, gently, the way you'd thank it. "What's that?" Julian asked. "Old habit," she said, and walked out through the door, and didn't look back at the window that had taught her.

In March, Julian Fairfax caught himself, for the third morning running, looking at the side window of Croft's shop instead of the door. Old habits died hard, and his had died hardest. He stood in the lane with his hat straight and his gloves on, a respectable gentleman presenting himself at a tradesman's premises at nine of a weekday morning, and his eye had gone automatically to the casement over the yard — low sill, worn catch, ivy on the boundary wall — the way a reformed drunkard's eye goes down the gin palace steps. He laughed at himself, quietly, and knocked at the door like a Christian. Inside smelled of oak shavings and raw paint. The benches were her father's pattern; she'd bought two of them second-hand from a cabinetmaker going under, and he had watched her scrape thirty years of another man's glue off them with a Cabinet scraper and something on her face that he had learned, over the winter, not to name aloud. "You're early," Nell said, not turning from the bench. "You're painting." "I'm painting." She set down the brush. On the bench lay the sign, bare pine, one word dried black at the left end: *CROFT.* The rest waited. A good deal had happened since Fernleigh, most of it paperwork. Mr. Pell's drafts had worked their quiet magic; Gerald, devout these nine weeks, had signed what he was told and released his nephew's portion, and Julian had sent the allowance back twice before asking Pell to pay it instead into his mother's comfort. Quill had sent the thirty-five guineas in February with a note apologising to both parties separately, in different hands, and a case of sherry marked *from a friend*. And that morning, before he'd set out, a letter had come from Brighton in a hand he had known all his life and mourned for nine years — upright again now, thrifty, pressing hard enough to emboss. *Dear J,* it began. *Brighton is nothing like so grand as its reputation. The dogs, I am told, are dead, which is a mercy, as they were dreadful snobs. My sister's house has windows that open, and I am allowed to open them myself, which I do, often, for no reason at all.* *Mr. Danvers calls on Thursdays with accounts for me to audit. I believe I frighten him.* *Your loving Mama.* He had read it four times, and the fourth time had had to sit down among the packing cases, and now here he was at a bench with paint fumes in his nose, about to ruin his life in the conventional manner. "Susan writes," Nell said, wiping her hands. "Her hands are in soda all day and she's proud of the blisters. She asks after you." A pause. "She spells your name with two esses." "She would." "You've come about articles," she said. It wasn't a guess. Mrs. Bagshaw had told everyone, Mrs. Bagshaw having told the county. "Seven years' indentures, at your age. You'd be thirty-five at journeyman. People would laugh." "People laugh at me in three counties already. I'd sooner it were for a trade." "And what trade would that be, precisely? Your hands are—" She stopped. Looked at them, laid palm-down on her clean bench. The glass-cames had scarred them at Wraye in November; the marks had faded to two pale ridges. "Your hands are improving," she amended, which from Nell was practically a sonnet. "I know every house in this county from the outside, Nell. Every weak sill, every bribed dog, every catch fitted by a man paid three shillings to hurry. You know them from the inside — the timbers, the ironwork, the making. Half the county's houses would fall to us in an afternoon." He turned his hat brim in his fingers. "We'd stop them falling at all. Locks fitted, sashes secured, advice given free to anyone who can't pay for it. It's honest work that's only dishonest work stood on its head." "Partner," she said. He blinked. "I beg your pardon?" "Not apprentice. Not clerk. Partner. Your capital's your head for houses; mine's the bench. Books open between us, drawings signed by both, quarrels settled over the bench and never in the street." Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write a short story set in Wales. Task: write a short story over several chapters. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. Over the course of the first scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. # Brainstorming ## Core Premise Angles The prompt gives us the inciting incident (paparazzi duck-in) and the central dynamic (charm vs. apparent immunity). The open question is *what the story builds from there*. Wide-net options: 1. **The Role-Research Engine** — He returns under a pretext: he's preparing to play a rare-books dealer and needs coaching. Gives structured reasons for repeated meetings, puts her expertise in demand, and plants a betrayal landmine (the role may be a lie, or half a lie). 2. **The Production Threat** — His film company wants to lease/buy her block for a location shoot; she's organizing local resistance. Enemies-to-lovers energy, but heavy machinery for 8,000 words. 3. **The Shared Past (light version)** — She recognizes him instantly and pretends not to. Or deeper: she secretly loved one obscure indie film he made at 24, the one role he assumes nobody remembers. This recasts her "immunity" as defense of an ideal rather than indifference — she's not immune to *him*, she's immune to *Rhys Blackwood™*. 4. **The Seasonal Countdown** — Autumn-to-Christmas structure; his shoot wraps December 20; ticking clock, cozy register, market-fair finale. These can hybridize: Variant 1 as the spine, Variant 3 as the emotional twist, Variant 4 as the calendar. ## The Actor - **Name options**: Rhys Blackwood (stage name), born Gareth Price in the Valleys — a Welshman estranged from Wales, rebranded. The gap between names *is* the theme. Alternatives: Kit Deveraux, Theo Kestrel, Dominic Vale. - **The fragile ego, sourced**: child actor with a father-manager who spent the money; a divorce scandal the tabs authored; a career built on being "likable" after a director told him at nineteen he was "nothing but charm, lad, so sell it." He flirts by reflex because approval is the only currency he's ever been paid in. - **Voice**: fast, superlative-laden, deflects with jokes, narrates himself in third person when performing ("Rhys Blackwood always says…"). Crucial tell: **when he stops being funny, he's being sincere.** The jokes are a gauge the reader learns to read. - **Sample register**: *"You've got the look. The 'I couldn't care less' look. Do you know how rare that is? People train for years for that look."* / *"That'll be seven forty."* / *"…I'm in the biggest franchise on earth."* / *"Bags are extra. We're green here."* ## The Bookstore Owner - **Name options**: Elin, Nerys, Seren, Carys — with a Welsh surname: Pryce, Bowen, Vaughan. Late 30s. - **Backstory options**: fled a London publishing career after burnout; came home to nurse a parent and stayed; inherited the shop from a grandfather; a quietly abandoned manuscript in the back-office drawer. - **Why she's immune (surface)**: she doesn't own a telly; or she's seen his films and found him "technically proficient but emotionally dishonest"; or she's simply met confident men before and catalogued them. - **The hidden flutter, externalized**: since we want dialogue-forward prose, her interiority needs *tells*. Best candidate: **when she's rattled, her Welsh slips out** — "Duw annwyl" muttered under her breath when he smiles; she code-switches back to English the way you smooth a wrinkled page. Other tells: mis-shelving, over-wiping the counter, recommending a book three shelves away from where it lives. - **Voice**: clipped, literal, weaponized politeness, book-trade metaphors. Answers questions with questions. Deadpan Welsh humor. ## Setting - **Hay-on-Wye** — the famous "town of books." Thematically perfect, possibly too expected; also too touristy to plausibly lack star-spotters. - **Invented coastal Ceredigion/Cardiganshire town** — e.g., **Aberdewi**: colored terraces, harbor, rain on glass, gulls, one pub, a fish van, a grapevine faster than Twitter. Keeps the paps plausible (nearby epic-fantasy shoot in Eryri) and the community intimate. - **Bookshop name**: **Yr Ail Argraff** — "The Second Impression." Double meaning available in English signage: *Second Impressions.* Second chances, second acts, and the whole point that his first impression is worthless to her. This feels like a gift; I'd hate to waste it. - **Shop texture**: a ladder on rails, a leaking skylight, marginalia in the secondhand stock, a shop cat (**Brân**, black, traitorous — loves him immediately, which infuriates her). ## Structural Devices Pool - **Alternating POV per chapter**: odd chapters hers (cool exterior / flustered interior), even chapters his (charm machine / private panic). # On Writing This Like a Human ## How a human writer would likely approach this brief A human taking this prompt would probably start somewhere other than structure. They'd start with a voice they've heard — a specific fast-talking man they once got cornered by at a party — or a place they know well enough to be annoyed by. They'd likely have one scene in their head they're writing *toward* (here, probably the lock-in, or the harvest supper), and they'd build backwards from it, letting earlier chapters exist mostly to earn that scene. They would not design five interlocking motifs. They'd have two, maybe, and one of those would be accidental — something they noticed on draft three and kept. A human would also trust boredom. Famous actors, in reality, are mostly tired and mildly dull; paparazzi work is mostly a cold man eating chips in a car for six hours. A human writer leans into that undignified texture. An LLM reaches for the glamorous version — lens glints, moped engines, dramatic near-exposure — because drama feels like story. But the *small* version is both truer and fresher: the menace is real but shabby, and shabby menace is scarier and funnier than cinematic menace. Most importantly, a human would resist explaining the central paradox. The prompt's engine is "immune on the surface, secretly flustered underneath." An LLM solves this elegantly — one tidy reveal ("she recognized him; she's seen his obscure indie eleven times") that retroactively organizes all her behavior. A human would leave her motive a braid of impure strands: professional contempt (she *manufactured* likability for a living), simple fatigue, attraction she's suppressing, the fact she's having a bad week, and yes, possibly that old indie film — but as one thread, not a master key. The elegant single explanation is an LLM tell. It's too satisfying. Real people don't know why they're flustered. ## General LLM failings relevant here **Symmetry sickness.** The deepest problem with my plan. Count the interlocking patterns: Pryce/Price surname rhyme; "Be good value, lad" / "Just make him likable" sentence-rhyme; a collapsed film literally titled *Marginalia* so the trade headline lands as metaphor; rain-and-skylight as relationship barometer opening and closing the story; chapter 8 explicitly mirroring chapter 1 (bell, rain, nobody chasing); the manager echoing the father; the interrupted kiss happening *twice*. That's not motif, that's a crossword. When everything pays off, nothing feels discovered — it feels executed. The reader starts spotting the machinery, and worse, starts predicting beats. A human keeps one or two of these and lets the others die on the cutting-room floor. The test for each: does it *cost* anything, or does it just reward attention? **The full bow.** My current trajectory ends with: roof repaired, gesture understood, career direction clarified, town charmed, cat vindicated, love confirmed, final image rhyming with the first. That's seven resolutions in 1,000 words. Genre romance promises emotional resolution, yes — but not *total* resolution. Something should remain broken, pending, or absurd. Ideally the skylight. **Tennis-match banter.** "Primarily dialogue" invites the airless version: two witty people exchanging perfectly responsive, fully grammatical volleys, each winning 50% of exchanges. Humans interrupt, mishear, answer different questions, repeat themselves, go quiet, land jokes that flop. Her deadpan shouldn't always *land* — sometimes he genuinely can't tell if she's joking, and neither can the reader. Silence needs to be a playable beat. And she should win some exchanges by simply *not responding*, which is more human and more devastating than a comeback. **Beat-labeling.** My chapter plan contains stage directions like "low point," "burn the playbook," "almost-kiss dies." Written mechanically toward these, you get scenes that are connective tissue — logistics montages ("then he went home, then the manager called") stretched between set-piece emotional moments. At 1,000 words per chapter there is no room for summary; every chapter must be one or two *live scenes*. Chapters 2 and 6 are the highest-risk for montage-itis. **Therapy-shaped arcs.** "Charm as addiction → seen clearly → burns the playbook" is a recovery narrative with clean stages. Humans relapse partially and embarrassingly. Worse: chapter 7's "no charm allowed" risks him performing sincerity *perfectly* — which is just charm wearing a hair shirt. His honest attempt should be slightly cringe, slightly too much, possibly a abandoned speech in his coat pocket. The intimate moment should be her laughing *at* him, and the laughter being the door opening. **Instrumental side characters.** Kitty Shaw (a predatory journalist named *Kitty* — straight out of cozy-mystery central casting) and the manager are currently devices with legs. The tabloid thread also arrives on schedule and detonates on schedule. A human lets the exposé *fizzle*: the town barely cares, the nan is delighted, the story dies in a week. Subverting the expected drama is warmer and truer. **Setting-as-costume.** Current Welshness inventory: rain, gulls, R.S. Thomas, "Duw annwyl," a chapel-adjacent harvest supper. That's a postcard. And here's the big miss: **the freehold purchase has enormous real-world charge I completely failed to register.** Wealthy outsiders buying up Welsh property — holiday homes, anglicization, "Nid yw Cymru ar werth" — is a living cultural wound, with actual protest history. Rhys buying her building via his company isn't just a personal-wound echo (money as love, his father); locally it reads as exactly the grotesque gesture a rich English-language celebrity would make. Elin wouldn't just be hurt that he used money — she'd be *mortified on behalf of her whole street*, and the town's assumption of the worst would arrive faster than any facts. This makes his gesture wronger, the repair harder, and the story finally *about* something. The plan stumbled into gold and treated it as a plot beat. ## Specific critiques of the stated Intention - **Her tell (Welsh leaking when rattled) will become a metronome.** Readers will clock it by chapter 3 and start ticking boxes: flustered = Welsh appears. Keep it, but starve it — twice, maybe three times total, at unexpected moments — and add a *contradictory* tell: when truly flustered she's ruder, overcorrecting into harshness, mis-pricing books. Blushing-equivalents are stock; pettiness under pressure is human. - **His tell ("when he stops being funny, he's sincere") is excellent and should be protected** — but it needs failure states. Sometimes he's funny AND sincere. Sometimes he uses the sincerity voice manipulatively, because rogues do that, and she should catch him at it once. - **The "rogue" label is undercooked.** Divorce scandal plus charm-addiction makes him wounded, not roguish. He needs a concrete rakish incident in his file — an on-set romance that ended someone else's engagement, a flirtation-with-a-journalist-to-kill-a-story that backfired — something that makes "rogue" a reputation, not a mood. - **"Eleven times" is LLM-cute.** A statistic engineered for charm. Better: a pirated DVD with a cracked case she's never replaced because replacing it would mean admitting something. Objects with shame attached beat round numbers. - **The returned-deed-with-margin-note gesture is twee.** It's the story complimenting its own motif. Her rejection should be blunter and less photogenic — maybe she doesn't respond at all for days, and *that's* the reply. ## Specific critiques of the Chapter Plan - **Chapter 2 is a logistics chapter wearing a scene's clothes.** Homework, wrapping lessons, surveyor's quote — that's a training montage. Needs one live interpersonal collision at its center. - **Two interrupted kisses is a formula.** The lens-glint (ch3) and the phone call (ch4) are the same beat in different coats. The phone-call version is far better (it's about *him*, his reflex, his choice — an interruption from inside, not outside). Cut or radically vary the first. - **Strict odd/even POV alternation is elegant and mechanical.** It will make chapters predictable in function: her chapters perform restraint, his perform confession. Either break it once meaningfully (stay with Elin for the opening third of a Rhys chapter, watching him through the shop glass) or keep the system but vary internal architecture wildly — one chapter starting mid-argument, one built around a single continuous scene, one with a letter embedded. - **Chapter titles "Page Nine" and "The Freehold" are plot-logistics titles.** Resonance or nothing. - **The silence week in chapter 6 is montage bait**, and his "effortless charm, feels nothing" hotel/garage vignettes are the addiction-narrative on rails. One of those scenes, done fully, beats four sketches. - **Kitty Shaw's armful-of-books purchase is a coincidence doing heavy lifting.** Acceptable at this length, but she should want the book for a *reason* that characterizes her — she's shopping for material, and the marginalia is professionally interesting to her. Predators collect. ## Brainstorm: moves that would make it more human **Cut the motif count to two.** Survivors: the marginalia correspondence (it's the spine — it connects title, theme, media thread, and gives dialogue-heavy scenes a visual second channel), and weather — *but* recast the leak as an economic problem (ruined stock, money she hasn't got), not a symbol. Demote or kill: Pryce/Price (at most let a *background* character notice it and get told to shut up), the *Marginalia* title (decide: either the headline coincidence is kept as dark comedy and never commented on, or rename the film something dumber and more realistic — development-hell projects have terrible names), the nan's *Steel Tide* poster (one-line runner only, never plot). **Make the freehold culturally loaded.** Research-adjacent texture: second-home resentment, a community land trust, the town assuming the worst, maybe an old boy at the pub who remembers the '80s. Resolution options worth weighing: he transfers it to a community trust (risky — savior-adjacent again); he sells it to her for £1 through a bewildered solicitor (funny, humiliating for him, right-sized); or the *town* intervenes before he can fix it and she has to defend him to her own neighbors — which flips the rescue dynamic beautifully. **Let the tabloid story fizzle.** One freelancer, cold and bored. Town reaction: nan thrilled, Mari selling screenshots' worth of gossip, everyone else shrugging. The real damage is private (Elin's guilt over page nine), not public spectacle. This kills the cliché *and* focuses the wound where it belongs. **Break the confession register.** Wounds exchanged as anecdote-plus-joke, never monologue. No therapy vocabulary anywhere. His father story should come out sideways, attached to something concrete — a receipt, a trophy, a specific Saturday — and he should try to turn it into a bit halfway through and fail. **Give the manager one humanizing beat.** He's been managing a fragile man for years; let him be tired and fond, not just a plot pump. One line of genuine care makes his warning land harder. **Vary the flustered choreography.** Pricing-gun errors, wrong change, recommending a book from the wrong shelf, sudden rudeness, over-long silence while she looks at his mouth then aggressively dusts something. Never the same tell twice running. **Ending candidates (to choose from later, not now):** 1. The Tuesday-routine ending — no kiss on-page, last image is domestic: two coffees, an argument about shelf order, the leak still dripping into a bucket they've stopped noticing. 2. Kiss happens early in ch8 and the remainder is aftermath — nan walking in, Brân on his lap, deeply unglamorous. 3. Unanswered margin note as final line — she's holding the pencil. Stop. 4. He leaves for a shoot; the last exchange is bad texting, which for these two is somehow a promise. 5. The freehold argument-as-foreplay ending — they're fighting happily about paint colors for a shop he no longer owns and she now does. My instinct: honor the genre contract (this is a romance; readers have paid for hope) but delay and de-glamorize the physical payoff, ending on commitment-of-intent rather than consummation, with one thread left literally dripping. ## Open decisions to carry forward Which two motifs survive; whether the film-title coincidence stays; how culturally explicit the freehold thread gets; whether to break POV pattern once; which interruption dies; ending shape. None decided today — but the direction of travel is clear: fewer gears showing, smaller stakes played bigger, bigger stakes played smaller, and at least one thing left unfixed.

Gareth was on stage at six (third shepherd, ad-libbed, got the biggest laugh), Welsh-language children's telly at eight (*Gareth Bach*, still occasionally airs at 6am to his horror), a BBC kids' serial at eleven, and a family adventure film at thirteen that actually made money. The money bought a conservatory extension that was never finished — the brick shell stood open to the sky for six years until Ken sold the house. By sixteen the account was empty; by seventeen Gareth understood the account had never been his. At nineteen, a London casting director told him: *"You're nothing but charm, lad, so sell it"* — and renamed him. Rhys Blackwood sounded like a leading man. Gareth Price sounded like somebody's nephew. He took the deal in under a minute, which is the fact about himself he likes least. # Chapter One — Something With No Feelings In It The rain came sideways off the harbour, the way it did in October, and the skylight above local history dripped its slow count into a bucket Elin had placed between the atlases and the jigsaws. *Drip.* She priced a box of Victorian sermons while she listened to it. *Drip.* Around sermon forty she put the kettle on. The bell over the door went, and a man came in wearing a cap, sunglasses, and enough cologne to qualify as weather. He was soaked through in the particular way of someone who had sprinted from a car park believing himself invisible. He shut the door with his heel and peered out through the rain-flecked glass like a man checking for artillery. "Sanctuary," he said. "I'll take the lot." "We close at five." "It's half two." "It closes at five regardless." She knew him before he'd finished dripping. You couldn't grow up in her nan's front room and not know that face — four *Steel Tide* posters, a cardboard cutout of Commander Jack Rourke standing guard by the telly since Christmas 2019. Rhys Blackwood stood on Emrys's welcome mat, ruining it. "There's a bloke in a grey Astra," he said, nodding at the window. "Been outside the chippy since Tuesday. I've started waving." "Have you." "We're practically friends now. I know his thermos." She looked. A grey Astra sat opposite, wipers going, some poor devil inside eating from a bag. "That's Col Prichard. He does the website for the rugby club." "The rugby club." "And other things." Brân appeared from behind the till, considered the visitor across the full length of the shop, and poured himself against the man's shin like syrup. "Traitor," said Elin. "Cats love me." He crouched, joints cracking, and read the collar upside down. "Brân. Giant king of the Britons. Good name. Head like a hill, if I remember Sunday school." He scratched the terrible chin. "You're letting me down, big man." Brân purred like a generator. "This is a proper shop, this." He straightened, turning, wet arms out. "Smells right. Old paper, dust, and — ambition? Some shops smell of nothing. This one smells like somebody cares." "It's the damp." "I did a film once with a bookshop in it. Two days' shooting. They built a set exactly like this and it looked like nothing, because nobody in it cared." He waited. The stamp went *thump*. The bucket went *drip*. "…The bookshop got better reviews than me, in fairness." Silence. "…Nothing?" "Do you want something, or are you hiding?" "I'm hiding," he admitted, "but I'd also like something." He drifted along the new fiction table, touching spines without pulling any, reading her handwritten labels. "You've got a look, you know." "No." "The look." He pointed at his own eyes, then hers. "The 'I couldn't care less' look. Do you know how rare that is? People train for years. I've paid good money for that look." "And here it is for free." "Here it is for free," he agreed, delighted, like she'd handed him a prize. "Best shop in Wales." "Right. I'm buying a book." "Congratulations." "A proper one. Poetry." He said it the way men announce marathons. "I want people to think I'm deep. Not sad. Deep. There's a difference." "Is there." "Huge difference. Sad is a mood. Deep is structural." "Structural." "Load-bearing depth." She looked at him for three full seconds, then wiped the counter, which was dry, and dried it again. "Follow me." She led him past biography, past the overstock of unsold local memoirs nobody had bought since Easter, and pulled the ladder along its rail herself rather than let him steady it. From the top shelf she took down a slim green volume and handed it across the gap between them. Their hands didn't touch. She made sure of that, which took planning, and annoyed her. "R.S. Thomas. Priest. Wrote about Welsh hill farmers, God, and how much he hated people. No feelings anywhere." He read the back cover. "This bloke looks furious." "He was." "Perfect. Will it make me look clever?" "It'll make you look worse than you are. Which is cleverer." A pause. "Was that a compliment?" "It was arithmetic." At the till she rang it through. "Seven forty." He produced a twenty like a magician. "Keep the change." "It's a shop." "I'm a big tipper." "Not in shops." "Every shop's a restaurant if you believe in yourself." She counted his change into his palm, exact, coin by coin, while he watched her do it with the expression of a man being shown a rare bird. Then he unwound his scarf — cashmere, expensive, the wrong colour for the coat — and draped it over the chair by the till. "I'll get that later. If I survive the Astra." "If." "Bolstering. Thank you." At the door he turned, cap going back on, sunglasses down like a visor. "I'll need more books, by the way. Loads. It's a whole thing I'm doing." "Is it." "Big thing. Very serious." The bell went. Through the glass she watched him cross the road into the rain, waving cheerfully at the Astra, and the Astra's wipers paused, just once, like a blink. Elin stood a moment. The kettle clicked itself off, forgotten. She found the scarf when she went to lock the till drawer. She held it by one corner, at arm's length, the way you'd hold evidence. Cashmere. It didn't come from anywhere round here. Then she tidied, because tidying was what hands were for. Three books went back in the wrong places — the canal book into gardening, the gardening book into psychology, and a third she simply held for a while, staring at the middle distance, before shelving it face-down wherever it landed. "Duw annwyl," she said quietly, to nobody, and put the scarf behind the counter, under the till, out of the damp. Outside, the Astra kept its vigil. Inside, the bucket kept its count. *Drip.*
+ Judge Evaluation (Chapter 1)
Judge Response:
[Analysis] This is an exceptionally accomplished piece of opening chapter writing. Let me work through it systematically. **Craft and Execution** The chapter opens with economy and precision: "The rain came sideways off the harbour, the way it did in October" establishes place, season, and a lived-in familiarity without tourism-brochure prettiness. The drip/bucket motif is introduced functionally — it's an economic problem, not a symbol — exactly as the plan specified. The counting of Victorian sermons is a lovely character detail that costs nothing and gives everything. The dialogue is the chapter's great achievement. The voices are genuinely distinct. Rhys's charm offensive is rendered with real wit — "Every shop's a restaurant if you believe in yourself" is the kind of line that's funny and also slightly exhausting, which is exactly right. His jokes have a quality of performance that the reader can feel even as they're charmed by them. Elin's responses are masterfully calibrated: short, dry, occasionally one word, occasionally a line that cuts ("It'll make you look worse than you are. Which is cleverer"). The exchange about "deep vs. sad" is particularly good — it lets him be genuinely funny while she refuses to reward it, and the reader can see both things simultaneously. The plan called for flusteredness to show in behavior rather than interiority, and this is executed with discipline. The counter-wiping (dry, then dried again), the three mis-shelved books, the book held and shelved face-down, the scarf held at arm's length "the way you'd hold evidence" — all of this is behavioral, observed, and earns its place. The single "Duw annwyl" lands with appropriate weight because it's been rationed. Brân's defection is handled with comic timing and serves the character dynamic without being labored. The Col Prichard detail — that the "paparazzo" is actually the rugby club website guy — is a quietly brilliant piece of Welsh-specific deflation that also plants a character for later. **The Charm Offensive and Its Derailment** The plan specified that the charm offensive should be "thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive." This is executed well. Rhys's delight at her responses ("Here it is for free," he agreed, delighted, like she'd handed him a prize) shows the derailment beginning — he's not getting the expected response and it's making him more genuine, not less. The "best shop in Wales" line feels like a man who's run out of script and is reaching for something real. **Minor Criticisms** The "cologne to qualify as weather" metaphor is slightly strained — it's trying a bit hard. "Poured himself against the man's shin like syrup" for Brân is good but "like syrup" is perhaps one word too many. The "rare bird" simile at the till is functional but not distinguished. These are small complaints against a chapter that largely earns its figurative language. The Astra's wipers pausing "like a blink" at the end is a nice touch — it anthropomorphizes Col Prichard without making him a symbol, and it closes the chapter with a quiet beat rather than a flourish. **Adherence to Plan** The chapter follows its plan with impressive fidelity: the R.S. Thomas sale, the "seven forty," the scarf left deliberately, the mis-shelved books, the "Duw annwyl," the hook of "I'll need more books." Brân defects. The bucket counts. The plan's instruction to avoid making Wales picturesque is honored — this is a working shop with damp and unsold local memoirs. The plan's instruction to keep interiority rationed is followed; we get Elin's perspective in behavior, not confession. **Overall** This is confident, controlled, funny, and emotionally intelligent writing. The characters are fully realized from their first lines. The dialogue carries the scene without feeling like a tennis match. The Welsh specificity is worn lightly and accurately. The chapter does exactly what a first chapter should: establishes voice, character, dynamic, and stakes, and makes the reader want more. # Chapter Two — Homework "No." Elin took the parcel off him. "You're strangling it." "It's a book." "It's a book being murdered." She undid his string with two pulls. "Watch. Paper down, book spine-left, fold the ends in like you're tucking it into bed. String twice round, knot on top. Knot on top matters — you want them to see it was tied by a person." "My grandfather wrapped everything in tape," Rhys said. "Christmas, birthdays. Once a sandwich." "Then your grandfather owed you refunds." She handed it back. He tried again, tongue between his teeth, and produced something that looked less like a parcel than a hostage. Brân, installed on the counter beside the till like a paperweight with opinions, opened one eye at the result and closed it. "That's a fail, that," Rhys said. "Mark it honestly." "Fail," she agreed, and made a small pencil tick on a card by the till, and he realised with genuine alarm that she was keeping score. She'd been at it twenty minutes. Condition grading first — she'd pulled a 1949 travel book off the Welsh shelf and walked him through it like a forensics lecture. Foxing. Shaken. Price-clipped. A bookplate inside the front cover, some dead vicar's name in faded iron-gall ink. "So it's worth less." "It's worth different. Condition's a fact. Value's an argument." She turned the jacket in the light. "Somebody loved this badly. Sun damage on the spine means it lived on a windowsill. Somebody's windowsill, somebody's room. It's been handled. My grandfather used to say let it show its life." "And if it's been handled by an idiot?" "Then it shows that instead." He looked at her. She was already looking at the book, which was somehow worse. The kettle went. She made tea in a pot — an actual pot, warmed first, which he hadn't seen outside his nan's house since the nineties — and set out two mugs that matched each other in no respect whatsoever, plus a sugar bowl. "How many?" "One," he said, and took four while she poured, stirring fast, like speed could hide a crime scene. She said nothing. She handed him his mug and looked at him for exactly as long as it takes to count to four, and he felt seen in a way no tabloid had ever managed. His phone buzzed against the counter. Then again. MAL: **call me tonight. PROVENANCE — the money's gone quiet. Not dead. On a gurney. Don't spiral.** He read it twice, turned the phone face down, and drank his tea. Somewhere behind his ribs a small door closed quietly, the way it had learned to. "Your film," Elin said, tying off her demonstration parcel. "*Provenance.* Rare books dealer. Which studio?" "Why?" "Because rare books dealers are thin, bitter men who hate everyone, and you've got the face of a man who does adverts for perfume." "That's — okay, that's hurtful, because it's accurate." He rallied. "It's a prestige thing. Small cast. Shooting spring, they're saying. Wales, possibly." "Mm." Just the one syllable. It went through him like a lance. He found himself filling the silence with the plot — the widowed dealer, the forged incunabula, the moral reckoning — embellishing freely, inventing a director, giving the whole thing a budget it will never see, and heard himself doing it from a slight distance, like watching a man wave at a grey Astra. "You've not read the script," she said. "I've read the script." "You've read pages. There's a difference." She untied her demonstration parcel, folded the paper along its old creases, and put it back in the drawer. "Homework. Ten books wrapped by Friday, graded, priced. You'll be wrong about all of them, but wrong in an instructive way." "What do I get if I pass?" "A passing grade." "People have burned villages for less motivation." His eyes went, again, to the bucket under the skylight. It had filled since Tuesday. "That's still going, then." "Mm." "What's it cost to fix? Properly?" "Four thousand." She said it the way you'd read out a parking fine. "Surveyor came Wednesday. Glass, flashing, repoint the frame, and while they're up there the rest of the roof will probably develop opinions." Something happened in his face. He felt it happen — the little forward lean, the mental wallet opening — and watched her watch it. "Don't," she said. "I didn't say anything." "You did it with your face." "I have a face. It does things." "It was about to do four thousand pounds' worth of things." She stacked his failed parcels and squared their edges, unnecessarily. "Anyway, I can't do Thursday. Trust meeting." "Trust what?" "Community land trust. This street. It's boring. It's minutes and spreadsheets and a man called Guto who loves a spreadsheet." "What's it for?" "Keeping things." She didn't expand, and he understood, with the particular frustration of a man locked out of a room he could easily afford to buy, that she wasn't going to. At some point she went up the ladder to reshelve the travel section, and he was alone with the green R.S. Thomas, propped by the till where she'd left it face-out. He picked it up meaning only to look busy. He read the way he read everything, without meaning to — mouth going, doing the voices, a low mutter — and somewhere around the middle of a page he stopped performing and just stood there. *The bright field.* It was about a field. Just a field, lit up for a minute, that everybody walked past. And the point of it was — he read it again — the point of it was that the field was the thing. Not the horizon you kept scanning. The field you were standing in. "Elin," he said. "This one. The bright field one. It's—" She looked down from the ladder. "—it's rubbish," he said. "Load-bearing rubbish. Very structural." She held his gaze for a moment, then went back to the shelf, and said nothing at all, and he stood there holding the book feeling like a man who'd been given a present and told to wait for his birthday. When she went through to the back room for more brown paper, he moved fast. Pencil from the till pot — hers, chewed at the end, which felt like handling evidence. He opened the display copy to the page, wrote small in the margin beside the poem, shut the book, and was examining a shelf of naval history with tremendous innocence when she came back. By the door, on his way out, he stopped at a noticeboard. A poster, laminated within an inch of its life: **HARVEST SUPPER — FRIDAY — Yr Hen Ysgol. Tickets £6 from Mari @ The Ship.** "Harvest supper," he read aloud. "Friday. I'm free Friday." "You weren't invited." "I'll buy a ticket. Six quid. From Mari." "She'll sell you one. She'd sell you the pub if you smiled right." "There we are, then." He got the cap on, the sunglasses down. At the door he turned. "Ten books by Friday. Graded and priced. If I pass, do I get a star?" But under the noise Rhys leaned across to her, and said, quietly, only for her: "Bouncy castle." "It was that or a horse." "It's a good horse story. I've got a horse story." She poured him tea she knew he wouldn't drink, four sugars waiting in the bowl, and hated how much she'd enjoyed it — the catch, the throw, the room laughing at her timing instead of his. Col Prichard was by the door with his camera. "For the rugby club website," he said to nobody, and took six photographs of the raffle, and one, casually, of the table by the radiators. Outside, later, the cold came off the harbour like a slap. The hall windows glowed behind them; inside, someone had started on the ship-shaped bottle. Rhys arrived at five-fifty with his homework under his coat and the coat lost anyway. "Ten books," he announced, dripping on the mat. "Graded. Priced. Marked harshly, I hope, by an impartial examiner." She went through them while he toweled off on the welcome mat like a large dog. Foxing mistaken for freckles. A first edition called a second because it *felt* like a second. One price so insulting she read it aloud twice for the pleasure of it. "Three out of ten." "Generous." "Instructively generous." She wrote it on the card. "It's still coming down." The skylight had given up pretending. Two buckets now, and a washing-up bowl stationed between the atlases and the jigsaws like a refugee. "I could take a look at it—" "You look at it with your eyes, same as everyone." Mari arrived at six, fighting the door, holding a bottle of red by the neck like a caught fish. "Roof fund," she said. "Don't argue, you'll wake the baby." She handed it over, clocked Rhys on the mat, and grinned the grin of a woman banking material. "Gareth. Swansea. Bouncy castle." "One incident—" "Ta-ra, then." She went. The wind took the door out of her hands and slammed it into the frame, and when Elin tried it afterward it moved a grudging half-inch and stopped, wood swollen fat with weather. "It'll shrink when it dries out," Elin said. "When will it dry out?" "Thursday, possibly." They looked at each other. Somewhere upstairs the storm shifted its grip and the bowl went from a drip to a patter, applause-sized. Right, he thought. Buckets, then. They repositioned the arsenal. She lit two candle stubs from a box of novelty lighthouses that hadn't sold since 2011, which threw enormous moving shadows and made the shop feel like a ship with opinions. He found a torch in the drawer under the till — big rubber thing, dented — and when he clicked it on, something in him clicked on with it. "My dad had a torch like this." He swept the beam along biography. "Every Saturday night. Pantomime season, I was in it every year, beanstalks, Ugly Sisters, once a horse, front half." The beam steadied. "And he'd sit at the back of whatever hall it was, with the torch, not for light — for counting. Counting the house. How many tickets, how many paid. Little torch-shield over his fingers so nobody saw him doing it." He heard himself winding up toward the voice, the bit, the impresario character with the catchphrase — reached for it — —and didn't. "He'd count the house," he said, plainly, "and my mum would collect me from stage door, and we'd drive home past a chippy, and he'd say, be good value, lad. That's all he ever wanted. Value." A pause. "There were four thousand quid of mine in that account by the time I was sixteen. I know because I found the statements. In the torch drawer." Silence, except the bowl going patter-patter. "Why ghostwriting?" he asked, because she'd been quiet in a way that invited company. She turned the bottle around once on the counter. "Footballer's autobiography, year before last. Six weeks, dictaphone tapes, he played golf through most of it. My editor read my draft and said—" Elin's mouth did something dry. "*Just make him likable.* Word for word. Like a spell you say over a man." She poured wine without asking. "Before that, a widow's memoir. Lovely woman, genuinely. Launch week she's on breakfast telly crying through the bits I wrote at two in the morning with a throat infection. Her name on the cover. My sentences coming out of her, performed back at me." She handed him a mug of wine. "So when your lot smile a certain way, I know what it's printed on. That's all." "Be good value," he said quietly, "and just make him likable." Neither of them said anything else about that. The candles moved their shadows around. He drank. Four sugars' worth of a different sweetness, wine gone down easy. "I did one proper film, you know. 2010. Boats. Widower mends them, hardly any words in it. Nobody saw it." Flat. "You'd not have seen it." "No," she said. Careful. Too careful, a word laid down level like a spirit measure. He looked at her a second longer than the sentence deserved. The candleflame leaned. Somewhere Brân relocated with dignity to the warm top shelf of Welsh history. Later — much later, bowls emptied twice, the storm easing from assault to siege — she was up the ladder re-homing books the damp had disturbed, and he picked up the green Thomas off the counter and opened it to show her, without planning to, what he'd been doing to his own copy at nights. Arguments in the margins. Objections. Underlines. On the page with the bright field, beside the poem, in pencil: *This one's true. Who do I tell.* She came down the ladder one rung at a time, slowly, looking. "You're supposed to hate him," she said. "Everyone starts by hating him." "I started by hating him. He grew on me like weather." He held the book up. "Who do I tell?" The gap between ladder and floor was one step. She took it, or the candle guttered, or the storm shoved the building — afterwards he couldn't have told you which of them closed the distance. Close enough now to see rain in her hair, close enough that her breath changed. His phone rang. He answered it. That was the obscenity of it — no thought at all, thumb moving before his heart did, spine straightening, voice lifting into its public register like a drawbridge going up. "Mal. Yeah. No, all good here — great, actually. Say it again? Right. Right." A laugh, bright, load-bearing. "Fine. Honestly. Fine." Down the line, tinny, Mal said, "You don't sound fine, you sound fine." "I've got to go," Rhys said, and hung up on his manager of fifteen years, and stood there in candlelight holding a phone and somebody else's face. When he turned, Elin was already at the door with a pry bar from the tool drawer, working the swollen frame with three efficient shoves. It gave. Cold came in like a verdict. "Door's free," she said. "Elin—" "Night, Gareth." He went. The storm walked him to the car. At the rental he didn't put the telly on, which was unprecedented. He sat with the green book and read it properly — aloud, at first, voices and all, and then somewhere in the middle of a poem about a chapel he ran out of performance and just read, mouth shut, eyes moving, the way other people apparently did it all the time. In the morning, grey and rinsed, he posted a pencil note through the shop's letterbox and walked away before it landed. *Tell me something true tomorrow. — R.*

# Chapter Five — Sources Say Mari arrived at twenty to nine, before opening, letting herself in with the key Elin had regretted giving her since 2021, holding her phone out like a summons. "Page nine," she said. "You're page nine." Elin dried her hands. Took the phone. Read it twice. Below a story about a sheepdog trials scandal and above an advert for a mobility bath, two paragraphs and two photographs. **STEEL STAR'S WELSH HIDEAWAY.** The first photograph was the harvest supper — the trestle table by the radiators, his head thrown back mid-laugh, her own shoulder blurred at the edge of frame like an intruder. Six pounds fifty, and she'd opened none of the stack because he'd kept talking about the weather. "You sold the evidence," said Mari, delighted. "To the journalist. While he stood there." "I know what I did, Mari." "*Sources say*," Mari read aloud, savouring it, "'he's been spotted browsing in a secondhand bookshop, where staff were reportedly unaware of his identity.'" A pause. "Staff." "One staff. Me." "'The bookshop babe declined to comment.'" Mari looked up. "Babe. You're a babe. At your age. Congratulations." "It's nothing." Elin handed the phone back and squared the pile of Saturday's unsold papers, edges flush. "Two paragraphs. No picture worth printing. It'll die by Wednesday." "Sources say," she added, because she couldn't help it. "Two sources. Source one is Emlyn, who'd sell the story of his own christening for a pint. Source two is the man who took the photograph. There's no other way that page got shot — it left this shop in his bag." "That's a very professional breakdown." "I used to write those." It was out before she'd decided to say it. "Two paragraphs, no legs. 'Sources close to the star.' I've written that sentence forty times. It's a machine. You wind it up, it walks to page nine, and it dies, and nobody remembers by Friday." Her hands were wiping the counter again. It was dry. "Except somebody's kept the clippings." Brân, with flawless timing, walked onto the newspaper spread on the counter and sat down on his own headline. "Even the cat's embarrassed," said Mari. Then, quieter, because she was her sister underneath everything: "Has he seen it?" "He'll come in today." "He always comes in," said Mari. "Ta-ra, then. I'm telling Mam you're a babe." --- Col Prichard came in at ten past five, buying nothing for a long time, and then a 1978 almanac he clearly didn't want. "Tide tables," he said, by way of conversation. "Never know." Elin rang it through and gave him his change exact. "For what it's worth," Col said, pocketing it, "I don't print what hasn't got legs. That piece had none. Sheepdog story above it, bath advert below. Nobody reads page nine." He adjusted his glasses. "I've done this thirty years. Local stringer, mostly. Rugby results, fêtes, the occasional famous face eating chips." A shrug. "It's not the Guardian. It's not supposed to be." "No," said Elin. "But I read the trades." He said it mildly, the way you'd mention the forecast. "Three weeks on the trade sites, back when. *Provenance.* Casting notices, a director attached, studio money. Then August — nothing. Rhys came in capless for once, wet-haired, and Col turned around with the unhurried calm of a man whose whole profession is other people's arrivals. "Mr. Blackwood," he said. The name hung there. By Friday nobody—" "When did it die?" He stopped. "What?" "The film. *Provenance.* When did it die?" She kept her voice level, purely English, every vowel doing as it was told. "Col's known three weeks from reading websites. Your manager's known longer. So. When." The silence stretched. Outside, the harbour threw small stones at the window. "The night of the storm," he said finally. "The phone call. That was Mal telling me the money was gone. Properly gone. On a gurney, he'd said that afternoon — I read the text while you were teaching me to wrap." He rubbed his jaw. "So. The lock-in. The wine. All of it — I already knew. And I stayed anyway, because it was the first evening in years where nobody wanted anything off me, and I thought—" "Don't do the voice." He blinked. "What voice?" "That one. The one where the jokes stop and you lean in half an inch and get quiet." She folded the tea towel along its crease, once, twice. "I've read that voice off scripts. I've *written* that voice. It's very effective. It's doing it now — you can feel it working, can't you, the room warming—" "This is me being sorry—" "I know. That's what I mean." She put the towel down. "You lied to me for three weeks. Not big lies. Little ones, daily. The film's shooting in spring. Wales possibly. You let me grade your homework against a job that doesn't exist, and I marked you three out of ten like it mattered—" "It mattered." "—and I keep landing on the stupidest part, which is that you didn't need the lie. I'd have liked you anyway. Probably. Against all my professional judgment." She stopped. Started again, lower. "You needed a stranger who didn't know your face. Somebody with no idea who you were. And I liked being her. That's the whole thing. That's the lot." He stood there holding nothing, in his expensive wrong coat. "You knew," he said slowly. "That first day. Before I said a word. You knew and you sold me Thomas for seven forty—" "The door's free." It was the line from the storm, given back to him. He heard it land. Whatever he'd been building toward in his throat, he swallowed it, and nodded once, and went, and the bell went over him, and the street took him. Elin locked the door behind him, which served no purpose whatsoever. She did not put the kettle on. She went through to the back room, moved a box of unsold local memoirs, and took the DVD out from under the till drawer where it had lived since Tuesday beside a cashmere scarf. Case cracked across the corner. Cardiff market, 2011, three quid. The old television took an age to wake. Rain on the skylight. The bucket keeping its count. On screen, grey water, a jetty, a man sanding a boat in silence. Hardly any words in it at all. Just work, and weather, and a face doing nothing for anybody. Elin sat down on a box of stock and watched.
